items.content:
Protecting and restoring Australia’s nature since 1970.

For more than 55 years we have brought First Nations organisations, governments, businesses and communities together to protect Australia’s natural heritage, restore vital ecosystems and save threatened wildlife.

Partner with us Explore our impact
Our purpose

Together, we can create a lasting legacy for nature.

Australia is home to extraordinary landscapes and wildlife found nowhere else on Earth, but habitat loss, a changing climate and other pressures threaten the places and species that make this country unique. We work with Traditional Custodians, scientists, governments, communities, businesses and supporters to protect what matters and restore what has been lost.

Growing National Parks

Saving Species

We protect Australia's most vulnerable species by restoring habitats, creating wildlife corridors, and supporting targeted conservation programs.

We restore landscapes affected by bushfires, floods and unsustainable activities through our Landscape Resilience Program.

items.static_title: We protect and restore Australia, with the people who know it best.
items.content:
Home/About
Who we are

We protect and restore Australia, with the people
who know it best.

Since 1970 we have been leading conservation across the country alongside First Nations partners, scientists, community groups, governments and corporates.

How we work

Three ways we work.

We focus where the need is greatest, across three connected areas of work, all of it aligned with Australia’s commitment to protect and conserve 30 per cent of its land and 30 per cent of its marine areas by 2030. With more than 2,000 native species now at risk of extinction, that focus matters.

Growing National Parks

We expand and protect conservation spaces to safeguard critical habitats and support resilient ecosystems. Working with First Nations groups, scientists and local stakeholders, we identify, acquire and protect high-value ecosystems so they are preserved.

See the projects

Saving Species

We protect Australia’s most vulnerable species by restoring habitats, creating wildlife corridors and supporting targeted recovery programs. By addressing threats like habitat destruction, invasive species and climate change, we help prevent extinctions and strengthen ecosystems.

See the projects

Healing the Land

We restore landscapes affected by bushfires, floods and land clearing through our Landscape Resilience Program. With 30 native plant nurseries, we grow and plant climate-adaptive and fire-resistant species, working towards 9 million trees by 2030 to bring back habitat for wildlife.

See the projects
How we make it happen

Organising the work, and seeing it through.

Protecting a landscape almost never comes down to one organisation. It takes the community group who knows the ground, the scientists who can measure what is changing, the landholders and agencies who manage access, and the people willing to pay for the work. Rarely does any one of them hold all the pieces.

That is the work we do. We find the places and species that need help most, bring the right people around them, and organise the project so it can actually be delivered. We help fund it, and we report on what changed.

It is why a community nursery, a state government and a corporate partner can end up working on the same patch of country, each doing the part only they can do. Our job is to make that possible, and to stay with it long after the first season.

600,000+hectares protected
50national parks and reserves
55years of doing it
Since 1970

55 years of impact.

drag back through the decades →
2025

We mark 55 years of conservation, and partner to help secure 1,900 hectares at Mundoo Island Station in South Australia for permanent protection.

2024

A major milestone: the successful planting of one million trees in key priority areas across Australia, delivered in collaboration with 30 community nurseries.

2023

The Curb Wombat Mange Program launches to address the effects of mange on wombat populations across Australia, providing treatment and resources to community groups and volunteers.

2022

The Gondwana Project begins at Luke’s Farm. The 1 Million Turtles Project, the Fire Wise Program and the Bandicoot Super Highway Project all launch.

2021

Named Australian Charity of the Year. Construction begins on the Mountain Pygmy Possum Breeding Centre at Secret Creek Sanctuary, and the $10 million Remarkable Southern Flinders Project begins, aiming to connect 30,000 hectares of established parks and state land.

2020

Healing our Land launches after the 2019–20 bushfires, with a commitment to plant one million trees in key priority areas over five years. Our Patron, the Governor-General David Hurley, acknowledges our 50th anniversary at Admiralty House.

2019

Wildlife Heroes commences, supporting over 10,000 wildlife rescue and rehabilitation volunteers across Australia. With the SA Government and the Flinders Ranges Ediacara Foundation, we acquire 60,000 hectares of Nilpena Station. Three co-funded Saving our Species projects commence across NSW.

2018

We acquire 229 hectares of land to extend Woomargama National Park in NSW, home to some 25 endangered or vulnerable species.

2016

We embark on a campaign to save the Murray River turtle, contributing funding to the first and largest national river study of turtles.

2015

Our first crowd-funding campaign rallies the community to support Manly’s Little Penguins. Cameras, lights and nesting boxes are installed to prevent fox attacks.

2012

The Voluntary Heritage Estates Land project supports our mission to acquire heritage sites for the public estate, and to preserve and celebrate cultural heritage.

2010

The Backyard Buddies microsite launches.

2008

The Private Land Conservation Grant Program launches to increase high-value conservation areas on private land.

2005

Green Gully is acquired as a stronghold for the endangered Brush-tailed Rock-wallaby.

2001

The Wollemi Pine Recovery Program launches to protect the species in the wild.

2000

We expand our focus from NSW to Australia-wide.

1996

The Friends of National Parks community is established, with the support of AGL.

1994

Bushfires ravage NSW. We achieve over $1 million in funding to support the response.

1993

The Gap Bluff Centre is established as the “flagship” of our Foundation, providing education on wildlife.

1983

Maroota Historic Site in the Hornsby Local Government Area is reserved to protect Aboriginal art and engravings.

1980

Operation “Cheese lift” to Lord Howe Island provides protein supplement for the woodhen population, part of over $250,000 of funding for the species.

1979

We acquire Mallee Cliffs National Park, 58,000 hectares in SW NSW, to protect Malleefowl habitat.

1972

We launch our first donor appeal at Greycliffe House, Sydney Harbour National Park HQ.

1970

On 29 June, our Foundation is established by the Lands Minister of NSW, the Honourable Thomas Lancelot Lewis AO, who later became the state’s Premier. On 31 July, we announce our first acquisition: Mount King Station in NW NSW.

Reconciliation Action Plan

Our commitment to reconciliation.

We acknowledge that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples are the Traditional Custodians of lands, seas, waters, flora and fauna, possessing crucial knowledge that supports our shared efforts to achieve a sustainable and healthy country. Our vision is to create such country, led and driven by First Nations peoples, through fostering deep engagement with one of the oldest living cultures on earth; a culture that remains a shining example of community and environmental sustainability.

Our Innovate RAP mirrors our ongoing commitment to strengthen relationships between Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and non-Indigenous Australians, and to ensure our policies, processes and programs are culturally appropriate and accountable. We are determined to advance reconciliation through meaningful partnerships and continual learning, building a unified Australia where First Peoples’ histories, cultures and expertise are celebrated to drive self-determination and a sustainable future for all.

Chair

Kelly O’Shanassy

  • Elected Chair in 2026 | Appointed Director 2026
  • Finance & Risk Committee member
  • Nominations Committee member

Kelly absolutely loves nature, with wombats, towering gums and tranquil rivers being her favourites. This love of nature drove Kelly to become a distinguished and transformative leader at the forefront of nature and climate.

Kelly was the CEO of the Australian Conservation Foundation and is experienced in executive roles in business, government and the community sector. She has been at the forefront of Australia’s most consequential nature and climate wins over the past two decades, and is trusted by environmental and political leaders, community, business and philanthropy.

She brings thought leadership, a ‘can do’ attitude, curiosity, kindness and fun to shape innovative, high-impact organisations to drive outcomes for people and nature.

Treasurer & Deputy Chair

Mark Arnold

  • Elected Treasurer and Deputy Chair in 2026 | Appointed Director 2026
  • Finance & Risk Committee Chair
  • Nominations Committee member

Mark is a Non-Executive Director of Freshmark, Blue Knot Foundation, and Afford, and chairs the Finance, Audit and Risk Committees of Blue Knot Foundation and Freshmark. He is also Chair of Afford’s Corporate Development Committee, a member of its Asset, Audit and Risk Committee, and an Advisory Director to two early-stage financial services technology businesses.

Mark has over 30 years’ experience in global financial services, having held senior regional and global Chief Financial Officer roles with major UK banks, primarily based in London, with international experience in Hong Kong and New York. He later became a Partner at Deloitte in Australia and South Africa within the Transformation, Technology and Strategy consulting practice, advising boards and executives across financial services and other industries.

He specialises in financial reporting including budgeting, including governance, organisational change, and risk management, with a strong focus on financial stewardship, regulatory oversight, and technology-enabled transformation. Mark is a Fellow CPA (Australia) and a Graduate of the Australian Institute of Company Directors and holds a Bachelor of Accounting from the University of Canberra.

Director

Jane Danziger

  • Appointed Director 2020

Jane is a proven leader in driving growth and transformation through customer centricity, digital, loyalty and data & analytics. She has a strong track record of driving customer centric change in both her senior executive and Advisory roles.

Jane spent 4 years in Executive roles at Woolworths, where she led customer, brand & marketing, loyalty, digital, the call centres, privacy, Group strategy and Group transformation. Jane was also Chair of Woolworths First Nations Advisory Board, spearheading Woolworths RAP commitments and delivery.

Prior to Woolworths she spent over 20 years with the Boston Consulting Group, where her experience includes incubating and launching innovative new digital businesses, working cross functionally with large teams to develop and implement machine learning personalisation tools, launching new products and brands, identifying growth opportunities and optimising brand portfolio positioning in airline, travel and consumer facing industries.

Jane is passionate about building high performance cross functional teams. She is also passionate about increasing the representation of women in Digital. At BCG she led GAMMA, BCGs data and analytics business, in Australia and also led Gamma’s global women’s initiative. Over 10 years she shifted the dial on diversity in BCG ANZ.

Jane loves the outdoors (hiking, kayaking, skiing) and has been actively involved with the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife for several years. Jane is also a member of Chief Executive Women (CEW).

Director

Tim Jarvis AM

  • Appointed Director 2023
  • Projects Committee member

Environmental scientist, author, adventurer and public speaker Tim Jarvis AM is committed to finding pragmatic solutions to major environmental issues related to climate change and biodiversity loss and uses his public speaking engagements, films and books to progress thinking in these areas. He has worked in the environmental field for over 30 years both in an environmental advocacy capacity as well as providing strategic and practical environmental advice to both government and corporate organisations.

Tim is well known for his historically authentic recreations of the Antarctic survival journeys of Sir Douglas Mawson and Sir Ernest Shackleton and campaigns actively for better protection of Antarctica. He is founder and leader of The Forktree Project, a native revegetation project on South Australia’s Fleurieu Peninsula, Global Ambassador and Governor of WWF, Vice President of conservation NGO Flora and Fauna and was made Australian of the Year 2024 for South Australia.

Director

Natalie Kyriacou OAM

  • Appointed Director 2024
  • Fundraising & Marketing Committee Chair

Natalie is an award-winning environmentalist, presenter, and charity director on a mission to spark curiosity about the natural world. She is the author of Nature’s Last Dance: Tales of Wonder in an Age of Extinction.

Natalie was awarded the Medal of the Order of Australia and the Forbes 30 Under 30 Honour for her services to wildlife and environmental conservation in 2018. She was a United Nations Environment Programme Young Champion of the Earth Finalist. She is one of LinkedIn’s 2022 ‘Top Green Voices’ and named as one of The Australian’s 2022 ‘Top Innovators’. In 2025, she was named as a Marie Claire “Women of the Year” nominee.

Natalie is the Founder and Chair of My Green World, a Board Director at Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife, a former Board Director at CARE Australia, a W20 Delegate (official G20 engagement group), a UNESCO Green Citizens Pathfinder. She sits on the XPRIZE Global Brain Trust for Biodiversity and Conservation. She is a National Ambassador for the Australian Conservation Foundation.

Director

Leisa Bacon

  • Appointed Director 2025
  • Fundraising & Marketing Committee member

Leisa has over 25 years of strategy, marketing and partnerships experience, spanning both Corporate and Government. Leisa is passionate about the Arts, Culture and the Environment, and has just commenced as Executive Director Partnerships and Development at Creative Australia, after a decade at the ABC.

Prior to that, Leisa predominantly worked for large, global organisations at a Director level, from P&G to the Coca-Cola Company. She was ranked #1 CMO in Australia in 2020, is a fellow of The Marketing Academy and has a Degree and Masters in Business from the Queensland University of Technology. Leisa has also completed Executive studies in design thinking at Stanford, and Leading Change at Harvard, and currently sits on the Boards of the AANA and Legs on the Wall.

Director

Dr Lucas Carmody

  • Appointed Director 2025
  • Projects Committee Chair
  • Finance & Risk Committee member

Dr. Lucas Carmody is an environmental economist and sustainability leader. Lucas is committed to helping organisations better understand the ways in which they rely on health of our natural environment and the risks posed by further degradation.

As Executive Director of PwC’s Global Centre for Nature Positive Business, he has guided organisations worldwide in understanding and managing the financial and economic impacts of climate change, and of nature and biodiversity loss. Lucas has played a key role in driving the development and adoption of frameworks, standards and methodologies essential for addressing the private sector’s role in halting and reversing nature loss. This includes partnerships with leading initiatives such as the Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures (TNFD) and the Science Based Targets Network (SBTN).

Lucas’ commitment is rooted in the view that our economic prosperity and societal well‐being depend on the sound management of natural systems that sustain all life.

Director

Kinjia Munkara-Murray

  • Appointed Director 2026
  • Projects Committee member

Kinjia Munkara-Murray is an Indigenous scientist with a strong commitment to integrating Western and First Nations knowledge systems to drive lasting environmental, biodiversity and community outcomes. She has experience across government, corporate and research contexts. She works at Melbourne Water, amplifying Indigenous-led perspectives in land and water management and statutory decision-making.

Kinjia is a Graduate of the Australian Indigenous Governance Institute’s Emerging Directors Program, and is a Non-Executive Director of Watertrust Australia. She is also an Ambassador for DeadlyScience and holds a Master of Science (Bioscience).

Kinjia has expertise in environmental policy, waterway and catchment management, and science-informed community engagement processes. She also has a particular interest in biodiversity conservation and environmental stewardship.

Director

Nick Tubb

  • Appointed Director 2026
  • Fundraising & Marketing Committee member

Nick Tubb is Head of Financial Services & Travel for Australia and New Zealand at Meta, where over 11 years he has led strategic partnerships with major Australian organisations.

Nick has been involved with FNPW since 2020, initially as an observer and contributing through the Marketing Sub-Committee for over five years. He brings commercial insight, experience operating at scale, and a focus on measurable, data-informed strategy to support the Foundation’s mission.

Home/Get Involved/Gifts in Wills
Gifts in Wills

Leave a legacy.

A gift in your will keeps the nature you love living on for the generations who come after you. Whenever you are ready, we would love to talk with you about it.

Talk to us in confidenceDownload our guide (PDF)
The nature you love, living on

Imagine the world your legacy keeps alive.

There is a kind of love that asks for nothing back: a love for places you may never see change, for creatures you will never meet, and for a forest that will stand long after you have gone. A gift in your will for nature is love exactly like that.

Picture the people who come long after us, generations we will never meet, still free to do all the small and ordinary things that make this country feel like home. Picture one of them stopping mid-walk to watch a wedge-tailed eagle ride a thermal across an open sky, or glancing up from the garden as the birds return, season after season, to a country that still has room for them.

A gift in your will helps make certain that world is there, waiting. There are few finer ways to be remembered than as someone who left the future a little wilder, and a great deal more hopeful, than they found it.

A legacy made real

Barbara Harris, and the island her gift helped save.

Some gifts change a single life. Barbara Harris left one that changed an entire landscape.

When Mundoo Island came onto the market after more than a century of farming, its 1,900 hectares of wetland, saltmarsh and coastal habitat at the Murray Mouth had a narrow window to be saved.

A transformative gift from the Estate of the Late Barbara Harris became the foundation of our contribution. Building on it, we worked with the Ngarrindjeri Aboriginal Corporation and the Australian and South Australian Governments to secure the whole island in 2025, and it is now being added to Coorong National Park.

Mundoo is home to 65 nationally listed threatened species and is a refuge for migratory shorebirds on the East Asian-Australasian Flyway. For thousands of years it has held deep cultural meaning for the Ngarrindjeri people, whose connection to this Country continues to guide its care. Where the land was once grazed, restoration has already begun, rebuilding the island’s natural hydrology and healing its wetlands.

None of it would have happened without Barbara. One person, thinking of the future, can protect an entire island for every generation that follows.

Read the Mundoo Island story →
Legacies that live on

Their names are written into the landscape.

For decades, people have written the wild into their wills. Because of them, whole corners of national parks, reserves and walking tracks exist today, and they will still be there for the generations who follow.

2,086 ha
Morton National Park, NSW

‘Kitty’ Catherine Clare White

Thanks to Kitty, 2,086 hectares of bushland were acquired and added to Morton National Park, for future generations to enjoy.

Restored
Cecil Hoskins Nature Reserve, NSW

Kenneth Hoskins

Thanks to Kenneth, the reserve was revegetated and given upgraded tracks, new signage and a bird-viewing platform. Kenneth was related to Sir Cecil Hoskins, who helped establish the reserve through a donation to us many years ago.

80+ birds
Mother of Ducks Lagoon Nature Reserve, NSW

Eulie Sandrey

Thanks to Eulie, important wetland research was supported at a reserve that is a haven for more than 80 species of birds and two species of endangered frogs.

7 km
Fitzroy Falls, NSW

Janet Cosh

Thanks to Janet, the East Rim Wildflower Walk near Fitzroy Falls, a much-loved 7 km walk, was upgraded for everyone who walks it.

Your gift could leave a lasting legacy for nature.

Talk to us in confidence
What your gift protects

Some things deserve to be protected forever.

You can direct your gift to the work closest to your heart, or trust us to place it where the need is greatest. Either way, it keeps caring for wild places and wildlife long after your lifetime.

Growing National Parks

Add land to national parks

When land of high conservation value comes up, often right beside an existing park, we work with our partners to acquire it and see it added to the national park estate, protected for good.

Projects like Mundoo Island and Remarkable Southern Flinders
Saving Species

Bring species back

We fund recovery programs run with Traditional Owners, researchers, carers and land managers, for flagship species and overlooked ones alike.

Projects like the Warddeken Mayh Recovery Project and the Curb Wombat Mange Program
Healing the Land

Heal damaged country

Through our Landscape Resilience Program we restore country affected by bushfire, flood and clearing, and we stay for the watering, weeding and replanting that follow.

Projects like Yarrahapinni Wetlands and Fire Wise
Thank you for considering it

No pressure, and no hurry.

To be reading this at all, turning over the idea of giving something of yourself to the natural world, is a quietly remarkable thing. It means that somewhere in the way you think about the years ahead, you have made room for the wild.

A gift in your will is one of the most personal decisions you will ever make, and it deserves time, conversation and care. After you have provided for the people you love, even a small share of what remains can help protect a place for good.

When you are ready, it takes three steps

  1. Talk it through with the people you love

    A conversation with family or close friends brings clarity, and means your wishes are understood.

  2. Talk to us

    Helen can answer your questions in confidence, with no obligation. Get in touch.

  3. Ask your solicitor to add it to your will

    Our guide has our legal details and the ways you can leave a gift, and your solicitor will make sure your will says exactly what you intend.

For professionals

Advising a client or managing an estate?

Our page for professionals brings everything together in one place: our legal details and suggested wording, how we handle gifts for a specific purpose, support for executors, and one direct contact for you and your clients.

  • Estate lawyers and will writers
  • Financial and estate planners
  • Trustee companies
  • Executors
  • Funeral directors
  • Insurers
Information for professionals → Or call us on 1800 898 626
Frequently asked

Questions about gifts in wills.

Do I need to tell you if I leave a gift in my will?
No, you are never obliged to. If you feel comfortable letting us know, it allows us to thank you and to understand your wishes properly. Your decision stays private, and entirely yours.
What kinds of gift can I leave?
Most people leave a share of what remains once their family is provided for, known as a residual gift, or a percentage of their estate. You can also leave a set amount or a specific asset, such as shares or artwork, and you can give through a trust, which your adviser can help you arrange. Our guide explains each option.
Can I choose what my gift supports?
Yes. You can dedicate your gift to a cause or region that means something to you, such as protecting native species or healing a particular landscape, or you can trust us to direct it wherever the need is greatest. If you would like to direct your gift, please talk to us first so we can make sure your wishes can be fulfilled.
How will my gift be used?
Your gift supports the work at the core of what we do: expanding protected areas, restoring ecosystems and protecting threatened species. In 2025, 80 per cent of our funds were invested in our core purpose.
Do I need a great deal of money to leave a gift?
Not at all. A gift of any size makes a real and lasting difference.
What does my solicitor need?
Our legal name, Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife, and our ABN, 90 107 744 771. Both are in our guide, and our page for professionals has suggested wording and our full organisation details.
Is a gift in my will tax-effective?
For many people, a gift in their will is a tax-effective way to give, and as a registered charity with Deductible Gift Recipient status we are able to receive gifts of this kind. Everyone’s circumstances are different, so we always recommend talking it through with your solicitor or financial adviser.
Can I leave land to you in my will?
No. Land can’t be left to us in a will, but you can give land in your lifetime so it becomes national park. Find out about donating land.
Can I change my mind later?
Of course. Your will is always yours to update as your life changes. If you already have a will, your solicitor can advise whether a codicil (a formal amendment) or a new will is the better way to add a gift.
How do you work with Traditional Owners?
Respectfully, and always in partnership. We work alongside Traditional Custodians to care for Country through shared decision-making and co-design, so that cultural knowledge and leadership guide how land and species are protected.
Talk to us

We are here whenever you are ready.

Whether you have already included us in your will, you are still thinking it over, or you simply have a question, we would be glad to hear from you. If you have already included us, please let us know through the form so we can thank you and understand your wishes. Every conversation is confidential and carries no obligation.

Your contact for Gifts in WillsHelen Dusevic1800 898 626fnpw@fnpw.org.au

Gifts in Wills enquiry

Ask us a question, or let us know you have included us in your will. We will come back to you personally.

The form is taking a while to load. Email fnpw@fnpw.org.au or call 1800 898 626 and we will take your enquiry directly.

Everything you share is kept confidential and handled in line with our privacy policy.

items.content:
Every September, Biodiversity Month highlights why we must protect diverse ecosystems. This is a chance to dive into the world of biodiversity, grasp its importance and learn how to protect it. In this blog, we'll explore Australia's unique biodiversity hotspots and why nature preservation is vital.

What is biodiversity and why should we care?

Biodiversity is a blend of "biological" (living things) and "diversity" (variety). It's all about the variety of life on Earth. This diversity ensures clean air, water, robust ecosystems and sustains us with food and medicine.

Currently, we've identified only 1.2 million of an estimated 8.7 million species on Earth. This gap reveals countless undiscovered species. Globally, there are 36 biological hotspots, two of which are in Australia: Southwest Australia and the forests of eastern Australia.

Australia's biodiversity hotspots

1. Southwest Australia (Kwongan)

Southwest Australia, isolated by deserts for millions of years, birthed unique plant species found nowhere else. Sadly, only 30% of its original vegetation remains due to agriculture. Remarkable species like the Albany pitcher plant, honey possum, and numbat call this place home.

Albany Pitcher

2. Forests of East Australia

East Australia's forests host over 2,144 plant species exclusive to this region. However, 77% of their habitat is lost. Among these, you'll find rare creatures like Boyd's Forest Dragon, the Yellow-Spotted Bell Frog and the ancient Wollemi pine.

Wollemi Pine

How can we help biodiversity?

Everyone – governments, industries, corporations, communities, and individuals – can support Australia's unique species by adopting sustainable practices. Start by learning about the species in your backyard and creating a habitat for them. For instance, websites like Backyard Buddies offer valuable guidance.

The Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife (FNPW) plays a pivotal role in preserving Australia's natural landscapes and biodiversity. FNPW collaborates with First Nations groups, donors, local communities, government agencies, corporations and environmental experts to prioritize three areas:

Growing Parks

National parks are vital for diverse ecosystems. We help acquire and expand national parks, in line with the Global Biodiversity Framework's goal of protecting 30% of land and marine areas by 2030.

Saving Species

Each species plays a unique role and their loss impacts ecosystems and human well-being. FNPW actively works to protect habitats and vulnerable species, addressing Australia's high mammal extinction rate.

Restoring Habitats

Bushfires and floods have ravaged Australian wildlife habitats. Through our Landscape Resilience program we are growing and planting 9 million trees by 2030, creating wildlife corridors and mitigating climate change's effects.

This month reminds us of Earth's incredible diversity and the urgency of its protection. By understanding biodiversity, appreciating Australia's unique hotspots and supporting organizations like FNPW, we can ensure a sustainable future for our planet's remarkable biodiversity. Together, we make a difference, celebrating the beauty and importance of biodiversity year-round.

Home/Corporate Governance
About us

Corporate governance.

We are accountable to our supporters, our partners and the ACNC. Here is how the organisation is run.

Our legal status

Incorporated
29 June 1970
ACN
000 744 516
ABN
90 107 744 771
Status
Company limited by guarantee
  • We were incorporated on 29 June 1970 as a company limited by guarantee ACN 000 744 516, regulated by the Australian Securities and Investment Commission to protect consumers, investors and creditors.
  • We were established as a national not-for-profit organisation to grow appreciation of and raise funds for the benefit of the natural environment and cultural heritage of Australia, under our Constitution as amended 2 February 2000.

How we are governed

  • We have a voluntary, unremunerated President, Treasurer and Secretary, and Board of Directors. These positions are elected annually to oversee our activities.
  • The Board is supported by the Finance & Risk Committee, Fundraising & Marketing Committee, Projects Committee, and Nominations Committee. The committees are comprised of staff, board members, and external representatives as appropriate.
  • The Board meets six times a year and its Committees meet between three and six times a year. They are guided by our Constitution, corporate strategies, annual business plans, as well as supporting marketing and other strategies and plans.

Reporting and accountability

  • We provide an annual report on the previous year’s performance with externally audited financial accounts to our Members, the Governors and Life Members, at our Annual General Meeting.
  • A copy of our annual report and financial statement is provided to the Commonwealth Department of Environment and Heritage as part of our statutory requirements.
  • As a national entity, we also seek approval in each relevant State and Territory to undertake fundraising activities.

Registrations and tax status

  • We are registered with the Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission (ACNC) as a charity focused on advancing the natural environment.
  • We hold an Authority to Fundraise for Charitable Purposes with the Department of Gaming and Racing.
  • We are registered with the Australian Taxation Office for Goods and Services Tax (GST), ABN 90 107 744 771.
  • We are endorsed by the Australian Taxation Office as a Deductible Gift Recipient (DGR) as a public museum, and as an Income Tax Exempt Charitable Entity (ITEC) as a charitable institution.
  • We are exempted by the Office of State Revenue from pay-roll tax.

Related entities

  • We are the Trustee of the FNPW Gift Fund Trust ABN 42 651 974 301 (Deed of Settlement 2 February 2000, DGR, ITEC), entered into the Register of Environmental Organisations kept by the Commonwealth Department of Environment and Heritage on 9 February 2001 and entitled to receive tax deductible donations of money and property.
  • We are the registered office of The Gondwana Program BRN T2383504, a membership loyalty program for national parks and wildlife supporters.
  • We are the registered office of Friends of National Parks BRN R3566341, a community-based volunteer program for conservation of national parks and wildlife.

Home/Partner With Us/Corporate partnerships
Corporate partnerships

Big conservation commitments need a partner who can deliver them.

We work with businesses ready to commit serious capital to conservation of national significance, from securing land for new national parks to restoring habitat across whole regions.

Explore OpportunitiesEnquire About a Partnership
Our partners
Ways to partner

Choose how your business wants to make an impact.

Every partnership is shaped around what your business wants to achieve. Pick one to see what it involves and the kind of work partners back.

Fund Conservation at Scale

Fund land for national parks, the restoration of native habitat or recovery work for a threatened species, with the scope and the outcomes your funding will deliver agreed from the start.

Good fit for: Businesses with a regional footprint, or a species or place that means something to your brand.

Our projects
  • Mundoo Island StationSA
  • Remarkable Southern FlindersSA
  • Hindmarsh IslandSA
  • Nilpena National ParkSA
Enquire About a Partnership

Build Conservation Partnerships

Commit to a landscape, a species or a cause over several years. We shape the program with you and grow it as the results come in, so the partnership lasts well beyond a single project.

Good fit for: Organisations ready for long-term, reportable impact at scale.

Our projects
  • Landscape Resilience ProgramNational
  • Native Plant Nurseries30+ nurseries
  • Black Cockatoo CorridorSA
  • Yarrahapinni Wetlands RestorationNSW
Enquire About a Partnership

Invest in Nature’s Future

We’re exploring how business, philanthropic and public capital could work together on long-term landscape outcomes. This work is still being developed, and we’d welcome businesses who want to help shape it.

Good fit for: Organisations exploring co-investment alongside government and philanthropy.

Enquire About a Partnership
How we work

From first conversation to results you can report.

Whatever you choose to fund, the way we work stays the same, and your business has a clear role at every step.

  1. 01

    Identify

    With Traditional Custodians, scientists and government, we find the places and species where your support will make the biggest difference, then agree the scope, budget and milestones with you.

  2. 02

    Deliver

    We bring the partners and funding together and engage the specialists who do the work, from Traditional Owner rangers to community nurseries, against clear milestones. You can see the work on the ground for yourself.

  3. 03

    Demonstrate

    We track the ecological, financial and partnership outcomes and report back, so your business can stand behind the results in its own reporting.

See the projects that are ready for a partner to fund now.

Explore Opportunities
Flagship program

Landscape Resilience: on the way to nine million trees.

What began after the 2019–20 bushfires as a promise to plant one million trees is now one of Australia’s largest community-led nursery restoration programs. We reached the millionth tree in 2024 and have set our sights on nine million by 2030. Partners fund the seed collection, nurseries and planting that restore habitat at the scale of whole regions.

1.2M
trees, shrubs and seedlings planted up to 2025
9M
trees in total, the goal for 2030
30+
community nurseries from around Australia
1.2 million planted9 million by 2030
Enquire About a PartnershipRead how the program began →
Partnership in focus

Restoring a Ramsar wetland on Hindmarsh Island.

15 ha
restored on Hindmarsh Island in 2025
10,000
local provenance plants across five sites
2,500+ ha
of habitat restored across the wider program

On Hindmarsh Island (Kumarangk), inside the Coorong and Lower Lakes Ramsar Wetland, L’OCCITANE’s $90,000 contribution in 2025 helped restore coastal woodland and wetland alongside the Ngarrindjeri, the Kumarangk Hindmarsh Island Landcare Group, local nurseries and park managers.

The partnership began in July 2020, when L’OCCITANE Australia helped fund our first Bushfire Recovery Nurseries through the L’OCCITANE Ecosystem Restoration Fund. Alongside One Tree Planted, they are one of the key partners behind the program that reached its millionth tree in 2024.

“As a brand that originated from nature and the use of botanical ingredients, it has long been a commitment of ours to respect and support biodiversity. So, we are thrilled to be able to support the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife in its mission of planting one million trees around Australia.”

Pierre-Emmanuel Joffre, Managing Director, L’OCCITANE Australia

Enquire About a Partnership
Also in 2025

Safer access through koala habitat at Bongil Bongil.

Gowing Bros Ltd · Bongil Bongil National Park, NSW

With NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service, we upgraded an existing boundary track using funding from Gowing Bros, owner of the adjoining land. The work improved safe public access while protecting habitat inside a declared Koala Asset of Intergenerational Significance.

Your people and customers

Bring your people and customers into the work.

Share of sales

Zorali

Now in its third year, our partnership with Zorali gives 10 per cent of the proceeds from each limited-edition fleece to our work. The July 2025 Sundown edition followed earlier releases, and the collaboration has raised more than $12,000 so far.

A contribution on every product

For every bucket of its S2 screws sold (1,000 screws to a bucket), AnchorMark contributes $1 to our tree planting partnership, so a building product helps fund restoration.

We are registered with the ACNC and governed by a voluntary, unremunerated board supported by four committees, and our financial accounts are externally audited every year.

Hands-on conservation

Give your team a day to bring back the bush.

Australia is home to plants and animals found nowhere else on Earth, and your team can play a practical part in protecting them. Step away from the office for a hands-on day outdoors, working alongside park rangers and community nurseries to care for places that need it.

Enquire now
Corporate volunteering · $3,500 + GST · weekdays Enquire now
What your team will do

Get hands-on with nature.

Depending on the site and season, your team might remove invasive plants, restore habitat, help out in a community nursery or, when planting is in season, put native plants in the ground, all while learning about the local wildlife you are helping to protect.

Your day in the bush

Every day is different. Activities and timings may vary depending on the site, season and conservation needs.

  1. Arrive & connect

    Welcome, Acknowledgement of Country and introductions.

  2. Get stuck in

    Site overview, safety briefing, then team bonding and hands-on activities.

  3. Refuel

    Lunch break. Catering is included.

  4. Keep going

    More hands-on conservation work, where most of the day’s progress happens.

  5. Wrap up

    Reflection, and a guided site walk where available.

Two ways to spend a corporate volunteer day.

Activity 1
Support bushfire recovery nurseries

Grow the plants that bring nature back.

Volunteer with our network of community-led bushfire and flood recovery nurseries, which supported the planting of our one millionth tree in October 2024. Our goal is now 9 million trees by 2030, helping rebuild ecosystems and strengthen landscape resilience.

Your team will nurture seedlings, learn from experts about native species, and understand the critical role these plants play in healthy ecosystems. A hands-on experience that aligns with your ESG or CSR goals.

1.2M planted to date · 9M trees by 2030
Activity 2
Restore national & urban parks

Bring habitat back, by hand.

Take part in on-ground restoration that supports the health, maintenance and cleanup of Australia’s parks and urban green spaces.

Your team will work outdoors to remove invasive species, plant native vegetation, and restore habitats that support wildlife and improve community green spaces. These sessions not only protect nature, but help maintain parks as places for connection, wellbeing and shared enjoyment.

Outdoor on-ground restoration · All equipment provided
A day in the field

What a volunteer day looks like.

Where we run

Explore corporate volunteering sites across Australia.

Included in every day

Why it is worth the day

Good for people. Good for business. Good for nature.

Get your team outdoors, working together and making a difference. Practical action in nature can strengthen teams, support communities and help nature thrive.

For your employees

  • Connect with nature and experience Australia’s wild spaces firsthand
  • Make a difference and contribute to environmental restoration and biodiversity
  • Strengthen team bonds through hands-on, meaningful team-building
  • Learn & grow, gaining insights into local ecosystems, native plants and wildlife

For your business

  • Boost employee engagement and strengthen teamwork, morale and culture
  • Enhance CSR & brand reputation and demonstrate genuine commitment to sustainability
  • Create a positive public image: consumers favour businesses with environmental values
  • Offer a unique experience where employees step away from screens to make a tangible difference

For communities

  • Restore & protect ecosystems and support restoration and enhance biodiversity
  • Build climate resilience and help communities adapt to bushfires and environmental change
  • Improve public spaces and contribute to healthier national parks and green spaces
  • Strengthen community ties and foster collaboration between businesses and locals
Aligned with the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework

Our corporate volunteering program aligns with the UN Sustainable Development Goals, including:

  • 15Life on Land
  • 13Climate Action
  • 11Sustainable Cities and Communities
  • 3Good Health and Wellbeing
Get involved

Ready to get into the field?

Let’s make it happen. Tell us where you’re based, how many people are on your team and when you’d like to get out there, or call our team direct for a chat.

1800 898 626
How it works
  1. Tell us what you need Share your state, team size and preferred dates.
  2. Choose your experience We’ll send you options that suit your team.
  3. Get ready to get outdoors Once you’ve chosen your experience, we’ll sort the details. You just need to show up in closed shoes and a hat, and get stuck in.
fnpw@fnpw.org.au 21 days’ minimum notice required GPO Box 2666, Sydney NSW 2001

Plan your volunteering day

The form is taking a while to load. Email fnpw@fnpw.org.au or call 1800 898 626 and we will take your enquiry directly.

We’ll be in touch within two working days. By submitting you consent to us contacting you about your enquiry.

FAQs

Your questions, answered.

The most common questions about running a corporate volunteering day with us.

What is the cost, and what does it include?

The cost is $3,500 + GST per day, whatever the group size. This amount is fully tax-deductible and directly funds our projects across Australia. If catering is required at NSW National Parks, the cost is $3,700 + GST (also tax-deductible).

The participation fee covers expert guidance, all equipment, materials (native plants, seeds), insurance and permits, and educational briefings on local ecosystems.

Why is the volunteering experience paid for?

Corporate Volunteering is paid for due to its substantial coordination, resource allocation and cost recovery. Companies invest in these experiences to foster team cohesion, provide meaningful engagement, and develop employees’ connection to nature. It also supports alignment with CSR/ESG goals, which helps enhance brand reputation and contribute to sustainability initiatives.

Why is the corporate group size small?

Group sizes are kept small to enhance hands-on participation, foster a deeper connection to the environment, and facilitate a better learning opportunity. Smaller groups ensure efficient coordination, meaningful contributions from every participant, and ease in logistical arrangements.

How much notice is required to book a day?

We require 21 days’ prior notice to arrange a corporate volunteering day.

Can you provide free volunteer opportunities?

Unfortunately, we are unable to offer free volunteer work. As a charity, we rely on donations and corporate volunteering events to help fund vital programs across Australia.

What are the timings for corporate volunteering days?

Corporate days run on weekdays only, approximately 9:00am–2:00pm (timings vary by state):

  • NSW & VIC: 9:30am–2:00pm
  • QLD: 8:30am–2:00pm
  • SA & WA: 9:30am–2:30pm
Do you offer weekend volunteering?

No, we do not run corporate volunteering events on weekends.

Can smaller groups or half-day sessions be arranged?

Yes, we can arrange half-day sessions (3 hours) and groups of fewer than 10 people. However, the cost of the day remains $3,500 + GST. Smaller groups may be combined with other corporate teams.

Is equipment provided?

Yes, all equipment required for the activities is provided on the day, including tools, gloves and safety gear.

Is catering included?

Yes, catering is included. For NSW National Parks sites, if catering is required, the total cost is $3,700 + GST, which is also fully tax-deductible.

What is the postponement and cancellation policy?

If extreme weather or another occurrence makes the day unsafe to run, we and the rangers will let you know as soon as possible and reschedule your day for another date. If your organisation no longer wants to reschedule, a $500 administration fee applies.

If you decide to cancel or postpone for any other reason: 21+ days 0% fee · 16–20 days 25% · 11–15 days 50% · 0–10 days 100%.

All these amounts are tax deductible. If you have any other questions, please call or email us.

Can my company plant trees?

Tree planting corporate volunteering can only occur at certain times of the year, typically from June to September, and varies by location. Tree planting is less common at sites closer to the CBD.

While tree planting may not always be an option, there are other impactful activities available, such as supporting recovery nurseries and participating in restoration sessions in national parks.

items.static_title: A gift you can walk through.
items.content:
Home/Get Involved/Donate Land
Donate land

A gift you can walk through.

Most gifts to nature are counted in dollars. A few are counted in hectares. If you own land with real conservation value, you can give it to become national park, protected for good, and we will guide you through every step.

How a gift of land works

Your gift becomes national park. We make sure it gets there.

A gift of land is a gift to the nation. We work alongside Traditional Owners, landholders and government to see it through, and we don’t keep the land: the government adds it to the national park estate so it is protected for good.

You

Offer the land

You tell us about land you would like to protect, and you decide with your own advisers whether to go ahead. Nothing commits you until the documents are signed.

Us

Make it happen

We assess the land, secure the government’s agreement to take it, and coordinate the valuation, legal work and transfer. Where it’s needed, the land passes through our Gift Fund Trust for the moment of transfer, but we never hold it long term.

Government

Protect it by law

The national parks agency in your state receives the land and formally gazettes it as part of the national park estate. From then on it is protected by law and can’t be sold.

Is my land suitable?

Not sure your land counts? That is worth a conversation.

People often assume we are only interested in the spectacular. In truth, some of the most valuable country in Australia is quiet and unremarkable to look at: a paddock with the last remnant scrub in the district, a scrappy gully that happens to hold a creek, forty hectares of regrowth sitting between two reserves that have been waiting decades to be joined up.

There is no cost and no obligation in asking, and no question is too small to put to us. We would far rather have the conversation and tell you honestly what we think than have you decide on our behalf that it was not worth raising.

Every property is assessed on its conservation value and on whether the government wants it for the national park estate. Not every property will be right, and if yours isn’t, we will tell you honestly and as early as we can.

Start a conversation
The quiet places count too
What happens

Five steps from your land to a national park.

A gift of land is a significant decision, so every step is careful and nothing is rushed. The government agrees to take the land before any valuation or legal work begins.

How long it takes

Every gift of land is different. Government agreement, valuation and the legal work all take time, and we will give you a realistic picture of the timeline once we know your land.

01. We assess your land

It starts with a confidential conversation about where the land is and what you know about it. Our projects team then looks at its biodiversity value, what it connects to and the species it supports, and commissions a biodiversity report if one is needed.

02. We secure the government’s agreement

We approach the government agency that manages national parks where your land is, such as the Department for Environment and Water in South Australia, where we do much of this work, to confirm it wants to receive the land and that it fits its priorities for the park estate. Nothing moves to valuation until the government has agreed in principle.

03. We coordinate the valuation and legal work

We agree the right structure for the gift with you and your advisers, arrange an independent valuation that meets ATO requirements, and prepare the donation agreement and transfer documents with your legal team and the government’s.

04. The land is transferred

The transfer is registered through the Titles Office. Where it’s needed, the land passes through our Gift Fund Trust for the moment of transfer on its way to the government.

05. It becomes national park

The government adds the land to the national park estate and formally gazettes it, so it is protected by law and can’t be sold. We give you the documentation you need and record the hectares your gift has protected.

Tax and costs

A gift that can carry a tax benefit.

Our Gift Fund Trust is a Deductible Gift Recipient on the Register of Environmental Organisations, so a gift of land may be tax deductible. An independent valuation is required for tax purposes, and we coordinate it as part of the process. We will also talk you through the costs involved, including valuation and legal fees, before you commit to anything.

Tax benefits for property donations

Since changes in 1999, the Income Tax Assessment Act:

  • Allows an income tax deduction in relation to gifts of property including land valued at more than $5000 by the Taxation Commissioner to eligible charities, regardless of when and how the property was acquired.
  • Allows apportionment (spread) of deductions over five years in relation to these property donations.

Tax rules for gifts of land are specific, so please get advice from your own accountant or financial adviser before you commit. For more information on tax incentives for property donations for conservation, please visit:

  • The Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
  • The Australian Taxation Office
Start here

Start with a conversation with us.

A gift of land is too significant to begin with a form and an automated reply, so it does not. Enquiries about land come to our Chief Executive, and the first conversation will be with someone able to give you a straight answer.

Ian Darbyshire
Chief Executive Officer, Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife
fnpw@fnpw.org.au 1800 898 626

What happens after you send this

  1. We’ll get back to you soonpersonally, by whichever means you have asked for.
  2. A first conversationat a time that suits, to understand the land and what you would like for it.
  3. Then it is your callwe will tell you honestly what we think is possible, and you decide whether to go further. Or not.

Tell us about the land

A few lines is plenty to start with. There is nothing you need to have decided, and nothing here commits you to anything.

Email fnpw@fnpw.org.au or call 1800 898 626 and we will help directly.

FAQs

Questions people ask.

Who will own the land?
The government. Once the transfer is complete, the land becomes part of the national park estate and is managed by the national parks agency in your state. We don’t keep it: where it’s needed, it passes through our Gift Fund Trust only for the moment of transfer.
How much land do I need to have?
There is no minimum. What matters is what is on the land and what is around it. A small block adjoining an existing reserve can be worth more to conservation than a large one in the middle of cleared country. If you are close to a national park, a reserve or a wildlife corridor, please do get in touch, whatever the size.
Will my land definitely be accepted?
Not always, and we would rather say so here than let you find out late. The land needs real conservation value, and the government has to agree to receive it before we go any further. If it isn’t suitable, we will tell you why as early as we can.
Can I leave land to you in my will?
No. A gift of land has to be made in your lifetime, through the process on this page. If you would like your will to protect land, a gift of money can do that, and it is how a gift in a will helped secure Mundoo Island. Find out about gifts in wills.
Can I protect my land and keep living on it?
Not through a gift of land with us. Our process transfers ownership, because the land has to pass to the government to become national park, and that is what lets it be gazetted and protected by law. If you are not ready to part with your land yet, we are still glad to talk it through with you, with no obligation, whenever the time feels right.
Can I say what the land should be used for?
Once it is gazetted, the land is managed as national park under the same rules as every other park in your state. Tell us early what matters to you about the land and we will share it with the government as part of the conversation. Conditions attached to a gift can also affect its tax treatment, so talk them through with your adviser too.
What if my family have views about this?
They usually do, and that is right and proper. Land carries family history in a way money does not. We would always encourage you to have that conversation before you have it with us, and we are very glad to talk to your family alongside you if that would help. A gift that causes hurt at home is not one we want.

Home/FAQs
Help

Frequently asked questions.

Answers about who we are, giving, receipts and the ways you can get involved. If your question is not here, we are only a call or an email away.

Jump to
About usDonatingTax and your donationReceipts and your detailsGetting involved

About us

What does FNPW stand for?

FNPW stands for Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife.

Are you part of the government?

No. We are a not-for-profit company limited by guarantee, regulated by ASIC, registered as a charity with the Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission and endorsed as a Deductible Gift Recipient. We work closely with federal and state governments and national parks agencies across Australia, but we are an independent, apolitical charity that relies on the generosity of our supporters and partners.

What do you do?

Our mission is to create powerful partnerships that protect and restore Australia’s unique natural environment, and our vision is to be the natural partner for the protection of Australia’s priceless biodiversity. Our work sits across three pillars: Growing National Parks, Saving Species and Healing the Land.

Conservation on this scale cannot be done alone, so we bring First Nations communities, scientists, government agencies, corporates and everyday Australians together to care for Country. Our work blends modern science with 65,000 years of Indigenous knowledge, focuses on high-impact regions and species under threat, and supports Australia’s commitment to protect and conserve 30 per cent of its land and 30 per cent of its marine areas by 2030.

What difference have you made?

Our 2025 Impact Report records 29,479 hectares of land added to National Park status, including the 1,900 hectares of Mundoo Island now being added to Coorong National Park. It also records 647 hectares under restoration during 2025, and 1,215,443 trees, shrubs and seedlings planted in key priority landscapes, many of them grown by our network of more than 30 community nurseries.

Who leads the organisation?

Ian Darbyshire is our Chief Executive Officer and Kelly O’Shanassy is our Chair. You can meet our leadership team and Board on our About page.

Where are your offices?

Our head office is in Sydney, at Level 6, 10 Bridge Street, Sydney NSW 2000, and our postal address is GPO Box 2666, Sydney NSW 2001. Our projects and partners reach right across Australia.

What is your ABN and legal name?

Our legal name is Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife and our ABN is 90 107 744 771.

Donating

How can I make a donation?

You can donate online as a one-off gift, give monthly as a Habitat Hero, or call us on 1800 898 626. You can also give through workplace giving, or give a tree in someone’s name through Give a Tree.

Is my donation tax deductible?

Yes. We are a Deductible Gift Recipient, so donations to us are fully tax deductible in Australia.

How much of my donation goes to conservation?

In 2025 we invested $3.8 million in our core purpose, and our 2025 Impact Report records 80 per cent delivery of purpose. Our financial statements are published every year, so you can see how funds are used.

Can I see your financial statements?

Yes. Our financial statements and annual reports are on our Reports page, and they are also published on the ACNC Charity Register.

Can I give monthly?

Yes. Become a Habitat Hero and you will join the supporters whose regular gifts keep conservation going all year round. Your first gift is processed when you sign up, and later gifts are processed each month around that date.

Can I donate in honour or in memory of someone?

Yes. Give a Tree lets you plant a native tree in someone’s name, and we send them a certificate. For other gifts in honour or in memory of a loved one, please get in touch and we will help.

How can I leave a gift in my will?

Our Gifts in Wills page explains the types of gift you can leave and the wording your solicitor will need. To talk it through in confidence, contact Helen Dusevic on 1800 898 626 or fnpw@fnpw.org.au.

Can I donate land?

Yes, and gifts of land are among the most lasting gifts anyone can make. Our Donate Land page explains how it works and who to speak with.

Tax and your donation

Tax deductible charity donations are a fantastic way to give to a cause that is close to your heart. We are endorsed as a Deductible Gift Recipient (DGR), which means donations to us are fully tax deductible in Australia.

Below are answers to some frequently asked tax time questions.

What qualifies as a tax deductible donation in Australia?

Gifts of money to organisations endorsed as Deductible Gift Recipients (DGRs) are generally tax deductible in Australia, as long as you receive nothing in return for your gift. Not every registered charity is a DGR, so it is worth checking. Find out more on the ACNC website.

How much of my donation is tax deductible?

The amount of your donation that is tax deductible depends on the charity you donate to and the type of donation you make. Visit the ATO site to find out more.

How do I know if a charity is a Deductible Gift Recipient?

You can check any organisation's DGR status on ABN Lookup.

Do I need a receipt for my donation to claim a tax deduction?

Yes, you need a receipt or other form of written acknowledgement from the charity to claim a tax deduction for your donation.

How do I claim a tax deduction for my donation?

You can claim a tax deduction for your donation when you complete your tax return. You will need to provide details of the charity and the amount of your donation, along with your receipt or other written acknowledgement.

Are there any caps on the amount of tax deductible donations I can make?

No, there are no caps on the amount of tax deductible donations you can make. You may need to seek professional tax advice, for example if your total donations exceed 10% of your taxable income. Find out more on the ATO website.

How long do I have to claim a tax deduction for my donation?

You can claim a tax deduction for your donation in the same tax year that you made the donation. However, if you forget to claim the deduction, you can usually go back and amend your tax return for up to two years. Find out more on the ATO website.

Can I claim a tax deduction for donating goods or services to a charity?

You can't claim a deduction for donating your time or services. Some gifts of property or shares to a Deductible Gift Recipient can be deductible under rules set by the ATO, so check the ATO website or ask your tax adviser before you give.

Can I claim a tax deduction for donating to a charity through workplace giving?

Yes. Workplace giving donations to a Deductible Gift Recipient, including us, are tax deductible. Because they come out of your pre-tax pay, you get the tax benefit each pay rather than waiting until tax time.

Can I donate land to a charity and claim a tax deduction in Australia?

Yes, you can donate land to a charity and claim a tax deduction, but there are some special rules that apply.

It's important to seek professional advice before making a donation, to make sure you understand the tax implications and any other legal requirements that may apply.

Find out more about donating land to FNPW.

Receipts and your details

Why haven’t I received a receipt for my donation?

Receipts for online donations are sent by email, so please check your junk or spam folder first. A tax receipt is emailed to you once each donation has processed, and that includes every monthly gift if you give as a Habitat Hero. If you still cannot find your receipt, call us on 1800 898 626 or email fnpw@fnpw.org.au and we will send you a copy.

How do I update my details or change my monthly gift?

Call us on 1800 898 626 or email fnpw@fnpw.org.au and we will update your details, or change or stop your monthly gift. You can read how we look after your information in our privacy policy.

Getting involved

Can I volunteer with you?

We run corporate volunteering days, where teams plant and restore habitat at sites across New South Wales, Victoria, South Australia, Western Australia and Queensland. If you would like to volunteer as an individual, your local national park or community conservation group is a great place to start.

How can I fundraise for you?

Our fundraising page has ideas to get you started and a Proposal to Fundraise form. Send it through and our team will be in touch.

How can my business partner with you?

We work with businesses on partnerships built around real, measurable conservation outcomes. Visit Partner With Us to see how we work together and who to contact.

Do you offer grants?

Yes. We provide grants for conservation projects run by community groups, scientists, private landholders and government agencies. When a grant round opens, we share the details and how to apply in our news and our newsletter.

Do you have a newsletter?

Yes. Our email newsletter brings you project updates, species spotlights and ways to help, straight from the bush. You can sign up here.

Still have a question?

We are happy to help.

Call us on 1800 898 626 or email fnpw@fnpw.org.au, and a member of our team will get back to you. You can also write to us at GPO Box 2666, Sydney NSW 2001.

Contact us Call 1800 898 626

items.content:
Home/Get Involved/Fundraising
Fundraise with us

Make a difference for wildlife and conservation.

Whether it’s a bake sale, a fun run or a morning tea at work, every fundraiser helps protect Australia’s wild places and the wildlife that call them home.

Getting started

Your idea, our support.

Tell us what you have in mind and we will help you make it happen. Start with our Fundraising Guidelines, then fill out the Proposal to Fundraise so we know what you are planning.

If you would like some inspiration first, the ideas below and our Community Fundraising Kit are a good place to begin. When you are ready, use the form at the bottom of this page to tell us about your plans.

Download

Fundraising GuidelinesPDF Community Fundraising KitPDF Proposal to FundraisePDF
Ideas to get you started

Pick a fundraiser that suits you.

Some people bake, some people run and some turn a workplace morning tea into a cause. Here are a few ideas to spark your own.

Community event

Hold a garage sale, bake sale or sausage sizzle in your neighbourhood.

Workplace event

Host a morning tea, or ask colleagues to donate the cost of their coffee.

Raffle or auction

Gather donated prizes, then sell raffle tickets or auction them off on the night.

Sale of products

Make something you love and donate the proceeds from every sale.

Challenge event

Run, ride or hike a distance that tests you, and ask people to sponsor you.

School fundraiser

Rally the whole school behind a cause, or run a stall at the next fete.

You will find plenty more ideas in our Community Fundraising Kit.

Two ways in

Start your own event, or join one that’s already running.

Create your own event

You might collect donations in lieu of wedding presents, set yourself a personal challenge or simply ask friends to give. Each of these makes a real difference for Australia’s wilderness and wildlife.

You can set up your own fundraising page and raise money securely online through GoFundraise, or directly with us. Get in touch and we will help you set it up.

Join an existing event

Marathons, ocean swims, bike rides and plenty of other challenge events welcome charity fundraisers. Take one on yourself, or put together a team of colleagues, friends or family so everyone can be part of it.

We can also set up a fundraising page for your company or team, which collects donations securely online and sends your donors their receipts automatically. Get in touch to find out more.

We cannot thank you enough

For loving Australia the way you do.

Thank you for taking that extra step for Australia’s environment. Together we can protect habitat and the wildlife that depends on it, and leave something future generations will be glad we did.

We can’t wait to hear what you have planned.

Let’s go

Tell us about your fundraiser.

Fill out the form with your question or your fundraising plans, and our team will be in touch shortly.

You can also email fnpw@fnpw.org.au or call 1800 898 626.

The form is taking a while to load. Email fnpw@fnpw.org.au or call 1800 898 626 and we will take your enquiry directly.

By submitting you consent to us contacting you about your enquiry.

Your donation grows national parks, saves species and heals the land.

Government partnerships

Trusted by government since 1970 to deliver conservation at landscape scale.

For more than 55 years, Australian, state and territory governments have worked with us to expand protected areas and recover threatened species. We bring Traditional Owners, funding and delivery partners to one table, and we stay with every project until we can show what changed.

Explore OpportunitiesEnquire About a Partnership
Mundoo Island, Murray Mouth, South Australia
Our record with government

Fifty-five years of delivering with government.

55+years

working alongside Australian, state and territory governments, since 1970

600,000+ha

protected across 50 national parks and reserves

29,479ha

added to national park status in 2025

Australian Government→$5.4mCaring for our Country grant we managed at Heritage Estates, adding 530+ lots to Jervis Bay National Park.SA and Australian Governments→$10mRemarkable Southern Flinders project, which joined four reserves into one national park, at the heart of a 30,000 ha precinct on Nukunu Country.NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service→18,582wombat mange treatments through $2m in rapid response grants we designed and ran, 2023 to 2025.Queensland Government→185+ haadded to Lamington and Main Range National Parks in 2023, our $340,000 within a $600,000+ partnership.Australian and SA Governments→1,900 haat Mundoo Island Station, secured in 2025 with us as an acquisition partner and now being added to Coorong National Park.SA Government→60,000 haNilpena Station, acquired with the SA Government and the Flinders Ranges Ediacara Foundation, proclaimed a national park in 2021.
Agencies we have delivered with
Ways to partner

Find the partnership that fits your commitment.

Every partnership is shaped around the outcomes you need to deliver.

01

Fund Conservation at Scale

Fund land for the national reserve system, threatened species recovery or landscape restoration, with the scope and the outcomes it will deliver agreed from the start.

02

Build Conservation Partnerships

Work with us over several years on a priority landscape or species, across state borders where the work needs it, and grow the program as the results come in.

03

Invest in Nature’s Future

We’re exploring how public, philanthropic and private capital could work together on long-term landscape outcomes. This work is still being developed, and we’d welcome governments who want to help shape it.

04

Deliver Grant Programs

We design and run grant programs on your behalf, getting funding to the community organisations, rangers and specialists already doing the work.

Enquire About a Partnership
How we work

From first idea to final report.

  1. 01
    Identify

    With Traditional Owners, agencies and scientists, we find the priority and shape it into a project that meets your program objectives.

  2. 02
    Deliver

    We bring the partners and co-funding together and engage specialist delivery partners against clear milestones, managing the grants and contracts along the way.

  3. 03
    Demonstrate

    We track ecological, financial and partnership outcomes and report against them, so you can show what the investment achieved.

Conservation and the visitor economy

Tourism budgets can fund conservation too.

Governments are bringing parks and tourism closer together. That opens a second route to fund environmental outcomes, through visitor-economy objectives, and we help design projects that meet both briefs at once.

A 38 kilometre Epic trail in the Southern Flinders Ranges.

Designed in close consultation with the Nukunu Wapma Thura Aboriginal Corporation, the Epic Mountain Bike Trail near Melrose opened in October 2023. It was a major part of the $10 million Remarkable Southern Flinders agreement, funded by the South Australian and Australian Governments and supported by us.

What the partnership delivered

  • The Remarkable Epic, a 38 km closed loop from the Remarkable Trailhead in Melrose, opened in October 2023
  • 20 km of new mountain bike trails in Mount Remarkable National Park at Willowie
  • An upgraded Mambray Creek campground and day visitor area
  • New and improved day visitor facilities at Wirrabara

Underway: the Gorges Walks trail network, a multi-day hike in Wapma Thura–Southern Flinders Ranges National Park.

Read about the project →
First Nations partnerships

Conservation led by Traditional Owners, backed at scale.

Many of the largest outcomes we have helped deliver sit on Country, with Traditional Owners setting direction and co-managing what is protected. For government, that means projects that deliver cultural, social and biodiversity commitments together.

  • Nukunu Traditional OwnersWapma Thura, Southern Flinders Ranges, SA

    Traditional Owners of the national park at the heart of Remarkable Southern Flinders.

  • Ngarrindjeri Aboriginal CorporationMundoo Island, Murray Mouth, SA

    Shaping the management plan for the 1,900 ha now being added to Coorong National Park.

  • Warddeken rangersWarddeken Indigenous Protected Area, NT

    Indigenous-led recovery of threatened mammals across 1.4 million hectares.

  • Barengi Gadjin Land CouncilLittle Desert, VIC

    Redeveloping the native nursery and arboretum beside Little Desert National Park, with a focus on cultural heritage.

  • Ngurrawaana rangersMillstream Chichester National Park, WA

    Traditional Owners working with parks staff to protect Pilbara olive python and northern quoll habitat.

Accountable at every step

We are registered with the ACNC and governed by a voluntary, unremunerated board supported by four committees, and our financial accounts are externally audited every year.

Board and committeesHow we are governed→PDF reportImpact Report 2025→PDF reportYear in Review 2025→
Start the conversation

Bring us your biggest conservation commitment.

Whether you are planning a land acquisition, a landscape precinct, a tourism and conservation project or a grant program, tell us what you need to deliver and we will connect you with the right person.

Talk to us directlyIan LaingChief Commercial Officerilaing@fnpw.org.au · 1800 898 626

Enquire About a Partnership

Email fnpw@fnpw.org.au or call 1800 898 626 and we will help directly.

Common questions

How will we know what our funding achieved?

Every partnership has agreed outcomes and a reporting schedule, and we publish our overall results each year in our Impact Report.

What can we say publicly?

We agree what each partner can say before any announcement, so every claim is accurate and backed by evidence.

items.title: Growing National Parks
items.content:
Home/Projects/Growing National Parks
13 projects across Australia

Growing National Parks

We expand and protect conservation spaces to safeguard critical habitats and support resilient ecosystems.

Credit: tsvibrav
29,479Hectares added last year

Land acquired and transferred into the national parks estate in the last reporting year. FNPW Impact Report.

13Projects funded

Land acquisitions and park expansions funded with partners, supporters and government.

4States and territories

From the Flinders Ranges to the New South Wales coast.

Why it matters

What this work does

National parks are the strongest protection Australian law can give a landscape. When land with high conservation value comes up, we help acquire it and pass it to government to become national park, so it is safe from clearing and development for good.

It started with our founding gift in 1970 and it has never stopped: from wetlands at the Murray Mouth to outback stations beside Boodjamulla, these projects are how the map of protected Australia grows.

How we do it

  • We identify land of high conservation value, often adjoining existing parks
  • We fund or co-fund the acquisition with partners and supporters
  • The land is transferred to the national parks estate, protected forever
Featured project

Remarkable Southern Flinders

Linking established parks, newly protected land and open reservoir country into one vast, connected park precinct for South Australia, on Nukunu Country.

It is the clearest picture of what growing a national park actually takes: patient negotiation, co-funding, and Traditional Owners at the centre of how the land is managed afterwards.

Australia's ecosystems are broken into smaller and smaller pieces, and wildlife pays the price. Adding land to the national park estate reconnects those fragments, protects whole systems and gives threatened species room to recover.
