items.title: Healing the Land
items.content:
Home/Projects/Healing the Land
28 projects across Australia

Healing the Land

We restore and rehabilitate landscapes affected by bushfires, floods, and human activities like unsustainable land clearing, through our Landscape Resilience Program.

1.2MPlants in the ground

Trees, shrubs and seedlings planted across priority restoration sites. FNPW Impact Report.

28Projects funded

Revegetation, wetland repair, bushfire recovery and cultural land management.

6States and territories

Across the eastern seaboard, the Top End and the west.

Why it matters

What this work does

Much of Australia is damaged rather than destroyed, and damaged land can heal. These projects replant habitat, restore wetlands and waterways, recover country after bushfire and support First Nations cultural land management.

Healing the land is slow, patient work measured in seasons and seedlings. It is also the work that turns a map of loss back into habitat.

How we do it

  • We fund revegetation, restoration and bushfire recovery at scale
  • We support cultural fire and caring-for-Country programs led by First Nations communities
  • We stay for the follow-up: watering, weeding, monitoring, replanting
From seed to habitat

Where your support goes.

Healing the land takes more than putting a tree in the ground. Only about a tenth of Australia’s native plants are available as seed, so we built a network to grow the rest, and your support carries each plant through every stage.

  1. 01

    Collecting seed

    Volunteers collect seed from local ecosystems, so what goes back into the ground belongs there.

  2. 02

    Growing it on

    More than thirty community-led nurseries grow the seed into locally adapted plants and bank what is rare or threatened. Some species take one to two years to be ready.

  3. 03

    Planting

    The plants go back into degraded land in national parks and on public and private land, with First Nations partners, Landcare groups and landholders.

  4. 04

    Caring and measuring

    We stay for the follow-up of watering, weeding, monitoring and replanting, and report what survives and grows.

Give a TreeHow the nursery network works
Featured project

Yarrahapinni Wetlands

Floodgates and levee walls removed, tidal flows returned: a wetland on the Macleay coming back to life after decades of damage.

It shows what healing at scale looks like when you undo the original damage rather than work around it, and then stay long enough to watch the system come back on its own terms.

Donate

Where your money goes.

Every donation is put to work across our three pillars. Here is what that looks like.

Where your money goes

Your support has an enormous impact on conservation.

We rely on your help to fund critical conservation projects Australia-wide, partnering with First Nations groups, community groups, rangers and scientists, individuals and government agencies to have a direct impact on growing and protecting natural Australia.

01

Projects to protect our future environment

We support a range of projects to protect natural Australia for future generations. Since the 2019 and 2020 bushfires we have focused on healing our land in bushfire affected areas of Australia.

To see the impact we have on our environment, take a look at the diverse range of projects we are currently involved in.

See our projects →

84 projects currently funded across every state and territory.

02

Land acquisitions to grow our national parks

To conserve nature, we must preserve the land and water of our country, the lifeblood of environmental balance.

Species, including our own, cannot survive without a healthy habitat. That is why we add land to Australia’s national parks for permanent protection. We are not about locking nature up. We are about protecting it in the most secure way possible.

How we grow national parks →

29,479 hectares added to national park status in the last year, including the 1,900 hectares of Mundoo Island secured for Coorong National Park.

03

Grants that make a difference

Our grants have supported conservation projects run by government agencies, private landholders, community groups and scientists.

Our grant programs are currently closed to new applications. Sign up to our newsletter to hear when they reopen.

Get grant updates →

Our Community Conservation Grants have funded work from seed collection to species monitoring.

04

Environmental education for future generations

Learning about what you see outside encourages you to care, and to practise more positive environmental behaviours.

We believe environmental education is central to the projects and grants we fund. Backyard Buddies is our best known educational initiative.

See Backyard Buddies →

1,215,443 trees, shrubs and seedlings planted across priority landscapes, many of them grown by community nurseries and school groups.

Ready to make a difference?

Your donation grows national parks, saves species and heals the land.

items.static_title: Exploring koala facts: unveiling the secrets of Australia’s iconic marsupials
items.content:
Koalas, those charming marsupials adorning countless postcards and memes, are more than just cuddly creatures – they are fascinating and complex inhabitants of Australia's eucalypt forests. Welcome to our deep dive into the world of koalas, where we uncover koala facts that will leave you enchanted and enlightened!

1. Not a typical bear

First things first, let's address a common misconception: koalas are not bears! They belong to the marsupial family, sharing lineage with kangaroos and wombats. Found in eucalypt forests across New South Wales, Queensland, Victoria, and South Australia, these tree-dwelling wonders have captivated the world with their unique charm.

2. Fussy eaters

Koalas may be picky eaters, but their selective palate is a matter of survival. Despite the presence of over 600 types of eucalypt trees in Australia, koalas zero in on just a few species. Their diet mainly consists of specific eucalyptus leaves that are toxic to most other animals. Surprisingly, they can munch through up to a kilogram of leaves daily, a feat fueled by their specialised digestive system.

3. Eucalyptus leaves

Ever wondered why koalas seem so dozy? The myth that eucalyptus leaves make them drunk is just that – a myth. Koala food provides minimal energy, leading them to conserve their strength by sleeping or resting during the day. This way, they can save energy for their nocturnal foraging endeavours.

4. Koalas and hydration

Koalas are the embodiment of efficiency, even when it comes to staying hydrated. Over 90% of their water intake comes from eucalyptus leaves. Drinking becomes a necessity only when leaves lack sufficient moisture, such as during droughts.

5. Joeys and motherly communications

Koalas' motherly communication is a symphony of soft clicks, gentle hums, and squeaks. When joeys emerge from their mothers' pouches, this intricate vocal interaction helps them understand their surroundings and establish a bond.

6. Territorial tree-dwellers

Koalas are creatures of habit, establishing long-term communities and territories within their preferred habitats. Their attachment to specific trees is vital for survival. If relocated, koalas struggle to adapt, often leading to unfavorable outcomes. This highlights the importance of conserving their natural habitats.

7. Breeding season and communication

Koalas' breeding season, from September to March, is marked by male koalas' unique vocalizations. Loud grunts attract potential mates, while gurgling sounds warn off rivals. Additionally, males release a powerful musky odor to attract females, marking their territory as they climb trees.

8. Threats and conservation

Sadly, koalas face threats like habitat loss due to urbanization, dog attacks, and vehicle collisions. With over 80% of their habitats located on private land, individual efforts play a crucial role in their conservation. Simple actions such as keeping pets indoors at night and planting eucalyptus trees contribute to their survival.

9. Koala-approved tips

To support koala populations, consider planting native trees, creating safe travel corridors, and driving cautiously in koala habitats. By respecting their needs and habitats, you become a valuable ally in their preservation.

From debunking myths to discovering their peculiar habits, koalas are undoubtedly captivating creatures. As stewards of our environment, it's our duty to ensure the survival of these iconic marsupials. By embracing these koala facts and incorporating small changes into our daily lives, we can safeguard their future and keep the magic of koalas alive for generations to come.

One Animal at a Time

Koalas: Taking care of an icon at risk

Amidst heartbreaking koala bushfire scenes, hope blooms in New South Wales. Despite habitat loss and disease, koala numbers are rising on Sydney's outskirts. A heartwarming collaboration on Liverpool Plains dispels myths and helps koalas thrive during extreme weather. We explore groundbreaking research amid declining koala numbers, while the NSW government's Koala Strategy aims to stabilize and boost their populations through actions like reserves, road safety, training, and funding.

Meet dedicated individuals like Valentina Mella, Robert Frend, and Morgan Philpott. Learn more about the Wildlife Heroes who care for our beloved Australian wildlife.

items.static_title: Mitigating the effects of environmental change on Australia’s fragile ecosystem
items.content:
Despite its remarkable resilience, the Australian ecosystem is being pushed to its limits by the persistent impact of human-induced environmental change. Every year, the country is struck by catastrophic natural disasters, including devastating floods, damaging cyclones, record-breaking droughts, and raging bushfires , wreaking havoc on its precious landscape.

Although we are approaching the point of no return to halt the detrimental effects of environmental change, there is still hope. We can make a difference if we take swift action.

Discover how to save Australia's precious ecosystem from environmental catastrophe in the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife's (FNPW) latest eBook, Mitigating the effects of environmental change on Australia's fragile ecosystem, that outlines collaborative strategies to combat environmental change, including:

  • Prioritising a whole of system approach
  • Coordinating funding and resourcing for projects, and
  • Establishing short term and long-term goals.

Take action today to create a brighter future: Download the eBook and learn how you can make a meaningful and proactive contribution in 2023 and beyond.

Explore OpportunitiesEnquire About a Partnership

Together, we can achieve more for Australia’s wild places.

From a single project to a long-term landscape partnership, we shape each opportunity around the priorities we share.

Corporate partnerships

Philanthropy, trusts & foundations

Ways to partner

Find the partnership that fits.

Fund Conservation at Scale

Fund the acquisition of land for national parks, the growing and planting of native habitat, or recovery work for a threatened species. Every project starts with an agreed scope and what your funding will achieve.

Our projects: Mundoo Island Station, Remarkable Southern Flinders

Build Conservation Partnerships

The most lasting results take years, not a single funding round. We build long-term partnerships around a landscape, a species or a cause that matters to you, and grow them as the results come in.

Our projects: Landscape Resilience Program, Native Plant Nurseries, L’OCCITANE Australia

We’re exploring how public, philanthropic and private funding could work together on long-term landscape outcomes, and we’d welcome a conversation with organisations who want to help shape it.

How a partnership runs.

    Identify

Privacy policy.

How we collect, use and protect your information.

Effective November 2026

1. Purpose and scope

Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife (FNPW), ABN 90 107 744 771, respects the privacy of people who support, work with or engage with us. This policy explains how we collect, hold, use and disclose personal information, and how individuals may access or correct it or make a complaint. It applies to our websites, fundraising, conservation programs, partnerships, events and other activities. We handle personal information in accordance with the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) and the Australian Privacy Principles (APPs), where applicable.

2. What information we collect

Depending on your relationship with FNPW, we may collect your name, contact details, organisation, role, communication preferences, donation and engagement history, payment transaction details (generally handled by payment providers), volunteer or event participation, correspondence, and information relevant to grant applications, projects and partnerships. For conservation projects we may collect site addresses, property or location details, project contact details, monitoring records and other information needed to deliver and demonstrate outcomes. Website information may include device identifiers, IP addresses and analytics data. We collect sensitive information only where reasonably necessary and permitted by law, including obtaining consent where required.

3. How we collect information

We generally collect information directly from you through forms, donations, enquiries, events, meetings, correspondence and our websites. We may also receive information from authorised representatives, delivery partners, community nurseries, government agencies, professional advisers, public registers and publicly available sources where lawful and appropriate. Where reasonable, we explain why information is collected and any likely disclosures at or before collection. You may interact anonymously or using a pseudonym where lawful and practicable; however, some activities require identification.

4. Why we use information

We use personal information to process donations and issue receipts; administer fundraising, bequests and supporter relationships; communicate about our work and opportunities to support it; manage partnerships, grants, volunteering and events; assess and deliver conservation projects; map and monitor restoration outcomes; meet reporting, governance and legal obligations; improve our services and websites; manage enquiries and complaints; and protect people, systems and organisational assets. We use information for other purposes only where permitted by law, including with consent where required.

5. Conservation sites and location information

FNPW may require accurate restoration site locations and appropriate project contact information for project planning, mapping, monitoring, verification, acquittal, impact reporting and future stewardship. A site address may be personal information when it identifies or can reasonably identify an individual. We restrict access according to operational need and consider whether published maps or reports should use aggregated, approximate or de-identified locations. Delivery partners providing third-party information must have an appropriate basis to collect and share it and should give individuals suitable notice. This policy does not replace collection notices or data-sharing terms in partner agreements.

6. Who we share information with

Where reasonably necessary and permitted, we may disclose relevant information to contracted technology, payment, fundraising and communications providers; conservation delivery partners, nurseries and contractors; government agencies and funders for authorised project reporting; auditors, insurers and professional advisers; and regulators or other parties where required or authorised by law. We seek to limit disclosures to what is needed for the relevant purpose and apply suitable contractual and organisational safeguards. We do not sell personal information. We do not provide donor information to unrelated organisations for their own direct marketing without an appropriate legal basis.

7. Storage, security and retention

Information may be held in secure electronic systems, cloud platforms and, where necessary, physical records. FNPW takes reasonable steps to protect personal information against misuse, interference, loss and unauthorised access, modification or disclosure, including access restrictions, staff awareness and appropriate service-provider controls. No electronic system is completely risk-free. We retain information only for as long as needed for lawful business, conservation, accountability and recordkeeping purposes, then securely delete or de-identify it where reasonable and legally permitted.

8. Overseas handling

FNPW uses technology platforms and service providers to support its operations, fundraising, communications and conservation programs. Some of these providers may store or process personal information outside Australia or provide access to information from overseas. Where FNPW discloses personal information to an overseas recipient, we take reasonable steps to protect that information and comply with our obligations under the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth), including the Australian Privacy Principles. Where practicable, FNPW identifies the countries in which overseas recipients are likely to be located. These countries are the United States and Canada. FNPW maintains appropriate contractual, organisational and technical safeguards for personal information handled by its service providers.

9. Fundraising and communications

We may contact supporters and prospective supporters about conservation outcomes, appeals, events, partnerships and opportunities to give, where permitted by law. We may use engagement and donation information to make communications more relevant. You may opt out of promotional communications using the unsubscribe facility or by contacting us. Transactional, legal or essential project communications may still be sent where appropriate. We comply with applicable direct marketing and electronic messaging requirements.

10. Website, cookies and third-party links

Our websites may use cookies and similar technologies to operate website functions, understand traffic, measure campaign performance and, where configured, support relevant advertising. Some tools may collect online identifiers or enable third parties to receive information. The technologies actually in use, their purposes and available choices should be accurately described in a website cookie notice following a technical audit. You may adjust browser settings and other available consent controls, although some features may not function as intended. External websites and payment pages have their own privacy practices.

11. Artificial intelligence and automated tools

FNPW may use approved digital and AI-enabled tools to support administration, analysis, communications and project work. We apply human oversight and privacy safeguards and do not intentionally enter sensitive or confidential personal information into unapproved public AI services. If FNPW uses automated decision-making arrangements that trigger specific statutory disclosure requirements, we will update this policy as required by the applicable commencement dates.

12. Access and correction

You may request access to personal information we hold about you or ask us to correct information that is inaccurate, out of date, incomplete, irrelevant or misleading. We will respond within a reasonable period and explain any lawful refusal. We may need to verify your identity. We do not charge for making a request; any permitted charge for providing access will be reasonable and explained in advance.

13. Privacy incidents and complaints

If we become aware of a privacy or security incident, we will assess and respond to it, including notifying affected individuals and the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) when required under the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme. If you have a privacy concern, please contact our Privacy Officer. We will acknowledge and investigate complaints and aim to respond within 30 days. If you are dissatisfied with our response, you may be able to complain to the OAIC at www.oaic.gov.au.

14. Contact and updates

Privacy Officer, Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife, GPO Box 2666, Sydney NSW 2001. Telephone: 1800 898 626. Email: fnpw@fnpw.org.au

We may update this policy to reflect changes in law, systems and operations. The current version will be available on fnpw.org.au with its effective date.

Home/Reconciliation Action Plan
About us

Innovate Reconciliation Action Plan.

Advancing reconciliation with First Nations Peoples.

Photo: Donal Sullivan

Our commitment

At FNPW, we’re committed to fostering reconciliation by building meaningful partnerships with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities. Our Innovate Reconciliation Action Plan for 2025-2027 formalises this commitment, guiding our efforts to support cultural recognition, environmental stewardship, and sustainable conservation efforts led by First Nations peoples.

Our vision for reconciliation

FNPW recognises that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples are the Traditional Custodians of Australia’s lands, waters, and biodiversity. Our vision is to honour First Nations knowledge, cultures, and contributions by embedding respect, recognition, and collaboration into our conservation initiatives. Through our RAP, we aim to:

  • Strengthen relationships with First Nations communities
  • Enhance cultural understanding within our organisation
  • Recognise and integrate the scientific and cultural knowledge of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities to support their leadership in conservation efforts
  • Support community-led environmental programs

Key initiatives in our RAP

  • Community partnerships: working with First Nations communities to grow national parks, save native species, and restore degraded lands.
  • Cultural recognition: promoting cultural learning, participating in National Reconciliation Week and NAIDOC Week, and embedding Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cultural protocols.
  • Employment & procurement: increasing opportunities for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander employment, professional development, and business engagement.
  • Governance & accountability: establishing a strong framework to measure our progress and impact.
The full plan

FNPW Innovate Reconciliation Action Plan 2025-2027

For a deeper look into our initiatives, goals, and commitments, read the full plan.

Home/Projects/Saving Species
44 projects across Australia

Saving Species

We protect Australia's most vulnerable species by restoring habitats, creating wildlife corridors, and supporting targeted conservation programs.

Credit: RichLindie
18,582Treatments delivered

Mange treatments delivered through the Curb Wombat Mange Program, against a target of 10,000. FNPW Impact Report.

44Projects funded

Recovery programs run with Traditional Owners, researchers, carers and land managers.

9States and territories

From Christmas Island to the Tasmanian midlands, including two external territories.

Why it matters

What this work does

Australia is home to plants and animals found nowhere else on Earth, and one of the worst extinction records anywhere. These projects fund the unglamorous, essential work of recovery: breeding programs, monitoring, nest boxes, disease treatment and the science that underpins all of it.

From koalas and quolls to enigma moths and endangered wattles, if it is on the brink, this is the work fighting for it.

How we do it

  • We fund recovery programs run with researchers, carers and land managers
  • We back both flagship species and the overlooked ones
  • Every project reports real outcomes: populations, hectares, hollows, seedlings
Featured project

Warddeken Mayh Recovery Project

Indigenous rangers run a network of permanent camera monitoring sites across 1.4 million hectares of the Warddeken Indigenous Protected Area, recovering threatened mammals through right-way fire and feral animal management.

It is the largest single landscape we work across and the clearest demonstration of what this work funds: local knowledge, long timeframes, measured outcomes.

Stories from the species we’re saving

Saving Species
July 2026 · Story

A wildlife corridor is only as wide as its narrowest point

Urban sprawl rarely wipes out a wildlife corridor outright, it pinches it. Four of Australia's fastest growing regions show what width, continuity and permanence actually decide, from a chlamydia free koala population in south west Sydney to an overpass in Brisbane that has worked since 2004.

Read more
Saving Species
July 2026 · Story

Your Backyard Is Habitat Too: Help Native Wildlife

Most of the green on a city map is mown lawn and imported hedge, which native animals cannot use. A backyard, a courtyard or a balcony planted with local natives becomes the next safe step for bees, lizards, microbats and birds.

Read more
Saving Species
March 2026 · News

Bringing Back the Growling Grass Frog

The Growling Grass Frog is listed as Vulnerable and has vanished from much of its former range. At Winton Wetlands in north-east Victoria, a founding population of 60 to 65 frogs is now in place, with monitoring running to March 2026 to see whether they breed.

Skip the socks. A native tree planted in a recovering landscape, with a certificate sent to the person you love. It cleans air, shelters wildlife and outlives us all.

Perfect for birthdays, memorials and Christmas, and popular with businesses gifting clients something that means something.

  • A real tree in a real FNPW project site
  • Personalised certificate for your recipient
  • Bulk gifting for business
Give a Tree today
quick + mighty

Donate to Bring Back the Bush

A single gift, toward replanting degraded Country and habitat, funding recovery science, and acquiring land for national park status. You choose the amount; we make it count.

Your donation is fully tax deductible, and your receipt arrives by email straight away.

  • Goes to work across all three pillars
  • Fully tax deductible
  • Instant receipt for tax time
Donate now
the inner circle

Become a Habitat Hero

Recovery is slow, patient work measured in seasons. Monthly giving is what lets us commit to it: rangers stay funded, monitoring keeps running, seedlings get watered in year two, not just planted in year one.

Habitat Heroes get updates from the field showing exactly what their support is doing.

  • Steady funding for long-term projects
  • Field updates from the projects you power
  • Change or pause anytime
Join monthly
the long game

Leave a gift in your will

After family and friends are looked after, a gift in your will protects what you love about this country beyond your lifetime. Gifts in wills have secured some of the most significant land in our 55-year history.

We can provide the exact wording your solicitor needs; every conversation is confidential and without obligation.

  • Land protected forever
  • Suggested wording for your solicitor
  • Confidential, no-obligation conversations
Learn how
Time and influence

Your time, worth every bit as much.

You can spend a weekend with your hands in the dirt, bring your business in behind the mission, or get your whole workplace giving together. There are five ways in, and we lean on all of them.

01

Corporate volunteering

Bring your team out for a planting or restoration day with our project partners. Tools, guidance and safety covered; most teams call it the best team day they have done.

→02

Workplace giving

→03

A simple way for businesses to celebrate milestones, say thank you or share a little appreciation. We can arrange Give a Tree certificates in bulk, featuring your company logo.

→04

Fundraise for us

Run, bake, climb or host in support of FNPW. We supply logos, photos, impact stats and encouragement.

→05

Donate land

Land with conservation value can become part of the protected estate, safe forever. Every conversation is confidential.

→

Funding conservation at scale for a government agency, foundation or business? Partner with us →

Let’s not beat around the bush any longer. Australia’s wilderness and wildlife need our help.

Home/Why Your Support Is Needed
Donate

Why your support matters.

Australia is home to species found nowhere else, and one of the worst extinction records on Earth. Support is not optional; it is the whole mechanism.

Why it matters

Together we are making conservation happen.

We are the charity partner of national parks and wildlife services across Australia. We are a non-government organisation with a mission to safeguard our ecosystems, wilderness and wildlife for future generations.

We believe in conservation, not only because it protects native plants, birds and animals, but also because it protects us. After all, you simply cannot be healthy in an unhealthy environment.

Protectnature
Preventextinction
Providea better future
The scale of it

Species in trouble, and lost forever.

In Australia today, millions of hectares of habitat have no permanent protection. Without a lasting form of protection, habitats can be degraded or destroyed, and a high rate of species extinctions is the result.

To date almost 2,000 plant and animal species are in trouble or extinct. Australia has the highest rate of vertebrate mammal extinction in the world, and nearly one in three of our unique mammals is at risk of extinction.

507fauna species in trouble or extinct
1,375flora species in trouble or extinct
104endemic Australian species listed as extinct by 2021
One thirdgrowth in threatened species and ecosystems over the past 20 years
What is driving it

Three pressures, all of them reversible.

Invasive species

Invasive animals are the number one threat, affecting 82% of all threatened species, with cats and foxes the biggest threat to our mammals. Invasive plants are a problem too: escaped garden plants account for over 70% of all environmental weeds.

Habitat clearing

Australia’s native forests now cover only 19% of the total land area, and over 40% of forests and woodlands have been cleared, mostly for agricultural expansion. About 8 million hectares of threatened species’ habitats were cleared between 2000 and 2017.

Fire and climate

Climate change threatens to increase the rate of losses. In New South Wales alone, over 37% of the state’s national park estate was impacted by the Black Summer fires.

Sources: Australian Government threatened species lists for fauna and flora; CSIRO on invasive species; State of the Environment.

Impact you can see

Acting now, as we have since 1970.

We work with local, state and federal governments to gain permanent protection for habitats and species, and to grow Australia’s national parks system. We do that work in partnership with First Nations groups, scientists, community groups, and with individuals and companies who want the same thing.

55 yearsand counting

Since 1970 we have been protecting land and species for future generations, so that all Australians can enjoy these natural gifts.

Every stateand territory

Our work spans hundreds of conservation projects across all states and territories. There are many ways you or your company can be part of it.

See how your contributions help Ways to get involved

Home/Workplace Giving
Get involved

Workplace giving.

A small amount from each pay, before tax, often matched by your employer. Set and forget, and it adds up to habitat.

Giving from your pay

Together with our corporate supporters and their employees, we can make a positive difference to improve our environment and help protect natural Australia for future generations.

We invest workplace giving donations in projects that protect and preserve our national parks, and rehabilitate our precious native species and their vital habitats across Australia.

What is workplace giving?

Workplace giving, also known as payroll giving, lets you make tax deductible donations to charities straight from your regular pay. A small regular donation makes a big difference when combined with other regular donors, helping us protect and care for our unique wildlife.

Donations are deducted from your salary before tax, so you receive the tax benefit immediately rather than waiting until the end of the financial year. In some cases your employer may match your donation dollar for dollar, so do ask whether your company will match it.

How it works

Three steps, then it runs itself.

01

Ask payroll

Ask your payroll or people team to add us as a workplace giving recipient.

02

Pick an amount

It comes out of your pre-tax pay each period, so you get the tax benefit straight away.

03

Ask about matching

Many employers match dollar for dollar, which doubles what your gift does.

If your workplace already has a program

To donate regularly, simply ask your payroll department to deduct your nominated donation from your gross, pre-tax salary each pay period. It really is that easy.

For details on implementing a program, or questions about setting up a workplace donation, get in touch and we can provide you with more information.

We also have profiles on Benevity and GoodCompany, where employees can donate, volunteer or fundraise for us.

If you are an employer

Workplace giving works for employees, employers and for us. Employees see how small pre-tax amounts add up collectively, and companies find that a program brings organisational values to life, increases employee morale and supports engagement.

By matching employee donations you demonstrate a real commitment to your people, help build engagement, and of course double the financial support towards protecting natural Australia for future generations.

  • Recognition of your company and employees supporting us on our social media channels
  • Educational presentations: invite us to a morning tea so we can engage your employees on the work we do and the impact of our projects
  • Impact reports that demonstrate your company’s CSR impact, your employee engagement initiatives, and the impact of the projects your company makes possible
  • Corporate volunteering event opportunities

If there is no program yet

If your company doesn’t offer a workplace giving program, you can still support us with a regular donation as a Habitat Hero.

And if your company or business would like to start one, let us help. Our fundraising team would be happy to talk through your options.

Start a program

Talk to our fundraising team.

Call us on 1800 898 626 or send us a message, and we will walk you through your workplace giving options.

Contact us 1800 898 626

Home/Gifts in Wills/Professional advisers
For professional advisers

Help your clients leave a legacy for nature.

For solicitors, estate planners, financial advisers, trustee companies, funeral directors and insurers. When a client wants to leave something for nature, we make the gift simple to write and easy to administer, with one person to call at every stage.

Contact our gifts in wills teamWording and organisation details
Gifts your clients can point to
1,900ha
Mundoo Island, secured in 2025 with a gift from the Estate of the Late Barbara Harris and now being added to Coorong National Park
2,086ha
added to Morton National Park thanks to a gift from Kitty White
80+bird species
find a haven at Mother of Ducks Lagoon, where a gift from Eulie Sandrey supported wetland research
Why clients choose us

A gift that outlasts everyone in the room.

Clients who care about nature want to know their gift will be used well and will last. We have been protecting Australia’s wild places and wildlife since 1970, and we look for outcomes that endure for generations.

01

Lasting outcomes

Gifts in wills have added land to national parks from Morton to the Coorong, supported wetland research, and restored reserves and walking tracks that people still enjoy today.

02

Wishes honoured

Clients can leave a gift for our general purposes or for a specific purpose, such as land acquisition or a particular species. We confirm specific wishes can be met before the will is finalised.

03

Accountable and audited

We are registered with the ACNC and endorsed as a Deductible Gift Recipient, governed by a voluntary, unremunerated board, and our financial accounts are externally audited every year.

80%invested in our core purpose in 2025Impact Report 2025
Drafting the gift

Everything you need in one place.

Please use our full legal name and ABN. If your client wants to direct their gift to a specific purpose, contact us before the will is finalised so we can confirm the wording.

I give to the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife (ABN 90 107 744 771) of Level 6, 10 Bridge Street, Sydney NSW 2000, [a percentage of my estate / the residue of my estate / the sum of $______ / the following specific gift] for its general purposes. I direct that the receipt of the Chief Executive Officer or authorised officer shall be a sufficient discharge to my executors.

Gifts for a specific purpose

We welcome gifts for purposes such as acquiring land for national parks or protecting a particular species. Talk to us first and we will help make sure the client’s wishes can be carried out.

Land

Land can’t be left to us in a will. Clients who want to give land can do so in their lifetime, so it becomes national park. How a gift of land works.

For executors

If you are administering an estate that includes a gift to us, contact our gifts in wills team and we will confirm what we need and help the estate finalise the gift.

Incorporated as a company limited by guarantee and regulated by ASIC. Registered with the Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission and endorsed as a Deductible Gift Recipient.

Raising the question

Clients are glad to be asked.

Many people would include a charity in their will if someone simply raised it. A short question, asked once the family is provided for, gives clients the chance to leave something for the causes they care about.

A question that works

Include a Charity, the national campaign for gifts in wills, suggests asking: “Are there any causes or charities that are particularly important to you?”

The evidence

When UK solicitors raised charitable giving, the share of wills that included a charity rose from 4.9 to 10.8 per cent, and 65 per cent of Australians say it is fine for their lawyer to ask. Source: Lawyers Weekly

Work with us

Part of your network, and you part of ours.

We want to be the organisation advisers think of when a client mentions nature, wild places or wildlife, and a reliable partner when it is time to administer the gift.

01

Information for your clients

Our gifts in wills page and guide set out the ways to give and who to contact, ready to share with clients. Gifts in Wills

Talks for your team or members

We are glad to talk to your firm, association or network about our work, the places gifts in wills have protected, and how gifts are received and used.

03

One direct contact

One person to call for questions from the first draft of a will to the final distribution of an estate.

Contact us

Talk to our gifts in wills team.

Whether you are drafting a will, administering an estate or would like to work with us, we would be glad to hear from you.

We acknowledge the Traditional Owners of Country throughout Australia and pay our respects to Elders past and present of the lands and waterways of the area now known as Queensland.

Corporate Volunteering at Daisy Hill Conservation Park

Location: Daisy Hill Rd (approx. 25km from Brisbane CBD) Timing: Weekdays, typically 8:30am – 2:00pm

Bring your team together for a hands-on corporate volunteering opportunity in Brisbane at Daisy Hill Conservation Park, one of Southeast Queensland's most important conservation areas.

Surrounded by eucalypt forest and rich wildlife habitat, Daisy Hill plays a critical role in koala conservation and bushland protection. Corporate volunteering here gives your team the opportunity to contribute directly to wildlife habitat health while building connection, purpose and environmental awareness.

Why corporate volunteering at Daisy Hill matters?

Daisy Hill Conservation Park is a vital refuge in Southeast Queensland, supporting a large population of native wildlife and providing essential habitat for koalas.

In a boost for conservation, the Queensland Government recently announced a 213-hectare expansion of the park, significantly increasing protected land and opportunities for ecological restoration. This makes now an ideal time for organisations to get involved and support long-term conservation outcomes through volunteering.

The park also serves as an important space for environmental education and community connection. By volunteering at Daisy Hill, your team helps protect biodiversity while contributing to a healthier, more resilient landscape in QLD.

What your team will do

Corporate volunteering days at Daisy Hill are practical, educational and rewarding. Activities may include:

  • Learning to identify native plants and invasive weeds
  • Weeding and land care to support habitat health
  • Assisting with bushland restoration activities
  • Restoring bushland and wetland habitats
  • An exclusive visit to the Daisy Hill Koala Centre, learning about koalas, their habitats and current conservation challenges

items.featured_alt: Two people beside a newly planted row of tree guards along a fence line
items.static_title: 10,000 Native Give-Away Trees and Shrubs Hit the Ground
items.content:
The Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife (FNPW) has been very active with bushfire recovery and restoration, providing funds to Greening Australia along with many other nurseries in the region to grow masses of plants of local native species.

With funds from FNPW, Upper Snowy Landcare Network (USLN) put its hand up to disseminate 10,000 tree and shrub give-aways to interested local landholders. All up, 47 landholders responded and received an average of 200 plants each.

The project is almost complete, thanks to Bernie and Michelle McDonald from Rock Flat who agreed to look after the seedlings at their property and helped facilitate the trees going out. USLN also helped by covering the cost of the tree guards which are necessary for the survival of seedlings in the Snowy Monaro.

Margaret Mackinnon, USLN Chair says, “The reality of landholders planting trees themselves is really encouraging. Ground preparation, planting, guarding, watering and follow-up care does take time and is a big commitment. Some of the landholders took bold steps to plant biodiversity sized plots. We hope to do it again next year.”

USLN also helped by providing their ’USLN tree and shrub planting guide for the Monaro’ which tells people everything they need to know to establish their own biodiversity plot.

FNPW is the charity partner of Australia’s national parks. They are a non-government organisation with a mission to safeguard our ecosystems, wilderness, and flora and fauna now and for future generations.

To keep abreast with Upper Snowy Landcare Network’s efforts, please find us on Facebook or go to www.uppersnowylandcare.org.au and join.
For information on the USLN contact:

Lauren Van Dyke
Upper Snowy Landcare Coordinator, 0411 402 978
Email: contact@uppersnowylandcare.org.au

items.featured_alt: Supporters gathered at Lane Cove National Park to mark one million trees planted
items.static_title: A million reasons to say thank you
items.content:
The last few years have been significant ones for our Foundation. A national strategy that is already delivering. A tree planting program that has passed one million trees in the ground. Partnerships that are deeper, more ambitious, and built for the long term. None of it happened by accident, and none of it happened alone.

David Knowles has been part of this organisation for eight years, three of them as President & Chair, and as he steps back from that role, we wanted to take a moment to reflect on what we have built together.

Strategy

Thinking bigger, acting bolder

If there’s a thread that runs through everything FNPW achieved during David’s time on the board, it’s the shift toward thinking at a national scale.

“The organisation has taken a leap forward in its approach to tackling the problems we are here to solve,” David reflects. “Taking a national view and focusing on the most important areas, where we can have the greatest impact, across Australia, is absolutely the right thing to do.”

That thinking took its clearest form in FNPW 2025-2028 strategic plan, Partnering for Impact, which David helped shape alongside the board and executive team. “Being part of developing that strategy was really enjoyable,” he says, “and we are already starting to see its impact. Its impact should be felt well beyond 2028.”

The milestone

One trowel, one million reasons

Ask David to name a moment that has stayed with him, and he goes straight to Lane Cove National Park, and the day our tree planting program hit one million trees.

“It was a standout moment because it involved marking a milestone as well as actually planting a living tree into the Earth,” he says. “I still have the trowel and I intend to keep it.”

That detail says a lot. One million is a number that matters. A trowel pressed into soil is the feeling behind it.

Growing

Growing with the urgency of the moment

Conservation has become a more urgent, more scrutinised space over the past eight years, and FNPW has grown with it.

“As well as the environment itself, we have evolved our thinking in terms of who we partner with and who funds our work,” David says. “Those funders and partners have all become more sophisticated over the last few years, and I expect they will continue on that path.”

What held steady through all of that change was a clear sense of purpose. “With any charity, it is always about the mission and vision,” he reflects. “You can never lose sight of the reason you exist.”

Convening

What makes us different

When we asked David what he believes sets FNPW apart, his answer was simple. “FNPW has the ability to bring everything together. We can bring important initiatives to life and we can often turn good ideas into bigger and better ideas that result in more impact.”

That capacity to convene, connect, and amplify is something we see reflected in every partnership we hold, from Traditional Custodians and scientists to corporate supporters and on-the-ground conservation teams.

Thank you

To everyone who made it possible

David also had something he wanted to say to the donors and supporters who have backed this work.

“The first thing I would do is thank them for their support, and their care for the environment and our amazing wildlife. I would say that they support a great organisation doing important work well. Their support will be critical going forward as we look to continue our increasingly urgent work.”

We couldn’t put it better ourselves.

The people

What we’re proudest of

Beyond the milestones, what David says he’s most proud of is the people. “When I look around the boardroom table, I think we have a group of really high-calibre, experienced and committed people.”

A strong strategy and the right people to carry it forward. At our most recent AGM, David passed the role of President & Chair to Kelly O’Shanassy, and left behind an organisation well placed to meet what comes next. That’s not a bad thing to leave behind at all.

“I care about the things that drew me to FNPW in the first place, so I’ll stay involved. At the same time, I’ll create a bit more space in my life.”

David, from everyone at FNPW, our partners, our supporters, and every species this work exists to protect: thank you. It has been a privilege to do this alongside you.

items.featured_alt: A koala crossing a road at the edge of a growing suburb
items.static_title: A wildlife corridor is only as wide as its narrowest point
items.content:
At dusk in Sydney’s south-west, a koala comes down out of a grey box and starts moving. She is not lost. She is doing what her mother did, and her mother before her, following a route between habitat patches her population has used for generations. The difference is what now sits across that route: roads, fences, and the steady spread of the city. Her population is one of the most important koala populations in the country, and its future depends on whether those old routes stay open.

We count habitat loss in hectares, because hectares are easy to count. Connectivity disappears without anyone tallying it, and connectivity is what keeps a population functioning. It lets young animals find territory. It keeps gene pools mixing. It gives species somewhere to go when fire or heat makes a patch unliveable. Remove it and you do not get a smaller version of the same population. You get islands, each one quietly running down.

None of which is an argument against building houses. Sydney, Melbourne, Perth and South East Queensland all need them, and pretending otherwise loses the argument before it starts. The choice in front of us was never koalas or first home buyers. It is whether the corridor written into the plan gets bought and protected before the estate is drawn, and whether we cluster development around contiguous open space or spread it thin across the routes wildlife already uses. Same dwellings. Very different outcome. Four regions show why.

Genetics

One: the last chlamydia-free koala stronghold in the Sydney Basin

South-west Sydney holds something rare: the only koala population in the Sydney Basin still free of chlamydia, the disease that has hollowed out koala numbers across the eastern states. Surveys through 2021 and 2023 confirmed the Campbelltown koalas remain free of it. That is a genuine stronghold, and it is worth everything to protect.

The catch is that being disease-free is not the same as being safe. Research published in early 2025 by the University of Sydney found these koalas are highly inbred, with low genetic diversity, precisely because roads and cleared land have cut them off from populations further afield. A population that cannot mix cannot refresh its gene pool, and a population with a narrow gene pool is less able to adapt when a new threat, chlamydia included, arrives at its edge.

This is the quiet argument for connectivity, and it is more important than any single road crossing. Corridors are how genes move. They let young koalas disperse, find unrelated mates and keep the population resilient. Narrow the connections and you do not just make the koalas harder to see. You make them more fragile in ways that only show up a generation later. For a population like this one, the movement route is not a convenience. It is the difference between a stronghold that endures and one that slowly closes in on itself.

Melbourne

3,750 hectares: the reserve Melbourne is still assembling

In 2010, in exchange for extending Melbourne’s urban growth boundary across the volcanic plains, the Victorian Government committed to a 15,000 hectare Western Grassland Reserve. Fifteen years on, roughly a quarter of that land has been secured. Call it 3,750 hectares of a 15,000 hectare commitment, with the rest still to come.

The lag is not a lack of will so much as a hard truth about this kind of conservation: buying land at scale is slow and expensive, and every year the acquisition takes, the land it is meant to protect keeps degrading under weeds and stock. Native temperate grassland is critically endangered, with around one per cent of its original extent remaining. The reserve is meant to hold what is left, along with the growling grass frog, the striped legless lizard, the spiny riceflower and the fat-tailed dunnart. This is exactly the kind of gap philanthropy and community effort exist to help close, alongside government, rather than wait on it.

The frogs show why the timing matters. Growling grass frogs survive as metapopulations strung along wetland chains, moving pond to pond across the Werribee, Merri and Darebin systems. Break the chain with a housing estate and the frogs upstream are not inconvenienced. They are alone.

Perth

12 kilometres a day: why Perth’s corridor problem is really a food problem

That is roughly how far a male Carnaby’s black cockatoo will fly in a day to feed his mate while she sits on the nest. A useful reminder that a corridor is not only a path. It is a food supply, spread across a distance an animal can physically cover.

Carnaby’s breed in the Wheatbelt and spend most of the year feeding on Perth’s Swan Coastal Plain, in banksia woodland now reduced to around 40 per cent of its original extent and listed as endangered. The plain as a whole retains less than a third of its native vegetation. Every new estate on the northern sandplain removes another feeding stop and stretches the gap between the ones still standing. Volunteer counts have tracked steep declines in the birds using the plain.

In Perth, you can lose the corridor without clearing a single one of the remaining patches. You only have to remove enough of the stepping stones between them.

What works

22 years: the crossing that has been working since 2004

In 2004, Compton Road in Brisbane’s south was widened from two lanes to four. Rather than simply severing Karawatha Forest from the Kuraby bushlands, the upgrade included a vegetated land bridge over the road, underpasses beneath it, glider poles and a rope canopy bridge.

The overpass was planted out with local species, and by 2009 about 95 per cent of those plantings had survived. Monitoring by Griffith University and others has since recorded koalas, gliders, wallabies, echidnas, microbats, frogs and reptiles using it. It works because it was designed as a continuation of the forest rather than as an engineering afterthought, and it has been working for twenty-two years. Compton Road is proof that the science is settled and the outcome is achievable. The opportunity now is to make that standard the norm on every growth front, not the exception.

Edges

The edge is not a choice

Ask why a koala turns up in a backyard, or a wallaby on a school oval, and the honest answer is almost always that the interior it used to live in has gone, and the edge is what is left. Animals are not moving into our suburbs. Our suburbs moved onto their range, and the strip between the last house and the last tree is now the only cover, food and passage available.

Edges are hostile in ways a map never shows. Light, noise, weeds and traffic all push inward from the boundary, and so do our pets. Roaming pet cats reach densities of forty to seventy per square kilometre in Australian suburbs, killing thousands of native animals per square kilometre each year, and cats whose homes back onto bushland range into that bushland far more than cats living a few streets away.

Australia also has its own edge specialist, and it is a native bird. The noisy miner thrives in remnants with a high ratio of edge to interior, where it aggressively drives out smaller woodland birds. Its behaviour is listed as a key threatening process under national environment law, and the Commonwealth’s own abatement advice is blunt about the fix: avoid increasing the ratio of edge to interior habitat.

A narrow corridor does precisely that. It is not a thin version of a forest. It is a long piece of edge.

Bad design

The corridor that makes things worse

A corridor can be designed so poorly that it does more harm than good. Drawn too narrowly, squeezed in around everything else on a busy site, it can end up working against the animals it is meant to help. It looks like habitat. It reads as green on the plan. It draws animals in, and then it can deliver them to a four-lane road, a dog fence or a dead end. Ecologists have understood this for decades: a strip that funnels wildlife toward danger concentrates mortality rather than preventing it.

The encouraging part is that this is entirely avoidable at the design stage. It is why width and continuity are not bureaucratic detail. They are the difference between a corridor and a funnel.

Design

What separates a corridor from a green line on a plan

Width. Narrow strips are all edge, and we have just seen what edge does. Width buys interior.

Continuity. A corridor with a break in it is a dead end, and a dead end is worse than nothing. It funnels animals into traffic and backyards.

Placement. Ridgelines, creek lines and wetland chains are where animals already move. Build across them and you sever the connection, no matter how much green space the plan contains in total.

Permanence. A corridor that can be rezoned is not yet secure. Land bought and reserved outperforms land still to be acquired, every single time. Melbourne’s grasslands show why locking in permanence early, and resourcing the acquisition to match, is worth the effort.

Buffers. Undeveloped land around high-value habitat lowers the edge to interior ratio and puts distance between wildlife and the things that kill it. Cluster the houses, keep the open space contiguous, and you get fewer collisions and fewer conflicts than the same number of dwellings spread thin across the same ground. It costs a developer very little, and it is one of the easiest wins to build into a plan from the start.

None of this is expensive next to the alternative. Retrofitting connectivity into a built-out suburb costs a fortune and rarely fully works. Protecting the route before the estate is drawn costs a fraction of it.

Where we come in

Where we come in

We have spent more than fifty years doing the patient version of this work, in partnership with governments, landholders and communities: buying the land that links the parks, funding the revegetation that closes the gaps, and backing the people restoring habitat on private property in the places the growth fronts are heading next.

The Bandicoot Superhighway in South Australia’s Mount Lofty Ranges is what that looks like on the ground. Delivered with the Hills and Fleurieu Landscape Board, the Sturt Upper Reaches Landcare Group, the Nature Conservation Society of South Australia and the Australian Government, it reconnects fragmented habitat for the endangered southern brown bandicoot. In two years it restored connectivity across 216 hectares of priority habitat, put more than 34,000 native seedlings in the ground, and drew in over 900 people through planting days and workshops. Camera traps and citizen-science sightings have since confirmed the bandicoots are using the route to move, forage and survive. That is a corridor doing exactly what a corridor is for.

The science on connectivity is settled. What moves it from the plan to the ground is partnership, and the funding to buy and restore the ground before it is gone.

Which brings us back to the koala in south-west Sydney. Her stronghold will hold, or it will slowly close in around her. Either way, her daughters will need room to move and unrelated koalas to find, and the work in front of all of us is making sure the connections are still there for them.

items.featured_alt: Bushfire glowing behind silhouetted trees at night
items.static_title: Are You Ready for Bushfire Season?
items.content:
As we come into the bushfire season many people are thinking about updating their Fire Safety Plan. It’s extremely important to have a plan in place before the fire season starts so everyone in your household knows what to do, and when to do it in order to protect their lives and the lives of your animals and livestock.

Bushfire Preparedness

This includes removing debris from around your property, cleaning out the gutters, checking pumps and sprinklers systems, slashing the grass and trimming back the trees.

But how many of you know planting particular species can actually help reduce the impact of fire and contribute to our bushfire preparedness?

What is a firewise plant?

Firewise plants are plants which are tolerant or resist heat from a bushfire or are not combustible when the bushfire engulfs them. They usually do not burn when the first wave of the bushfire hits, are difficult to ignite, can give off steam, or will not produce flame or embers. These traits help to deprive the fire the fuel initially, slowing down the spread of the fire and allowing more time for people and animals to move out of the way.

Important:

No Plant is Fireproof

Everything can burn under extreme heat

Why should we be planting them?

Fully cleared and open areas allow winds to increase in speed as there is nothing in its pathway. This also helps embers spread many kilometers ahead of the fire. Planting a Green Wall of fire-wise species can help stop the embers and break up the wind pattern. Remember, ember attack is the most common way houses catch alight.

Firewise plant examples

Some examples of fire-wise plants are listed here. But the best firewise plants for your garden or farm will come from your own environment. Not sure what they are? Check in with your local native plant nursery, Landcare or Bushcare group, or local government environment officer to find out what is available in your area.

The following firewise plants examples have been kindly provided by the Lakes Entrance Community Landcare group:

  • Sea Berry Saltbush (Rhagodia candolleana),
  • Tree Hakea (Hakea eriantha),
  • Boobialla (Myoporum insulare),
  • Lilly Pilly (Acmena smithii)
  • Kidney weed (Dichondra repens)

items.featured_alt: Banksia seedlings in tubes at the Yankalilla nursery
items.static_title: Baby Banksias thrive in volunteer run nursery
items.content:
Volunteers have rallied to save a once thriving Banksia marginata population at Charleston Conservation Park in the Adelaide Hills. Devastated by the 2019 bushfires, this banksia population, once the second largest population in the Adelaide Hills has struggled to regenerate. Banksia are often killed by fire and regenerate from seed released from the burnt cones. The harsh conditions preceding the 2019 wildfire meant there was very little banksia seed set and the remnant is now struggling.

In an attempt to rescue the population, the Friends of Charleston have collected seed and plated over 20,000 banksias since 2019. This year the group have partnered with the passionate volunteers at the Fleurieu Coast Community Nursery to grow more than 2000 banksias to further bolster the population. This partnership is made possible through funding provided by the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife who generously support the project.

Recently volunteers from the Friends of Charleston Conservation Park joined forces in a working bee at the Yankalilla based nursery to pot up the valuable seedlings. With a target of 1000 baby banksias for the year everyone was thrilled to double the numbers!

The seedlings will make their way back to Charleston Conservation Park in June where they will be planted and nurtured by the Friends Group to give the population a second chance. Banksias are keystone species in that landscape where they punch far above their weight in terms of what they contribute to the local ecology. They provide nectar and seed to birds, insects and even mammals like the Yellow Footed Antechinus and Western Pygmy Possum.

Organisation National Parks and Wildlife SA

items.featured_alt: Bossiaea seedling growing in sandy soil after fire
items.content:
Braving some tough terrain, staff from the Department of Planning of Environment (DPE), Upper Shoalhaven Landcare, Threatened Species Conservancy and an independent botanist have been searching for the rare Bombay Bossiaea (Bossiaea bombayensis) in recent months.

This species, listed as Vulnerable under the NSW Biodiversity Conservation Act, is only known from a stretch of the Shoalhaven River between Warri and Bombay. After fire tore through the area in late 2019, most plants were presumed to have been killed. Because of the species’ limited distribution and the impact of the fires, Bombay Bossiaea was among a list of plants requiring urgent attention by the Commonwealth Bushfire Recovery Expert Panel in 2020.

The aim of the survey was to map surviving plants and assess the species’ recovery after fire. A few pockets managed to escape the blaze and Bossiaea plants survived. Not only that, they managed to recruit new seedlings, which have just flowered for the first time nearly three years on from the fires. Best of all, in areas where virtually all plant life was incinerated, Bombay Bossiaea seedlings have sprung up in very respectable numbers!

This tough plant is well adapted to drought and fire. It has no leaves, photosynthesising by means of flattened stems or cladodes. Its seed has a hard coat, allowing survival in the soil for extended periods. Heat from the fires cracks the seed coat, allowing the seed to take up water and germinate. Initial counts of seedlings at Bombay Reserve looked spectacular, but numbers have been slashed after several flood events. However, it appears that this tenacious localized native is here to stay, with many hundreds of regenerated plants flowering and setting seed. Many thanks to landholders who kindly allowed access to the river and the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife for grant funds.

Authors: Christine Allen, Mary Appleby and Erin Brinkley

Organisation Upper Shoalhaven Landcare Council

items.content:
The best time to plant a tree was 20 years ago. The second best time is now. With the support of the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife Bushfire Recovery Restoration Grants, Whian Whian Landcare planted the foundations for future subtropical rainforest with more that 1500 new trees in the ground including over 40 species across 3 properties. A dozen Whian Whian Landcare volunteers rolled up their sleeves and made the best of the tail end of La Nina for planting. Trees are protected through their infancy with mulch and guards and will be tended with watering through the drier season to come. Looking forward to enjoying the shade of these trees in 20 years time!

items.featured_alt: Swamp wallaby standing in long grass
items.content:
A government adviser said not to use tree-guards in our revegetation; we had de-stocked and rabbits, hares or wallabies would graze on kikuyu, not seedlings. We planted 100 tubes with care, but without tree-guards. It was soon obvious the seedlings were being munched to the ground and most were killed. Red-necked and swamp wallabies were eating trees as fast as we could plant them.

We had wrongly viewed wallabies as grazers, not browsers. In fact, they feed on the foliage and young bark of a wide range of trees and bushes. We first tried plastic tubes around hardwood stakes; they were torn down immediately saplings became visible. When we electrically fenced the home paddock, the shocks merely made wallabies push through harder. So we fenced the paddock with ringlock, adding a one-way exclusion trap, which reduced their numbers. But eventually a panicked animal forced his way through the ringlock, teaching others how to do so. It was three years before one brave animal cleared the cattle grid; now many do it.

Rabbit netting tubes on hardwood stakes were heavy, expensive and time-consuming, and tree roots and branches, plus kikuyu runners, resisted removal. Instead, we stapled corflute to the stakes; these were moderately effective, but blocked light and air-flow and degraded quickly.

At last, we have an effective, economical approach that resists damage (photo). Three 17 mm x 1.5 m hardwood stakes are clothed in 1 m x 0.9 m of scaffolding cloth. Staples attach the cloth top and bottom to each stake. Occasionally, a wallaby reaching up to a tasty shoot pulls down the cloth, but it rarely kills the tree. The mesh allows air movement, and most of the necessary red light passes through. The system is relatively inexpensive and lasts for many years.

Organisation Rifflerun
