items.featured_alt: Australian native bushland and garden vegetation in summer.
items.static_title: Planning for Fire Season Starts in the Garden
items.content:
As the Australia summer heat starts to build, so does the risk of bushfire, not just in remote forested areas, but around homes, properties and in our wider communities. At the same time, this is a powerful moment for community togetherness, land healing and supporting our native landscapes to recover and thrive. We can work hand-in-hand: preparing our homes, supporting our neighbours, restoring our land.

In this blog we explore:

  • Why native plants matter in bushfire prevention and land-healing
  • What you can do at home or as a neighbourhood to make your place safer
  • How the Fire Wise Project and the Fire Wise Learning Hub offer resources and tools for action
The science

Why Native Plants & Smart Vegetation Matter

It’s tempting to think that bare ground or removing all vegetation is the safest route when fires loom. But fire science tells us a more nuanced story. Planting native vegetation with the right spacing and plant-types can actually help slow fires and save lives.

Here are a few key scientific points:

  • Fires move fastest through fine dry fuels like grasses and exposed ground litter, especially when driven by wind.
  • A moderately dense canopy of native trees/shrubs can provide shade, maintain moist soil, reduce local wind speeds and offer a barrier to ember attack and radiant heat.
  • After a bushfire, the ecosystem goes through stages of recovery: first colonised by short-lived species that protect soil and provide shelter, then gradually more mature vegetation returns.
  • Native vegetation isn’t inherently a fire hazard; in fact, with the right design and management, it supports both biodiversity and resilience.

So when we think about preparing for summer and restoring our land, the message is: don’t just clear everything, think about strategic planting, nurturing native plants, and working as a community.

At home

What You Can Do at Home

Here’s a checklist of practical steps you (and your neighbours/community) can take. Adapt them to your context, climate and local native plant list.

Secure your property and create defensible space

  • Remove or regularly clear fine fuels: dry leaves, grass clippings, bark mulch near buildings.
  • Keep shrubs and trees spaced so fire doesn’t readily climb from ground to canopy.
  • Prune lower branches of trees to reduce ladder fuels.
  • Ensure your house/garden access is clear for fire-engine access and evacuation if required.
  • Make sure your emergency plan is up to date, and your household knows it.

Use native plants (and the right ones!)

  • Choose native plants with lower flammability and plant them in the right locations. The Fire Wise project emphasises the strategic use of native vegetation rather than wholesale clearing.
  • Use design logic: e.g., waterwise, shade-keeping, windbreaks.
  • Maintain your plantings: keep them healthy, irrigated (where appropriate), remove dead material.
  • Consider ground-covers that hold moisture and reduce fine fuels.

Community and neighbourhood involvement

  • Talk with your neighbours: a bushfire-safe community is a connected, informed one. Share ideas, join planting days, form local groups.
  • Host or attend community native-planting days: these build local ecosystem resilience and social cohesion.
  • Visit, support or volunteer at local seed banks (native seeds) or community nurseries to grow local plants for fire-wise landscaping.
  • Share resources and knowledge from the Learning Hub (see below) so everyone is on the same page.

After a fire or during recovery

  • Monitor the site: photograph and revisit. Drops in vegetation or structure need attention.
  • Control invasive species quickly – they can outcompete native seedlings and create new fuel loads.
  • Re-plant missing or keystone native species if natural regeneration isn’t sufficient.
  • Consider cultural burning or Indigenous-led practices if your local context allows, honouring Country and traditional knowledge.
Working together

The Science + The Community: How They Connect

At its heart, fire-prevention and land-healing is both science (fire behaviour, ecology, vegetation management) and community care (neighbours, planting, shared land, Indigenous knowledge). Bridging these gives us real resilience.

For instance: the Fire Wise theory highlights three key fire risks: radiant heat, wind speed and ember attack. By planting the right natives, spaced and maintained, communities can reduce those risks: shade keeps ground moist, trees deflect wind/embers, and healthy vegetation slows flame spread. It’s a simple concept, but when executed across many properties in a neighbourhood, the effect multiplies.

And when a community plants together, shares seeds and knowledge, the social fabric becomes stronger. People know each other, share responsibilities, look out for each other, and that’s another layer of fire safety.

Go deeper

Resources & Links: Dive Deeper

Here are some top resources to help you, your neighbourhood or your organisation get started:

  • Fire Wise Learning Hub – Explore their learning resources, project case-studies and plant lists. Visit: https://firewisehub.online/
  • Fire Wise Resources page – https://firewisehub.online/resources/
  • FNPW Fire Wise Project – https://fnpw.org.au/project/fire-wise/ – gives project overview, science-background, how you can get involved.
  • Helping the Bush Recover (by Trust for Nature) – Good reading on ecological recovery, timing and weed control. trustfornature.org.au
  • Practical plant lists & fire-wise landscaping reports (e.g., The Crossing Land’s NSW report) thecrossingland.org.au

Tip: Bookmark those URLs, share them in your community newsletter or local social-media group, perhaps even organise a “bushfire-safe native planting” morning.

What's at stake

Why It Matters And What’s At Stake

When we don’t act, the stakes are high: the 2019-20 “Black Summer” fires illustrated how ecosystems, homes and communities can be devastated. Recovery takes years, biodiversity suffers, and our native species and cultural heritage are under threat.

But when we do act:

  • Homes become safer
  • Landscapes become more resilient
  • Biodiversity is supported
  • Communities become stronger, connected, proactive

And importantly: embracing native species and thoughtful vegetation means we’re healing our land, not just defending it.

This summer, let’s come together: behind our fences, in our streets, in our neighbourhoods. Let’s plant with purpose, look after our native landscapes, and support each other. Fire preparedness it’s about smart design, native planting, shared knowledge and community care.

items.featured_alt: Smiling volunteer beside a young acacia at the Burra planting site
items.static_title: Planting parties key to success on small properties
items.content:
In a family first, on the morning of Sunday 22 of May, Burra landholders Rachel Clarke and Lee Georgeson hosted neighbours, friends and family for their first ever planting party.

The trees and shrubs were provided through a partnership between Royalla Landcare Habitat & Wildlife Recovery Project supported by Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife with Greening Australia Bushfire Recovery Nursery with over 34,000 trees planted between Bredbo, Michelago , Burra & Royalla. The project was ambitious for small landholders – with a minimum allocation of 500 plants in tree lines or stepping stones of at least 20m wide.

Rachel was initially surprised by the number of trees.

“We have done a few plantings before, but no more than 200 trees. When we heard the minimum was 500, it became clear that we would need some help if we wanted to be part of the project. In the end we had about 25 or 30 people come to help us plant.  I was so surprised and delighted that so many people were happy to slave away on a Sunday morning, but it was a stunning day and everyone loved it! The kids had a ball, as well.”

“Another planting party was in progress in nearby Michelago on the Saturday. Belinda Sierzchula, of Michelago Landcare received 600 trees under the program. A last-minute call on the day yielded 28 locals, friends and family members keen to plant.”

“We were a bit disorganised – we just put a call out on Facebook on the Saturday morning and were so happy that people showed up. We had a barbecue and bonfire when we had finished – it turned out to be a great day,” Belinda said.

Royalla Landcare Chair and project organiser and champion Maryke Booth said that many people on small holdings don’t realise how much they can do.

“We allocate 410 plants (140 trees 270 Shrubs ) per acre in the project, so even if you are only on ten acres you can plant between 2000-4000. It all helps in restoring habitat and creating connections between different patches of vegetation. People have been extremely keen to participate – we had 34 landholders participate in this project on some 100 acres planting some 34,000 of trees & Shrubs.”

Apart from wanting to help restore the local Yellow Box woodland, there were social benefits from the plantings, Rachel said.

“With so many events and gatherings being cancelled with Covid it was really wonderful to get people together again- and in an outdoor environment that felt really safe. It was a lovely Autumn day and it felt healing – with so many trees and so much bushland destroyed in the fires, it was wonderful to be able to feel like we are doing something to try and help.”

Both Maryke and Rachel commented that small landholders have to be part of the solution to both climate change and biodiversity loss.

Small property owners have a role to play here. We live in heavily cleared environments, but most people don’t rely on the land for income, so they have more options for restoring their on-farm vegetation. We all drive cars and have impacts on our local environment, but this project shows we can have a positive impact, too.” Maryke said. Rachel agreed. One day I’d love to look out my window and see every hillside in the Burra region covered in trees like they should be– it’s my dream.”

Rachel Clarke

items.content:
Local volunteers, community groups, Council, and the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife (FNPW) have come together to support a revegetation program to boost biodiversity, increase habitat for local fauna and create linkages between important biodiversity spots from Mount Barker Summit down to the Laratinga Wetlands.

Over the last 12 months, 300 volunteers have planted and maintained 3500 native seedlings across three areas of 2 hectares each.

The newly established native plants are improving soil health, enhancing biodiversity, increasing wildlife habitat and reducing invasive weeds.

You can continue the effort and register for Planet Ark’s National Tree Day with a planting at Anembo Park on Sunday 30 July. Sign up at https://treeday.planetark.org/site/10027996

items.featured_alt: Eucalypt bushland in early morning light.
items.content:
Step onto a bush trail at daybreak and you expect the trees to burst with life. Yet across Australia the once bright chorus is fading to a hush. From rainforest canopies to inland salt-marsh, more than 2 000 native species now stand on a cliff edge. 

Many of the voices and colours that once defined our landscapes are fading fast. In this blog, we’ll explore why, spotlight the threatened species in Australia most at risk, and share the hopeful ground-level work already giving them a path back from the brink.

The stakes

Why losing Australia’s threatened species hurts us all

Healthy ecosystems quietly keep life humming, often in ways we notice only when something goes wrong:

  • Pollination and seed dispersal: birds such as the Regent Honeyeater and mammals like the Grey-headed Flying-fox move pollen and seeds across huge distances, supporting crops and regenerating bushland.
  • Clean water: Murray–Darling river turtles stir sediments, cycle nutrients and keep wetlands clear.
  • Rich soil: Southern Brown Bandicoots turn over several tonnes of soil each year while foraging, aerating soil and helping leaf litter break down.

When these “ecosystem engineers” vanish, services worth billions in agriculture, tourism and disaster resilience begin to unravel.

The numbers

Snapshot of a crisis we can still avert

Here’s why urgency matters:

  • More than 2,000 native species already sit on state or national threatened-species lists.
  • Koala numbers have fallen by over 50 percent in just two decades.
  • In parts of the Murray–Darling Basin, nine out of ten river-turtle nests are destroyed each breeding season.
  • The Regent Honeyeater counts fewer than 300 wild birds, while the Orange-bellied Parrot is down to double digits.

Unless we act swiftly, lifelines for many species will close within our lifetime.

On the edge

Meet the species on the edge

Woodland singers and night gardeners

Regent Honeyeater, Swift Parrot, Orange-bellied Parrot and Grey-headed Flying-fox are vital pollinators and seed couriers, but shrinking old-growth eucalypt woodlands and coastal salt-marsh put them between Endangered and Critically Endangered.

Fresh-water guardians

The Murray Short-Necked Turtle has cruised Australian rivers for sixty million years. Today, egg-raiding foxes, hotter summers and flash floods have wiped out up to 90 percent of some local populations.

Rocky refuges and grassy scrubs

Brush-tailed Rock-wallaby, Southern Brown Bandicoot and Greater Bilby cling to isolated strongholds, challenged by feral predators and shrinking habitat corridors.

Icon in the treetops

The beloved Koala is now missing from half of its historic range as land clearing, disease and hotter bushfires take their toll.

Plants we can’t afford to lose

It’s not only animals that are at risk of extinction; rare plants underpin entire food webs.

  • Kangaroo Island Spider Orchid (Caladenia ovata): a barometer of healthy, species-rich woodlands. After farmland expansion and altered fire patterns, FNPW and local partners are rebuilding the understorey on Kangaroo Island and the Fleurieu Peninsula to help this orchid rebound.
  • Davidson’s Plum (Davidsonia jerseyana): a nutrient-dense rainforest fruit that feeds birds and supports First Nations enterprises. Northern Rivers nurseries now raise thousands of seedlings for restored creek-line corridors.
  • Small Purple-pea (Swainsona recta): a bright wildflower that enriches box-gum woodlands by fixing nitrogen. FNPW nurseries in NSW and Victoria propagate plants for return to newly restored woodland plots.

When these keystone plants disappear, everything from pollinating insects to seed-dispersing birds feels the loss.

Our work

How we’re turning urgency into action

At FNPW, we’re working alongside Traditional Owners, researchers, volunteers and local communities to restore habitat, protect nests and rebuild wildlife corridors that can turn the numbers of Australia’s threatened species around.

Landscape Resilience Program

Thirty community nurseries across four states have produced more than 1 000 000 locally adapted seedlings since 2020, restoring 2 500 ha and reconnecting fragmented corridors rebuild salt-marsh and re-green fire-scarred country, exactly where birds, bats and marsupials need them. With the one millionth tree planted in October 2024, the program now scales toward 8 million trees by 2030. 

Saving our Species

  • 1 Million Turtles: Nest guards, wetland repair and hatchling releases lift survival from 10 % in the wild to near 100 % in protected sites.
  • Nectar Sippers: Flowering eucalypts planted as “stepping-stones” give Regent Honeyeaters and Swift Parrots safe refuelling stops.
  • Bandicoot Superhighway: In South Australia’s Mt Lofty Ranges, 34 600 native seedlings and habitat works have triggered 110 new Bandicoot sightings in 2023 alone.

Conservation Grants and First Nations Partnerships

In the Kimberley, Aboriginal rangers from seven language groups use cool patch burning and detailed burrow mapping to protect Greater Bilbies, combining traditional knowledge with modern science.

Fire Wise and Climate Resilience

Since the Black Summer fires, FNPW supporters have helped plant the one-millionth tree for burnt landscapes and restore 2,500 hectares of habitat. 12 nurseries are now growing low-flammability species, and more than 100 landholder workshops now share proven techniques that lower fire risk while boosting biodiversity.

Signs of recovery

Proof that hope is justified

Recovery is real.

  • Turtles back in the water: school-incubated hatchlings now thrive in revitalised wetlands. 
  • Birdsong returning: new eucalypts in the South-East Woodlands attracted Regent Honeyeaters within just two flowering seasons.
  • Bilbies on camera: motion-sensor footage shows Bilbies foraging in freshly managed country where cultural burns revived food and shelter.

These successes are milestones that prove wildlife rebounds quickly when we give nature a hand.

How to help

How you can help

Volunteer locally

Join tree-planting days, beach clean-ups or citizen-science surveys through our corporate volunteering program.

Give a Gift

Your one-time donation helps drive real, on-the-ground conservation, supporting urgent action for priority projects.

Become a monthly donor 

Join Habitat Heroes – a passionate community of monthly givers protecting wildlife all year round.

We put 78% of every dollar straight into field projects, not administration.

  • $50 plants a tray of native seedlings to rebuild lost habitat.
  • $100 restores critical woodland or wetland.
  • $200 funds nest boxes, predator control or Traditional Owner surveys.

A future worth fighting for

Envision a dawn where the chorus is strong, rivers run clear and bright wildflowers blanket the ground, an Australia where threatened species not only survive but thrive. By understanding the challenges, celebrating progress and supporting practical on-ground work, we can turn that vision into reality.

items.featured_alt: Man planting a young tree on cleared ground
items.content:
The 2019/2020 bushfires had a devastating impact on already dwindling populations of koalas in the Tenterfield district and Quoll Headquarters. A 160 Ha exclusion fenced nature reserve has been planned to help koala recovery and reverse the decline with a multi-faceted facility dedicated to the recovery of Koalas. With grant support from the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife, we have completed a pre-release rehabilitation enclosure for orphaned and injured koalas and also a koala food tree plantation.

Enclosure to help Koala recovery 

The 8 hectare pre-release enclosure is prime New England koala habitat of tall, old growth eucalypts now surrounded by a predator proof fence. This area will be utilised for the transition of both orphaned joeys and also recovering sick and injured koalas from a wildlife carer environment to a natural but predator proof ecosystem with all the requirements they need for further rehabilitation before release. The enclosure will provide a vital step to getting koalas back into the wild.

New koala food tree plantation 

Our new koala food tree plantation will also be crucial in the care and rehabilitation of the species. This plantation of endemic koala food trees, chosen by local botanist Sarah Caldwell, will be maintained for maximum leaf production and available for all koalas in care throughout the district.

With the help of our dedicated volunteers we have completed the project and we are working with local wildlife carers to give them the facilities they need to get koalas in their care rehabilitated and ready for release back into the wild.

This project will make a real positive and lasting impact on koala recovery in the New England district.

About the Quoll Headquarters

Quoll Headquarters Mission statement is ‘Protect, preserve and educate, creating a future for Australians threatened species whilst providing an educational facility for the public to understand, appreciate and learn about our unique wildlife’.

Thanks to the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife the New England district now has the facilities to care for and rehabilitate our precious koalas in the event of future catastrophic bushfires.

Steve Haslam
Founder of Quoll Headquarters

Our rewilding project has been a great success, achieving an impressive seedling success rate of around 95%.

This accomplishment was made possible by strategically planting during the wet seasons of the previous year. This approach ensured that the foundational tree roots could establish themselves strongly, enabling them to better endure drier conditions in the future. The main goal of this effort was to introduce approximately 2500 native plant species into the area. These species include Forest Red Gum, Coastal Banksia, Forest Oak, Grey Gum, and Creek Lilly Pilly, all of which contribute to the ecological diversity and health of the region.

This grant from the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife has made a significant impact as planting has now begun to flower, attracting many of the native birds and wildlife back onto the property.

items.featured_alt: Blue tree guards protecting new plantings in a grassy paddock
items.content:
At our Rifflerun site we propagated and planted 1000 seedlings with the aim to re-establish the native forest canopy on 37Ha of old farming country.

Approximately 40 native tree species expanded the site’s dry-rainforest community, together with species adapted to the riparian corridor and floodplain, and upland areas dominated by Eucalypts.

We recently held a final tree-planting effort last week, with replanting of the flood-damaged riparian and floodplain areas. Another 100 trees from six native species were added to the previous plantings, adding to survivors from the severe 2021 and 2022 floods

Weed control with herbicides, fertilisers, and mulching was used to ensure seedling establishment and growth. Browsing impacts of wallabies were managed with tree-guards based on a previously tested design using scaffolding cloth stapled to hardwood posts.

Alongside planting we cleared a lot of invasive weeds, notably lantana, castor-oil plant, tobacco bush, privet, tree of heaven, Johnson grass, wild turnip, Tradescantia, balloon vine, prickly pear, and Enredera. This involved spraying, tractor removal, and hand-pulling.

This project has seen revegetation increase local habitat availability for biota affected by bushfires and strengthened regional habitat linkages.

Revegetation work will continue in future, with application of both weed control and planting.

OrganisationJohn Hamlyn Harris

items.featured_alt: Rows of tree guards across a regenerating paddock beside a fallen log
items.static_title: Royalla Landcare Conservation Area Restoration Project
items.content:
Restoration Project – Royalla Landcare Planting

It’s been two months since we held a planting day on a Conservation property in Royalla. On the day we showcased planting techniques using an Electric auger & Hamilton tree planter.

With the ground being so wet the Hamilton tree planter came to the fore with the auger only used on slopes where the ground was harder. The electric auger was really great so much quieter than petrol ones & just as effective.

We also learnt that using a large bamboo 20mm stake instead of a hardwood stake more than halved the time to put them together. And no splinters or sore arms! Combined with a narrower bamboo stake put through the other two sides from top to bottom will stop them spinning & blowing away. To-date they are working really well with a biodegradable cardboard guard.
Altogether much more environmentally friendly solution !

We didn’t rip deciding not to plant in rows & adopted a more natural approach. We planted in groups & some thickets of same the species. Creating a series of stepping stones leaving the grasslands untouched in-between.

Over the week we got 2500 tubestock in mostly wattles to provide that all important understory layer which was missing due to grazing whilst a sheep property. The understory planted will provide valuable habitat for small nesting birds, an important food source for the sugar gliders & pollen for many native bees & nectar eaters. Providing a healthy balance in the Box Gum Grassy Woodland.

We would like to thank Greening Australia & Foundation of National Parks & Wildlife for their generous support in providing grants to enable this project, James Suthern & his team of planters and volunteers on the demonstration planting day.

For more information or to join Royalla Landcare email royallalandcare@gmail.com

items.featured_alt: A student holding a freshwater turtle hatchling at the wetland edge.
items.static_title: Students release turtle hatchlings in a conservation first
items.content:
It starts with curious minds, a walk to the wetlands, and a turtle in hand.

On Tuesday morning, students from Presbyterian Ladies’ College (PLC) Sydney gathered under the late-summer sun at Oatlands Golf Course to release eastern long-necked turtle hatchlings into the wild: hatchlings they had incubated, monitored, and cared for over the past five weeks.

This was no ordinary field trip. It was the culmination of months of learning, nurturing, and hands-on science. But more importantly, it marked a real-world environmental impact: where science class became species recovery, and students became conservationists.

The event is part of Turtles in Schools, a national education and conservation program supported by the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife (FNPW) and delivered through the 1 Million Turtles Project, led by Professor Ricky Spencer of Western Sydney University. A long-time champion of citizen science and student-led conservation, Professor Spencer has helped shape programs that turn local communities into active conservation partners.

A Species in Decline

Freshwater turtles across Australia are disappearing, largely unnoticed. In some regions, their populations have collapsed by over 90%. Foxes destroy most nests. Wetland habitat is vanishing. Climate change and disease are adding pressure.

These animals are far from ornamental. They recycle nutrients, control algae, and help keep rivers clean. When turtles decline, the health of our wetlands begins to break down.

A Classroom That Changes Everything

In November, PLC students worked alongside scientists and Oatlands Golf Course staff to relocate two vulnerable clutches of turtle eggs. The eggs were incubated in a simple, school-based setup, maintained daily by students. The goal: protect them from predation and give them the best chance at survival. Five weeks later, every egg hatched.

On release day, students gently returned the hatchlings, now bright-eyed, alert, and strong, to the wetland where they were originally found.

Professor Spencer called it “education at its most powerful.”

“It’s a great opportunity for schools to demonstrate that they can be a major part of conservation outcomes.” Said Professor Spencer. “It’s a combination of community conservation in action. This is the first school that’s ever done this and really doing what zoos and wildlife parks do: raising turtles from eggs to this release point as hatchlings”.

Turtles in Schools works because it turns abstract environmental issues into something tangible and personal. Students aren’t just learning, they’re contributing to real species recovery.

CEO of the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife, Ian Darbyshire, said “What we’re hoping is this is the first of many, many, many future releases where we create a sustainable program of protecting the turtles of the Murray-Darling Basin by getting schools to do this every year forever, so that we can protect the population of turtles.”

He added, “The turtles were laid on the floating islands that Ricky Spencer has created in part of the sponsorship with the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife.”

More schools are now introducing “hatchling hubs” into their classrooms, where students incubate eggs, monitor local wetlands, test water quality, and log turtle sightings through the national TurtleSAT platform.

A National Effort with Real Impact

Turtles in Schools is one part of the broader 1 Million Turtles Project, a national collaboration uniting researchers, educators, governments, and communities.

Partners include:

  • Leading universities: Western Sydney, La Trobe, Sydney, Murdoch, New England, and Ohio University
  • Conservation groups: FNPW, Aussie Ark, WIRES, and Turtle Rescues NSW
  • Government agencies and local councils
  • Schools and community groups, beginning with the pioneering efforts of PLC Sydney

A Scalable Model for the Future

At FNPW, we believe conservation is most effective when it’s hands-on, local, and connected to the next generation. Young people, with the right support, can lead real environmental change.

Every turtle released this week was one that wouldn’t have survived without intervention. And every student involved walked away with a deeper understanding of nature, and their power to protect it.

Turtles in Schools is more than a classroom initiative. It’s a scalable, national model for conservation education. And it’s proof that the next generation doesn’t have to wait to make a difference: they’re already leading it.

Discover more projects like this one and explore how you can be part of protecting Australia’s wildlife. Contact us.

items.featured_alt: Forested valleys and ridges under a hazy sky
items.static_title: Three key takeaways for mitigating the effects of environmental change on Australia’s fragile ecosystem
items.content:
Australia’s unique ecosystem has shown remarkable resilience over time yet is now facing unprecedented challenges due to the persistent impact of human-induced environmental change. Catastrophic natural disasters, such as devastating floods, damaging cyclones, record-breaking droughts, and raging bushfires, have become increasingly frequent, causing widespread damage to the country’s valuable natural resources.

Despite the urgency of the situation, there is still hope. Taking swift action can make a difference and help prevent reaching the point of no return in halting the detrimental effects of environmental change.

In our latest eBook, Mitigating the effects of environmental change on Australia’s fragile ecosystem, the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife (FNPW) discuss how we can help change the course of environmental change.

Download now:
Mitigating the effects of environmental change on Australia’s fragile ecosystem. How to take action now for the future

Key takeaway #1: Prioritise a whole-of-system approach
Protecting and restoring biodiversity is crucial to ensure that appropriate species thrive in their natural habitats. The relationships between fauna and biodiversity values are vital in preserving ecological balance. To sustain Australia’s fragile ecosystems, it is essential to protect and preserve native trees and plants that sequester carbon and help reduce the impact of environmental change.

What governments and organisations can do
To effectively mitigate the impacts of environmental change, it’s vital to adopt a whole-of-system approach that involves all stakeholders, including governments, businesses, non-government organisations (NGOs), Indigenous communities, and individuals. The invaluable knowledge and practices of First Nations peoples who have been working with the Australian landscape sustainably for tens of thousands of years can provide essential guidance and a framework for how Australia can contribute to a more sustainable future.

Recommendations:

  1. Prioritise collaboration and effective coordination among all stakeholders, including Indigenous communities, grassroots movements, governments, businesses, NGOs and individuals.
    2. Identify and engage organisations that can coordinate efforts among all involved parties.
    3. Work together to best position all relevant stakeholders to facilitate necessary change and achieve on-the-ground outcomes.

Key takeaway #2: Coordinate funding and resourcing for projects
Environmental change creates a harmful cycle, where each event exacerbates the other. It also poses a challenge to environmentalists’ work, as floods and fires can make sites inaccessible or too sensitive for new vegetation. This hinders efforts to mitigate the impacts of future natural disasters and to grow species with fire tolerance.

What governments and organisations can do
Volunteers and community organisations are making a difference; however, they face limitations in terms of numbers, availability, funding, and resources. Scaling their efforts to significantly impact the rate and scale of environmental change can be challenging.

Recommendations:

  1. Collaborate with stakeholders to coordinate funding and resources for environmental projects.
    2. Encourage organisations that facilitate coordination to take a more active role in coordinating funding and resources.
    3. Prioritise projects that have the potential to scale their impact with additional funding and resources.

Key takeaway #3: Establish short-term and long-term goals
Maintaining healthy vegetation and animal habitats requires effective connectivity. However, as environmental changes continue to persist, animals may need to relocate in search of suitable habitats, which can limit their ability to spread natural resources and vegetation.

What governments and organisations can do
Governments and organisations are taking steps to establish and meet long-term sustainability goals, including setting carbon emissions reduction targets and investing in more sustainable practices. While achieving carbon zero by 2050 is an essential goal, it’s important not to overlook the importance of what’s required right now, as well as offering directions to future generations. This includes acknowledging and incorporating the valuable knowledge and practices of Indigenous communities as well as committing to Healthy Country Planning with First Nations peoples to care for Country and the land, water, resources, and culture on which First Nations people depend on.

Recommendations:

  1. Prioritise setting and meeting short-term sustainability goals in addition to long-term goals and consider setting targets beyond current lifetimes to ensure the sustainability of the planet for future generations.
    2. Invest in research and development to find innovative and sustainable solutions.
    3. Prioritise transparency and accountability, regularly monitoring and reporting progress toward sustainability goals.

Take action today to create a brighter future
Don’t wait to take action – download the eBook today and discover how you can make a meaningful and proactive contribution to creating a brighter future for Australia’s ecosystem.

For more information on how environmental organisations, such as the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife (FNPW), can help governments and businesses make a more substantial contribution to environmental protection and sustainability, contact the team today.

items.featured_alt: Volunteers planting tree guards across a hillside
items.static_title: The number almost no one publishes
items.content:
There is a statistic almost every environmental campaign reports, and almost none of them follow up on:

Trees planted.

It is an easy number to produce and a difficult one to stand behind, because a tree planted is not the same as a tree that lived. Survival depends on species selection, on soil, on the season, on whether anyone came back to check. Across the restoration sector, the gap between the number announced and the number still standing five years later is rarely published, because it is rarely known.

That gap is the reason we have partnered with veritree.

What the partnership commits to

Together we are planting and verifying 100,000 native trees across Australia.

Thirty thousand of those will go into two Victorian restoration sites: the Yarra Valley, in partnership with Yarra Ranges Council, and South Gippsland, in partnership with the Nerrena/Tarwin Valley Landcare Group. The remaining 70,000 will restore Hindmarsh Valley in South Australia.

Planting has already begun. On Friday 31 July, more than 1,000 native trees went into the ground at Black Spur Creek in South Gippsland. The following day, Saturday 1 August, another 2,000 were planted at Woori Yallock in the Yarra Valley, alongside volunteers, Yarra Ranges Council staff and a visiting team from veritree.

Why verification is the point

veritree is a nature-technology platform that funds and verifies restoration. It uses field data and satellite monitoring to confirm that trees are not only planted but growing, and it has verified more than 182 million trees for over 300 organisations worldwide.

Every planting session under this partnership goes through veritree's three-level verification process. That changes what we are able to tell you. Instead of a single announcement number, we can report on how these sites are actually recovering, year by year.

It also changes the incentives on the ground. When survival is measured rather than assumed, species selection and site preparation stop being details and start being the whole job.

For a partner funding restoration, it is the difference between a contribution and an investment with a return you can see.

What 92% looks like

The Yarra Valley planting site is a good illustration, because the survival data already exists.

The Yarra Valley Biolink Project is a council-led restoration program along the Yarra Valley Trail at Woori Yallock, a council-managed wildlife corridor beside the Birrarung. Yarra Ranges Council has grown it from 9,000 plants in 2021 to around 70,000 native plants in 2025, and has achieved a 92% survival rate across that work.

Ninety-two per cent is an unusual number to see published. Most restoration programs cannot report it because they never measured it. Yarra Ranges Council can, and it is the single strongest reason this was a site worth backing.

The corridor is being revegetated to restore connectivity for native flora and fauna, with priority given to habitat that supports Koalas, Gang-gang Cockatoos, Powerful Owls and Greater Gliders. It has also become a genuine community asset, engaging 25 schools and more than 1,000 students, nine university placement students and nine environmental and community groups, with ongoing partnerships across Upper Yarra schools and Deakin University.

The 2,000 trees planted on 1 August form part of a 15,000-tree commitment for that site.

We acknowledge the Wurundjeri people, of the Woiwurrung language group of the Kulin Nation, as Traditional Owners of the Yarra Valley. Their connection to this land and to the Birrarung goes back tens of thousands of years.

Three landscapes, three different jobs

The Yarra Valley is a connectivity project. The Biolink restores a continuous corridor of native vegetation along the Birrarung so that wildlife can move safely through a landscape that has been opened up. Yarra Ranges Council leads the ecological design.

South Gippsland focuses on wetland restoration. The Black Spur Creek Wetlands Project is restoring around 60 hectares of high-value wetland at the confluence of the Tarwin River and Black Spur Creek, in the Tarwin River Catchment. It is critical habitat for the Strzelecki Koala, the Southern Brown Bandicoot, the River Blackfish and the critically endangered Slender Tree Fern. The Nerrena/Tarwin Valley Landcare Group has established more than 45,000 native plants there since 2016, replacing invasive weeds with local species. Our partnership builds on work that was already nine years underway.

We acknowledge the Gunaikurnai and Bunurong peoples as Traditional Owners of South Gippsland, represented by the Gunaikurnai Land and Waters Aboriginal Corporation and the Bunurong Land Council Aboriginal Corporation.

Hindmarsh Valley in South Australia is the largest of the three at 70,000 trees. It sits in the Hindmarsh River catchment on the Fleurieu Peninsula, where the southern Mount Lofty Ranges fall away toward Victor Harbor. Much of the valley is farmland today, and this planting will bring native vegetation back into the catchment, creating habitat that local wildlife can return to and move through.

The part that doesn't scale

Funding moves quickly. Ecological knowledge does not.

Every one of these sites depends on people who were already there. Council ecologists who know which species belongs on which slope. Landcare volunteers who have spent nine years building relationships with local landholders. Students who have been planting the same corridor since primary school.

We have spent over 55 years supporting exactly this kind of local work, and the pattern is consistent. Projects succeed where local commitment already exists. Our role is to remove the funding constraint, not to replace the expertise.

What happens next

The first 3,000 trees are in the ground, and there are many more to come across all three landscapes. We'll keep sharing what we see as these sites grow, from the Birrarung to the Fleurieu.

There are many environmental, social and economic benefits from planting native vegetation and rehabilitating natural areas. However, the success of revegetation projects is dependent on many factors and requires planning, site preparation, weed control, good planting technique, and a proper watering regime. The weather also has an effect on seedling survival.

While we cannot control the weather, we can help the success rate of plants by proper site preparation and follow up maintenance.

From May to July last year, and thanks to a $15,000 grant from the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife, council staff, local volunteer and community groups have successfully planted and cared for about 3,500 native seedlings around Laratinga Wetland with a 95 percent survival rate.

The new native plants are thriving with the added love, and will enhance biodiversity, increase habitat, reduce weeds, and provide vital wildlife corridors.

items.content:
The Upper Shoalhaven Landcare district was hit by the North Black Range and Currawan bushfires in the summer of 2019/20. Over 250,000ha was burnt in the region, with recent repeat floods causing even more damaged and biodiversity loss.

To help the network recover, the Upper Shoalhaven Landcare Council successfully sourced 2650 trees, shrubs and ground covers for Landcarers across the district. Over 92 volunteers, across 22 sites chipped in to help plant tubestock, including members of Bombay, Bungendore, Windellama, and Upper Deua Catchment Landcare.

A special focus of the project was learning how to conserve and create habitat for Glossy Black Cockatoos (Calyptorhynchus lathami). Feeding almost exclusively on she-oaks or Allocasuarina trees, this Vulnerable species requires large-scale revegetation efforts to restore habitat lost to ongoing natural disasters. Our project sourced 600 she-oaks and valuable revegetation advice from FNPW’s Greening Australia nursery in Canberra – an organization which has spent over 11 years studying and restoring Glossy habitat across the region.

Ultimately, the Trees for Fire Affected Landcarers was a success, with many happy planters across the district.

The Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife supported this project with a grant for $5,000.

items.featured_alt: Planted tree guards on a grassy slope beside a farm dam
items.content:
On a property in McCullys Gap the local Landcare have been involved in planting trees as a part of a process of restoring a wetland. The majority of the edge of several existing farm dams have been fenced off and these areas have been planted with a mix of eucalypts and understorey natives.

This is one stage of a larger plan involving returning parts of the gully to a swamp like character that was lost when the area was ‘cleaned up’ about 70 years ago. Low barriers are under construction to slow the movement of water and plants like lomandra have been planted.

In a second project, an extension has been planted to an existing tree lot that was created as a wildlife stepping stone (or corridor). A 600 m long tree lot which was planted in stages in 2015, has now been extended by another 250 metres.

So far 200 trees have been planted and another 150 will be planted by the completion of this project, once the final section of drip irrigation is installed. This has now increased the planting on this property 3.5 to 5 Ha.

OrganisationMcCullys Gap Landcare

items.featured_alt: Row of native seedlings silhouetted against soft green light
items.content:
With support from the FNPWS and FRRR we are working on our project “Youngman Creek Watershed Rehabititation”. We had a great day on Tuesday June 14th, planting trees in the Youngman Creek rehabilitation corridor. About 30 of us met and yarned about what’s going on at Namabunda. We cleared another 300 square metres of degraded creek line and created a rehabilitation area with an initial planting of 45 plants.

Then over 4 days between June 23 and 26, we had another busy time. The Bundjalung Tribal Society had its first board meeting since the floods – this meeting was held on the property and we harvested some bananas, chillies, greens, mandarins, lemons, and a couple of native yams and shared them out.

On Saturday Bundjalung leader, Anne Kelly provided a stirring welcome to country to the small group of 10 volunteers (including 3 Bundjalung community members). This time, instead of planting, we focused more on maintaining the existing plants, clearing space and surveying the ecosystem. What we found was fascinating. We have identified several priority areas on the site for planting out the rest of the trees.

These are areas where there are:
1. existing native species populating the area and we can support those with weeding, maintenance, and planting of supportive native species.
2. identified koala habitats where we can plant out koala food trees.
3. ephemeral water courses connecting standalone areas suitable for native rainforest species and koala food trees.

This was very exciting for us, because we didn’t realise we had so many native tress finding their way up amidst all the invasive species (on the property it is about 95% invasive species). It was encouraging to see that the ephemeral water courses are such important areas that support the native rainforest species. Thanks to all who have come along and brought the project this far. Oh and we still managed to plant out another 50 rainforest species too! This brings the total now to over 500 square meters and 150 trees planted. We have a way to go as the target for our rehabilitation grant is 1,000 plants.

Additionally, the shed now has hot and cold running water and a camp kitchen/food prep workspace. We also finished the landscaping around the shed including a grey water area for the run off from the kitchen. We also planted out a winter vegetable plot. In the next few weeks we will be installing the new compost toilet at the shed, making compost using the Johnson-Su Bioreactor method, and clearing weeds and planting more trees towards the bushfire recovery/creek rehabilitation project. Standby for more dates to come and participate.

Organisation Bundjalung Tribal Society

items.featured_alt: Grassy hillside dotted with tree guards beside remnant woodland
items.content:
Upper Snowy Landcare Network distribute 12,000 free native seedlings in the Snowy Monaro thanks to the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife.

The last two years have been totally gratifying as more than 60 local landholders put their hands up to plant more than 12,000 much-appreciated free native seedlings.

Upper Snowy Landcare Network has been responding since 2016 to the devastating tree dieback episode that has left a hole the size of the ACT in our functional biodiversity. Then along came the fires in the already stressed drought-affected landscape, and while the Snowy Monaro was not fully engulfed, the pressure on our vegetation was extreme.

In our reaction to the tree dieback, our initial instinct was to get straight out and plant local native rehabilitation plots which is what we have done, and to date, there are 50 of these plots successfully growing. Much of this planting was fully funded by government grants and we understood that the amount of revegetation was still very small considering the landmass devoid of trees and shrubs, and the price to install these plots is very expensive. We subsequently prepared a detailed paper on how to motivate landholders themselves to plant their own rehabilitation plots and or augment good habitats with missing species and keep them protected.

Our dream came true when the FNPW provided us with the free giveaway tree project. At first, as if we were weaning the local landholders into self-activation (planting their own plots) we provided support by supplying a free tree guard with each seedling for the first 10,000 seedlings and the latter 2,000 landholders were totally responsible for the guard themselves. Although 4 lucky landholders were delighted when a local new guard supplier offered free guards for 450 plants. Thank you to the Planting Systems Australia for this giveaway.

In two years 12,000 seedlings have made it into the ground. This is a great effort and we hope that this opportunity and desire continues so we ‘all’ act to replace what has been lost from historic tree clearing and strange episodes like dieback

OrganisationUpper Snowy Landcare Network

items.static_title: UPPER YANGO CREEK RESIDENTS GET PLANTING
items.content:
After devastating fires in December 2019 and subsequent significant rain events, including the July 2022 floods, residents of Upper Yango Creek Valley have teamed up with FNPW to identify, propagate and plant endemic species that will help address habitat loss and the considerable erosion that has occurred in Upper Yango Creek.
Working with FNPW Nurseries such as Upper Hunter Landcare and Trees in Newcastle, seed collection has begun and species linked to local providence have been identified and through a FNPW grant tube stock have been purchased or put on a grow order.
A Valley Planting Day on the weekend of 29th October 2022 saw the beginning of 600 tube stock being planted across 11 properties that front Upper Yango Creek. Land holders report that loss of plants thus far has been amazingly minimal.
Further rounds of planting including stock that is being grown by the above nurseries will take place in Autumn. In preparation for the next planting round significant weeds such as blackberry will be targeted and a spraying program begun.

OrganisationUpper Yango Creek Landholders Association

items.featured_alt: Volunteer planting tube stock along a restored creek line
items.static_title: Upper Yango Landholders Association Revegation Project
items.content:
Over the past twelve months members of the Upper Yango Creek Landholders Association have undertaken a revegetation project supported by a grant from the Foundation of National Parks & Wildlife (FNPW). The aim of the project was to revegetate riparian areas in and adjacent to Upper Yengo Creek that were devastated by the 2019 bushfires. Further urgency was added to the project due to flooding events of 2000-2022 that caused significant erosion of the creek.

Planting has been carried out in targeted sections areas of the creek as well as adjacent areas to try and create some habitat corridors for recovering native bird and wildlife populations.

After two Valley planting days, small group and individual work, landholders have spent over five hundred hours, planted over 1160 trees and 1400 grasses using tube stock supplied from FNPW nurseries, Trees in Newcastle Nursery and Upper Hunter Landcare Nursery. Of particular satisfaction was the collection of seed from the site between March 2000 and August 2022 that has resulted in the planting of Melelucca styphelioides , Eucalyptus dennii and Eucalyptus amplifolia on the Valley’s Autumn Planting Day. These species and others endemic to the area have been used to create diversity in the habitat.

In conjunction with revegetating sections of the creek we have been able to engage contractors to target blackberry, Japanese honeysuckle and tree of heaven which has made it possible to begin preparation for further planting in the coming months.

Without the support of the FNPW Grant we as a community would not have been able to embark on such an important project, for that we are grateful.

Comments from Landholders:
In an environment of very sandy soil, fires and floods have impacted badly on our creek banks. The only way to stabilise the banks is by planting grasses, trees and shrubs…The plants supplied by the FNPW grant, …lomandra and a range of trees and shrubs have helped us keep up the fight to save the creek banks.
Geoff and Rhonda Parkin UYLA Members

It was amazing to see how the valley community came together to support the project. To see so many tree guards scattered along the riparian area from [one end of the Valley to the other] . It has been just a wonderful initiative that will be giving back for generations to come.
North Sullivan, President UYLA
Planting these trees makes me feel we are at least trying to save the creek beds from eroding more as well as providing a greener canopy for the lower sections of the valley. Some of our trees have grown a metre in under a year and look very happy.
Helen McGrath ULA Member

..(We) are very grateful for the assistance provided by the grant. We have been able to strategically plant a number of areas along the creek that were damaged by fire and recent floods and were susceptible to further erosion. Blackberry treatment has made the task of regaining control over this weed seem much more achievable.
Carol and David Stiles, UYLA Members

OrganisationUpper Yango Landholders Association Inc

items.featured_alt: Home-school families planting trees on a valley floor at Araluen
items.static_title: Upper Shoalhaven Landcare’s Trees for Ongoing Disaster Recovery
items.content:
The Bushfire Recovery grant for Upper Shoalhaven Landcare was used to support ongoing disaster recovery and revegetation efforts across our Landcare network in the Queanbeyan-Palerang Council Region. Overall 1500 native tubestock, 1100 stakes, 600 guards, 500 jute mesh squares, fertilizer and catering for 2 community tree-planting events were purchased and distributed across 17 sites across Bombay, Braidwood, Bendoura, Mongarlowe and Araluen.

The key highlights of the project were two community tree plantings in the Araluen Valley with Upper Deua Catchment Landcare. The first planting was held on Saturday 27 May, with twenty-one volunteers turning up to help plant tubestock across two erosion control sites along the Araluen creek.

The second event, on Tuesday 30 May, invited parents and kids from the Braidwood home-school group to come down for a day of outdoor learning along the creek. Led by Araluen locals and out Local Landcare Coordinator, twenty-two participants, including eleven kids ranging from under 2 -14 years old, dug in and got their hands dirty planting an impressive 150 trees, shrubs and sedges.

Throughout the day the group learnt about the geology and gold-mining history of the Valley and why it contributes to high levels of erosion along the creek. The key message was the importance of ground cover and vegetation to help secure sediments and prevent them from being lost downstream. After a busy day’s planting and a quick splash in the creek for the kids, each family got a donated native plant to take home to grow and remember their planting day in Araluen.

items.featured_alt: Three rangers resting among granite boulders on Country
items.content:
Warddeken Rangers and the Karrkad Kanjdji Trust are working to protect vulnerable Mayh (species/animals) in the Stone Country of west Arnhem Land. Rangers are monitoring populations across the Warddeken Indigenous Protected Area to identify what land management interventions may lead to better outcomes, especially for culturally important mayh.

One of the most culturally significant species is the Northern Quoll, which is known as Djabbo in local language.

Djabbo are associated with the duwa patrimoiety and in the dreaming fought with the Dird (moon) man. The Djabbo wanted humans to die once and for all, but the Dird said there should be rebirth. They went their separate ways, the Djabbo dying like all creatures, but the Dird rose to be reborn every month. Today, the Djabbo’s curled-up claw is a symbol for death. The Djabbo is thought to be a semelparous mammal, meaning all the males die-off after the breeding season, placing great importance on the breeding females and survivorship of young to sustain Djabbo populations.

With the help of FNPW, Warddeken rangers are working to learn more about a population of Djabbo and their key threat, feral cats, at a place called Barradj. Rangers have recently deployed a 100 camera predator grid, spacing cameras approximately 400 metres apart on four land types and will process the data over the coming wet season.

Initially the location data of cats and Djabbo will be mapped and used by senior Traditional Owners to determine where to burn in the early dry season to best benefit the Djabbo. The second stage of data analysis will involve identifying individual animals to determine the size of populations and whether the species temporally or spatially interact. This knowledge will then be used to determine if other interventions can be used to support the persistence of Djabbo.

Organisation Warddeken Land Management Limited

items.featured_alt: Bushland with fallen logs, leaf litter and a dense understorey beneath the trees
items.static_title: What does healthy bushland actually look like?
items.content:
At the Mulligans Flat woodland experiment near Canberra, researchers added 2,000 tonnes of dead wood to the ground and waited.

Nine years later they counted significantly more reptile species than before. There was a clear dose response, so the more logs they had put down, the more lizards they found. And the effect was strongest exactly where the tree cover was thinnest.

This is awkward, because a healthy Australian bush looks, to most Australian eyes, like something that needs tidying up. Fallen timber. Leaf litter. Scrappy, prickly understorey. Almost every instinct we have about a well-kept landscape is wrong, and the science on this is not close.

It is National Science Week, and this year’s schools theme is Seeds of Science: Nurturing Knowledge for All, so it seems a good moment to say something we do not say loudly enough at the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife. Restoring the bush is not gardening at scale. It is applied science, it is harder than planting, and most of the difficulty sits in the parts nobody photographs.

Structure

A bush is a building, not a lawn

The mess matters, and not for sentimental reasons.

When Australian researchers compared remnant woodland against two kinds of revegetation, woodlots of trees alone and ecological plantings with trees, shrubs and understorey, bird richness tracked structural complexity. Floristic richness on its own showed no significant effect. At around twenty years both planting types had caught up to the remnants on raw species counts. The composition had not, and the remnants still held species that appeared in no planting at all.

More recent work using ground-based and drone LiDAR arrived at the same place from a different direction. The strongest predictors of bird abundance in a restored woodland were canopy roughness, vertical complexity in the ground layer, total vegetation volume and canopy height. The understorey, in other words. The layer satellites are worst at seeing, and the layer humans are quickest to remove.

A bush is not a surface with trees on it. It is a building with several floors, and the wildlife lives on all of them. Which is why NSW Government revegetation guidance recommends planting around 60 per cent shrubs, ideally dense and prickly, and keeping linear plantings at least 30 metres wide. Not a canopy. A structure.

Slow layers

The floors you cannot rebuild

Some of those floors can be re-established in a season. Others cannot be re-established inside a working lifetime, and those are precisely the ones that look most like neglect.

Dead wood is the first. In 2003, the NSW Scientific Committee formally listed the removal of dead wood and dead trees as a Key Threatening Process, alongside feral cats and land clearing. Not a shame. A listed threat. The determination names the broad-headed snake, the regent parrot, the pink cockatoo and the spotted-tailed quoll among the species affected, and notes that stripping dead wood out alters the soil microclimate and starves the invertebrate communities doing the nutrient recycling. Research at Mulligans Flat found soil beside fallen logs gained measurable carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus within two years, concentrated in the top centimetre. A log is not debris. It is shelter, slow-release fertiliser, and a nursery for the fungi that everything above ground depends on.

The second is older again. In eucalypts, hollows suitable for wildlife take between 120 and 200 years to form, through branch loss, fungal decay, termite activity and weather. Around 300 Australian vertebrate species use them. That timeline cannot be shortened with funding and the result cannot be manufactured. The powerful owl nesting somewhere tonight is in a tree that was already old when Australia became a country.

Put those two together and you have the real asymmetry of this work. A tree can be planted this winter. The hollow in it will not be available to wildlife until the 2200s. Which is why protection is not the cautious half of conservation. It is the only way to hold onto the parts of the system that nobody can replace.

The seed bank

What the soil remembers

If the oldest layers cannot be rebuilt, the question becomes what a landscape can still do for itself. Quite a lot, as it happens, by mechanisms stranger than most people expect.

Take a seed from many Australian natives and give it perfect soil, water, warmth and light. Nothing will happen. It will sit there, alive and refusing. What it is waiting for is smoke.

In 2004, chemists at the University of Western Australia isolated the compound in bushfire smoke that breaks seed dormancy. It works at concentrations as low as ten nanomolar. They named the family karrikins, after karrik, a Noongar word for smoke recorded in the Perth region in the 1830s. Australian plants are not passively waiting for rain. They are reading chemical signals in the soil, and much of the bush holds a store of dormant seed underground waiting for the right one.

But that store is a partial archive. In a study of eucalypt wetland forest at Yellingbo in Victoria, researchers germinated more than 6,300 seedlings from soil samples and found only about 24 per cent floristic similarity between the standing vegetation and what was held beneath it. Very few seeds of the wetland trees and shrubs were present at all. Exotic species made up 32 per cent of the standing vegetation but 41 per cent of the seed bank.

The soil remembers the ground layer. It remembers the weeds rather well. It does not reliably remember the canopy. That gap is exactly where the work sits, and it is why 145 living seedbanks and more than 30 community nurseries across four states sit inside our Fire Wise program, and why 110,000 fire-resilient natives have been propagated and planted rather than bought in from wherever was convenient.

Before planting

The question that comes before planting

All of which leads to a single diagnostic question, and it is not the one most people expect.

Australia’s national restoration standards set out a principle that should govern far more conservation spending than it currently does: restoration inputs will be dictated by level of resilience and degradation. Translated, the first question on any site is never what shall we plant. It is whether this place can still repair itself, and if not, what exactly is broken.

Get that wrong and you can spend a decade planting into a landscape that will not take it. On the Cumberland Plain west of Sydney, eleven years after planting and with 71 per cent of planted species established, species composition at all three restored sites remained significantly different from reference woodland. Only five planted species had produced recruits of their own. In the Western Australian wheatbelt, soil organic carbon under trees planted a decade earlier sat at 0.9 per cent, against 1.2 to 1.5 per cent under reference woodland. The trees were there. The system had not come back with them.

Planting is the beginning of the process. It is not the proof of it.

Connection

Distance is a habitat feature

There is one more variable, and it has nothing to do with the site itself. It is where the site sits.

A systematic review of 80 Australian connectivity studies found a mean gap-crossing distance of around 106 metres, and a threshold for dispersal between patches of around 1,100 metres. Those two numbers decide whether two patches of bush are one habitat or two. When the answer is two, the losses arrive slowly enough to be missed. Ecologists call it extinction debt: species still present in a fragment, still being counted in surveys, but no longer viable there. On the Swan Coastal Plain in Western Australia, banksia woodland patches were found to carry an average extinction debt of 13 species each, equivalent to 28 per cent of mean species richness. The bill had not been paid. It had only been deferred.

Scale is the counterweight. Research across Victorian farmland found landscapes with 1 per cent revegetation held an average of 11 woodland bird species. At 15 per cent revegetation, the average was 25.

This is why Growing National Parks is an ecological strategy and not merely a real estate one. Our 23,000-hectare acquisition at Undilla Station sits adjacent to Boodjamulla. Mundoo Island’s 1,900 hectares went into Coorong National Park rather than standing alone. We added 29,479 hectares to national park status across the last year, and the question we ask of every hectare is what it connects to.

The whole bush

What a full bush actually means

All of it. The canopy, the midstorey, the prickly scrub, the litter, the logs on the ground and the fungal networks underneath. Gaps narrow enough to cross and patches large enough to hold. Old trees left standing long enough to go hollow.

We measure that against a local reference ecosystem using six attributes and a five-star scale, and we publish what it produces: 647 hectares under active restoration last year, 1,215,443 trees, shrubs and seedlings planted across priority landscapes, and 80 per cent delivery of purpose. Numbers we put in writing because they can be checked.

Growing National Parks, Saving Species and Healing the Land are three answers to one question, which is what does this particular landscape need, and in what order.

Australia looks better with a full bush. Not a tidy one.

items.featured_alt: Native plantings in a restoration site, chosen for the species that depend on them
items.static_title: The science of plant selection, and why the species matters
items.content:
Who are you planting it for?

Put a Glossy Black-Cockatoo in a healthy forest and it can still starve.

Not because the forest is degraded. Because it is the wrong forest.

Last time we wrote that a bush is a building, and that its structure matters more than its tree count. This is the part where you decide who moves in. Because “we planted a bunch of trees ” is a volume statistic. The ecological question is narrower, and much harder. Which trees, and for whom.

One bird, two trees, no substitutes

The South Australian Glossy Black-Cockatoo feeds almost exclusively on the seed of the drooping sheoak, Allocasuarina verticillata. Not sheoaks in general. That one. And it does not forage evenly across the trees available to it either. Researchers on Kangaroo Island have spent years working out which cone and tree characteristics decide where these birds will and will not feed.

Then there is the second requirement, and it has nothing to do with food. Glossies nest in hollows, in large old eucalypts.

So the bird needs two entirely unrelated species, delivering two entirely different things, on two entirely different timelines. Plant only sheoaks and you have fed a bird that cannot breed. Plant only eucalypts and you have housed a bird that cannot eat. Plant both this decade and the food arrives in years, while the nest sites arrive next century.

The South Australian population climbed from 158 birds in 1995 to around 453 by 2023, which is a genuine recovery story. Then the Black Summer fires destroyed at least 54 per cent of their feeding habitat and 38.5 per cent of known nests in a single season.

That is what a species list is really deciding.

Timing is a species trait

Fewer than 400 Regent Honeyeaters remain in the wild. They are critically endangered, they depend on flowering eucalypts, particularly yellow box and mugga ironbark, and they range across more than half a million square kilometres chasing blossom.

They have to, because eucalypts are unreliable. Flowering is irregular, heavy in some years and absent in others, and it varies between individual trees in the same stand. A nectar feeder cannot settle down. It follows the food or it does not eat.

Which means a species list is not only what you plant. It is when those plants flower. A revegetation site that blooms gloriously in spring and offers nothing in July is a feast followed by a famine, and the famine is the part that decides whether anything stays.

Sometimes the plant is not the food

At Winton Wetlands in Victoria, we funded the translocation of around 60 Growling Grass Frogs to establish a new population, in a targeted recovery plan.

Frogs do not eat the vegetation. They need it for something else entirely. Growling Grass Frogs require cover in and around the water, and they also need to bask. Raising their body temperature helps them resist chytrid fungus, the disease behind amphibian collapses worldwide. So habitat work for this species means planting for shelter while deliberately leaving open, sunlit places to warm up in, and adding rock.

Same principle, completely different logic. Here the vegetation is chosen for what it physically does, not for what it feeds.

A thousand plants can be one plant

Here is the part almost nobody outside the sector thinks about.

Collect seed from three convenient trees, grow a thousand seedlings, and you have not planted a thousand plants. You have planted a very small number of plants, a thousand times over. The genetic variation that lets a population survive drought, disease and heat is simply not in the box.

And it gets worse in exactly the places restoration tends to happen. Small, isolated remnants produce less seed, of poorer quality, with narrower genetic diversity, because the plants that remain are increasingly related to each other. A landmark Australian paper by Broadhurst and colleagues concluded that the emphasis on strictly local seed sourcing will, in many cases, lead to poor restoration outcomes, and argued for concentrating less on how local the seed is and more on how genetically diverse and high quality it is.

This is why “locally sourced” in our reporting means seed collected across many parent plants, not simply seed collected nearby. It is also why community nurseries and seedbanks are infrastructure rather than sentiment.

Planting for a climate that has not arrived yet

Which brings us to the most interesting unresolved question in Australian restoration right now.

The traditional rule is local provenance. Use seed from as close to the site as possible, because local plants are adapted to local conditions. It is sound logic and it has guided planting for decades.

But the conditions are moving. So Australian researchers have proposed alternatives, most prominently climate-adjusted provenancing, which mixes local seed with seed collected from populations lying in the direction the climate is travelling, typically hotter and drier. The aim is to give a planting the genetic raw material for the climate it will face in fifty years, not only the one it faces today.

Both positions carry real risk. Stay strictly local and you may plant something exquisitely adapted to a climate that is on its way out. Move seed too far and you risk outbreeding depression, where mixing distant populations produces less fit offspring.

There is no settled answer yet, and anyone who tells you there is has stopped reading.

Which is why the nursery matters

We support community nurseries across four states, with living seedbanks and community groups that tend to them, and we have propagated and planted more than 110,000 fire-resilient natives.

Not because growing plants locally is charming. Because the species list, the seed source and the genetic spread are the three decisions that determine whether a planting becomes habitat, or just becomes trees.

The question is never how many.

It is who are you planting it for.

Help us bring back the bush.

items.featured_alt: Wildlife Heroes project manager Stacey
items.static_title: Wildlife Heroes Updates from the Field
items.content:
Wildlife Heroes Project Manager, Stacey Mole (pictured above), has been out on the road visiting with NSW volunteer wildlife rescue and rehabilitation groups. Currently, the Wildlife Heroes project is funded until the end of 2023, and there is an Action Implementation Plan to be written. This plan will underpin what the Wildlife Heroes Project will undertake over the next year and a half. Gaining insight into how groups are going, their needs, issues, and wish lists by meeting with members of wildlife groups in person will help inform this plan. Here is an update from Stacey about the trip so far:

“Over the past few weeks I have met with seven wildlife rescue volunteer groups, one wildlife hospital, and a representative from Taronga Institute of Science and Learning. I am now at the turn around point of my journey in the chilly town of Jindabyne where, for the first time, I have indulged in a motel room instead of sleeping in my camper. My weather app says ‘feels like -3.9°C’ outside!

I hope to visit more groups, and possibly independent licence holders on the way back to my home in the Northern Rivers, where I will catch up with local groups as well. So, the journey is not over yet…
[Editor’s Note: By the time this blog was published, Stacey had visited ten groups in total.]

My gathering of information this far has shown me the diverse needs of the different groups, and there is a lot of information for me to tease through. However, most groups will speak to the need for more people on the ground doing jobs that will help share the work load.

It seems most groups are based around a core group of individuals who are the key rescue and rehabilitators, who also tend to the 24-hour hot line and do all the administrative tasks. People are time poor; they are tired, some are emotionally wrung out – they need help.

If you’re a member of a group, please know that there is always, ALWAYS a way you can contribute. If the stress of rescue, or heartbreak of losing a patient in rehabilitation is not for you, there are many, many other tasks that need to be done. There’s the phone to answer, volunteers to coordinate, food to distribute, data to manage, grant applications to write, social media posts to make, cages to build, webpages to manage, fundraisers to organise, etc. etc. And, if you happen to have land in a quiet place away from traffic and dogs, and can devote an area to become a soft-release site, please contact your local wildlife group – they need you!

At this point, I just want to pay tribute to the dedication I have seen out there in the wildlife sector. I am truly humbled and inspired. Thank you, for all that you do.”

-Stacey

Wildlife Heroes is a project managed by FNPW and designed to help and support Australia’s 10,000+ volunteer wildlife carers. Funding for the project has been received through the NSW Government Environmental Trust in NSW, the Australian Government and FNPW donors and sponsors.

For more information on this project, visit https://wildlifeheroes.org.au/

items.featured_alt: Volunteers planting along a grassy creek flat
items.static_title: Wollombi and Laguna Primary School Earth Day Planting
items.content:
The Wollombi Landcare Group and 20 students from the Laguna Public School planted around 90 plants as part of the FNPW Bushfire Recovery Program on Earth Day 2021. The trees were provided by the Hawkesbury Community Nursery as part of a project supporting nurseries to grow bushfire restoration trees. Whilst the background may look green and “treed” this is a badly degraded part of Wollombi Brook where there are only a few native trees which were themselves planted years ago. It is also only a few kilometres from the 2019 fire fronts. Wollombi Landcare Group have been doing a lot of woody weed control it was the right time to plant as this has been the first good planting season we’ve had for at least five years. The school is just across the road and the kids love the planting. Their enthusiasm is exhausting for us oldies but wonderfully infectious at the same time.

Organisation Wollombi Landcare Group
