items.featured_alt: Common wombat looking towards the camera
items.content:
Wildlife Heroes Project Manager, Stacey Mole – update on Wildlife Heroes NSW 2022 Flood Emergency Funding. Seven volunteer wildlife rehabilitation groups assisted to the sum of $56,000. Wildlife rehabilitation groups that were flood affected and supported through this grant are now fulfilling their last milestone. Part of this process is to share a story in relation to the grant. It is very satisfying to see how the efforts of the Wildlife Heroes team, along with the hard work of wildlife volunteers, are able to help wildlife in need. We would like to share one of the stories…

LAOKO has received many reports of wombats needing help due to flooded burrows. Wombats have been attacked by other wombats, and have ended up under houses and in sheds, when heavy rain and local flooding have meant wombats have nowhere to sleep and there is competition for dry burrows. The Wildlife Heroes Emergency Flooding Grant has been wonderful and has helped with costs associated with wombat rescues, soft release enclosures, plastic dog kennels for temporary burrows, cameras to monitor wombats, a storage container for equipment, and reimbursement for some travel costs associated with these rescues. One classic example is when we received a call from Jindabyne about a wombat under a property owner’s veranda.  One of our volunteers went to investigate and found this soggy wombat:

This wombat was trying to sleep under a veranda so we setup a plastic dog kennel, under the veranda (similar to the photo below) to give the wombat a better, more comfortable place while burrows dried out.

Our volunteer would drive out and check the wombat each day to make sure it wasn’t getting sick.  After a few days the wombat had moved on and wombat tracks could be seen at nearby burrows. The kennel is then taken back, cleaned, and stored, ready for the next wombat in need. This photo is an example of one of the plastic dog kennels used to house wombats displaced by flooded burrows.  These dog kennels were also used for orphan wombats who lost their mothers during the floods. Author: Robyn George Wildlife Group: Snowy Mountains Wildlife Rescue LAOKO Inc

More stories can be found at: https://wildlifeheroes.org.au/stories/

The NSW Wildlife Heroes Project is managed by the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife with funding from the New South Wales Government through its Environmental Trust.

items.featured_alt: Aerial view of a waterfall dropping into a rainforest gorge in the Gondwana Rainforests
items.content:
In a world threatened by climate change and rapid deforestation, protecting our rainforests has become an urgent global imperative. These lush and diverse ecosystems are not just natural wonders; they are the guardians of our planet’s health and biodiversity.

In 2022, FNPW purchased a parcel of land to extend the UNESCO World Heritage-protected Gondwana Rainforests of Australia. The Gondwana Rainforests date back to a period 500 million years ago, before Australia was formed. These rainforests connect us to the foundations of our country and its unique biodiversity.

Protecting 189 hectares of vitally important biodiversity is a crucial step in preserving our natural heritage. This act of conservation helps protects more than 200 threatened species, ensuring they can continue to thrive for generations to come. It is our duty to preserve rainforests for a number of reasons.

Rainforests are biodiversity hotspots

Rainforests are teeming with life, housing an incredible array of plant and animal species found nowhere else on Earth. They are veritable treasure troves of biodiversity, making up only 2% of the Earth’s surface but harbouring more than 50% of all known species. Losing rainforests would mean the extinction of countless unique plants and animals, disrupting the delicate balance of nature and depriving us of potential life-saving discoveries.

Rainforests stabilise the climate

Rainforests act as natural climate stabilisers, playing a crucial role in regulating global temperatures. Through a process called photosynthesis, they absorb carbon dioxide, one of the main greenhouse gases responsible for climate change, and release oxygen. By protecting rainforests, we can help mitigate climate change and curb its devastating impacts, such as rising sea levels, extreme weather events, and loss of agricultural productivity.

Rainforests guard the water cycle

Rainforests are like giant sponges, capturing rainfall and releasing it slowly over time, ensuring a steady supply of freshwater for rivers, lakes, and underground aquifers. They help regulate local and regional rainfall patterns, preventing droughts and floods. By preserving rainforests, we safeguard the primary source of water for millions of people, maintaining the delicate balance of ecosystems and supporting human livelihoods.

Rainforests support First Nations cultures and traditional knowledge

Rainforests are not just biodiversity hotspots; they are also home to numerous Indigenous communities with rich cultural heritage and invaluable traditional knowledge. These communities have lived in harmony with the rainforest for millennia, understanding its intricacies and relying on its resources sustainably. By protecting rainforests, we respect and honour the rights of Indigenous peoples, allowing them to preserve their ways of life and share their wisdom with the world.

Help us protect rainforests

Protecting rainforests is a crucial step toward securing a sustainable future. By preserving these magnificent ecosystems, we can stand as guardians of our green lungs for future generations.

This winter, FNPW is raising funds to grow national parks like the Gondwana Rainforests. Habitat loss and change of land use have created an extinction crisis for our native species. Please help us purchase and protect the places extinction cannot reach by making a tax deductible donation before 30 June 2023.

items.featured_alt: Endangered orange daisies flowering in restored ground at Hindmarsh Valley National Park
items.static_title: Years of restoration, written in layers
items.content:
A morning in Hindmarsh Valley National Park, where a cleared paddock is becoming a forest again

A few years ago, this hillside off Hindmarsh Falls Road was nothing but pasture. Now it has layers: bushes, shrubs and trees taller than a person at the top of the hill, and new seedlings pushing through at knee height behind them. This is a 60 hectare section of Hindmarsh Valley National Park that was only recently brought into the park, and restoration here has been underway for a few years already. With the support of our partners at One Tree Planted, those layers are what years of steady, dedicated work look like on the ground.

We came down to the Fleurieu Peninsula in late May to walk the site with Anthony Abley, the regional ecologist leading this work for National Parks and Wildlife. What he showed us was a work in progress, done paddock by paddock as time and funding allow. You can never do it all at once, he told us, so you do it piece by piece and keep on top of it. But the pieces are starting to join up, and the species are starting to answer.

A valley found nowhere else

To understand why this corner of South Australia matters so much, you have to go back millions of years. Hindmarsh Valley, along with the neighbouring Inman and Back Valleys, was shaped by ancient glacial activity. Those old valleys created natural breaks and boundaries that, over an enormous span of time, produced something unusual: a dense pocket of endemic species, plants and animals that live here and nowhere else on earth.

That uniqueness is what makes the work urgent. When a species exists in only one valley, fragmentation is not an inconvenience, but an existential threat. For years, many of these species had been written off, hanging on along roadsides and in scattered remnants. The arrival of this park changed the maths. With 500 hectares now available to restore across the broader Hindmarsh Valley landscape, there is a genuine chance these species can have a future rather than a slow managed decline.

From pasture to wet and dry mosaic

The restoration here is not simply about putting trees in the ground. It is about rebuilding a whole ecosystem, including the parts you can’t see. The nationally endangered Fleurieu Swamps and their associated woodland are the heart of this site, and recreating them means recreating the way water moves through the land.

Walk the paddock at the end of winter and you would struggle to cross it without gumboots. It turns to bog. Rather than drain that away, the plan embraces it. The site has been mapped into a patchwork: forest along the watercourses, and discrete swamp patches set into the low, wet ground, each planted with a community of species suited to its conditions. The result, over time, is a gradient of habitat rather than a uniform block of trees, and that structural variety is what wildlife needs.

It is already drawing life back. The native swamp rat, an animal with an unfairly grim name, is one of the gentlest creatures you could hope to meet. Nothing like the introduced black rat, it looks more like a small guinea pig and will often put its paws up on your leg for a sniff before wandering off. Bush rats are turning up too. These small native mammals are a quiet proxy for recovery: when they return, it tells us the food web underneath them is starting to function again.

The hidden network underground

Some of the most important players here never see daylight. Beneath the soil runs a vast web of fungi, with best estimates suggesting ten times as many fungal species underground as plant species above. Plants and fungi depend on each other, and many native animals feed on the fungi and spread them as they go. When we talk about restoring nutrients to degraded land, this is much of what we mean. You cannot rebuild a forest by planting the canopy alone.

Why corridors change everything

The single most important idea on this site is connection. A patch of habitat on its own, no matter how healthy, can only hold so much. Genetic viability for most species needs something in the order of 500 interconnected individuals, breeding and moving freely across enough habitat to sustain themselves.

In a fragmented landscape, that is almost impossible to achieve.

Rosenberg’s goanna makes the point vividly. It needs roughly 100 hectares per animal, which means this park on its own might support only a handful. The only way to build a viable population is to connect this land to neighbouring parks and willing farmers, stitching the fragments into something whole. By doubling a 200 hectare remnant toward a 500 hectare contiguous patch, we give every species more room, more genetic exchange and more resilience.

Connected, multi-storied habitat does something else too. It gives animals a way to move when conditions turn dangerous. Plantings that include ground shrubs, a mid-storey and a canopy create escape routes through the landscape, koalas using the trees and smaller mammals using the cover below. It is the difference between a population that can survive a disturbance and one that gets wiped out with nowhere to run.

Living with fire

It would be easy to assume the great threat to all this new growth is fire. The reality is more interesting. Many of these species have evolved with fire over millions of years and actually depend on it.

Some plants, including Banksia, need the heat of a burn to release their seed. The danger is not fire itself but fire in a broken landscape, where a single blaze can erase an isolated population with no neighbouring habitat left to recolonise from.

The southern brown bandicoot shows how recovery is supposed to work. When most of the Scott Creek and Mount Bold remnant network burned several years ago, with seventy to eighty per cent lost, the bandicoots vanished from the burnt ground. Within three years they had recolonised most of the burn scar, and within five they were back to pre-fire numbers. That bounce-back only happens when connected habitat sits alongside the burn for animals to shelter in and return from. On this site, the team has even used a prescribed burn to regenerate long-unburnt understorey, because bandicoots favour habitat in that five to fifteen year window after fire. Done well, and increasingly in partnership with First Nations fire knowledge, fire becomes a tool for creating habitat rather than destroying it.

A future worth planting for

There is a lot of good news threaded through this landscape. The glossy black cockatoo, doing well on nearby Kangaroo Island, is visiting the mainland more and more often, and the answer to keeping it here is gloriously simple: plant a great deal of she-oak for it to feed on. The local bandicoot is the subject of genetic studies likely to confirm it as a species in its own right, distinct from its eastern cousins, with a new name drawn from Aboriginal language, Marti, and the scientific name Isoodon nauticus. Recognising it as its own species means we can protect it properly, and even guide where animals are reintroduced to rebuild the strongest possible populations.

That endangered orange daisy we found flowering through the paddock tells the whole story in miniature. Once locked into the roadsides, it now has a new home in ground that was recently just pasture, coming up everywhere across the restored block. It is no longer hanging on. It is spreading.

Stand on that hillside and look across to the cleared land opposite, and it is not hard to picture what it could become: a forested hill instead of bare ground, a new home for species that have spent decades surviving on the margins. Thanks to the support of partners like One Tree Planted and the people who fund this work, that picture is getting closer paddock by paddock. We intervene where the land needs a hand, and then we let nature do what it has always known how to do. What comes back is more than trees. It is a whole living system, finding its feet again.

Learn more about how we’re bringing back the bush.

With thanks to Anthony Abley and National Parks and Wildlife South Australia, and to One Tree Planted, whose support funds the plantings described here.

items.content:
DOWNLOAD THE 2022 impact report   We are delighted to present the annual Impact Report for 2022, showcasing the remarkable achievements of the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife in safeguarding Australia’s natural wonders. Significant progress has been made towards the mission of preserving these treasures for future generations. The year 2022 witnessed global strides in biodiversity, with Australia proudly joining 195 other nations in committing to protect 30% of the planet by 2030 through the signing of the Global Biodiversity Framework. Let’s explore the Foundation’s accomplishments and the positive impact they have made on our environment. Expanding National Parks and Protecting Threatened Species A core principle of the Foundation’s conservation approach has been acquiring land to grow national parks and protect Australia’s threatened species. Since our first land purchase in 1972, we have continued this effort, with notable achievements in 2022. Adding 60,000 hectares to our portfolio, we established the Nilpena Ediacara National Park, which was shortlisted for UNESCO World Heritage Status. In another milestone, the Foundation acquired 189 hectares to extend the UNESCO World Heritage Listed Gondwana Rainforests of Australia, forever preserving an area equivalent to 467 soccer pitches. These expansions contribute to the long-term conservation and preservation of our natural wonders. Recovering from Bushfires and Flooding The Foundation’s Bushfire Recovery Project, aimed at regrowing and planting over 1 million native trees in fire and flood-affected regions by 2025, continued to evolve in 2022. With over 400,000 trees grown and partnerships with local communities, we have rejuvenated over 550 hectares across Australia. This reforestation effort plays a crucial role in preserving wildlife habitats and enhancing the resilience of these areas for future environmental challenges. By replanting trees and restoring ecosystems, the Foundation is actively contributing to the recovery and protection of our natural environment. Supporting Wildlife Carers Another significant achievement of FNPW is the continued support of Australia’s wildlife carers. By expanding the capacity of carers and veterinarians, we ensure that injured and displaced animals receive the best possible care, increasing their chances of survival and eventual release back into their natural habitats. This support acknowledges the vital role of wildlife carers in preserving our unique fauna and ensuring their well-being. Creating Lasting Impact With renewed global goals and increasing recognition of the value of biodiversity and environmental health, the Foundation expresses gratitude for the continued support and dedication of its partners and supporters. Together, we are creating a lasting impact and driving positive social change. By protecting and cherishing Australia’s natural wonders, we are safeguarding these treasures for generations to come. FNPW’s efforts align with the global commitment to preserving biodiversity and ensuring the long-term well-being of our planet.

FNPW partners with corporate organisations, philanthropists, donors’ government and local communities to maximise environmental impact.  

If you want to discuss how you can support community projects or create environmental partnerships that achieve impact on a national scale then get in touch for a chat via fnpw@fnpw.org.au.

items.content:
We are delighted to introduce to you the 2023 Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife Impact Report. This report highlights the significant progress we have made together. It is your support that safeguards Australia’s natural wonders for future generations.

DOWNLOAD THE 2023 IMPACT REPORT

To deliver maximum impact and ensure that we’re funding priority projects which are pivotal in safeguarding and preserving Australia’s rich natural biodiversity, we align with international and national environmental objectives, including:

The Kunming-Montreal Global Diversity Framework(GBF) (Targets 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 8). United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals(Goals 13, 15 and 17). International extinction priorities via the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species. Australia’s EPBC Act List of Threatened Species alongside state listings. Since COP 15, our efforts have echoed the worldwide push for conservation. We’re dedicated to goals like protecting 30% of land and marine areas by 2030 and preserving Indigenous knowledge. Our partnerships extend to biodiversity reporting frameworks, guiding our investments for maximum environmental benefit. By expanding national parks, saving threatened species and restoring our land, we’re building a sustainable future for Australia. Some of the key highlights from our report:

Growing Parks  Supported 50+ land purchases since 1970. Developing the Wapma Thura Southern Flinders Ranges National Park, a world-class nature tourism destination. Expanding the UNESCO World Heritage Listed Gondwana Rainforests.   Saving Species Work alongside governments to prioritise the protection of threatened native species. Supporting 167 threatened plant and animal species across Australia. The Wildlife Heroes project aided over 700 species over three years, with over 50% being threatened mammals. Working to save 1 million turtles in the Murray-Darling Basin.   Healing Our Land Planting over 700,000 native trees for restoration. Building one of Australia’s largest community-led restoration projects across 4 states enabled by 19 local community nurseries and 10,000+ volunteers. The Fire Wise project, launched with CSIRO, is a catalyst for community engagement in best-practice bushfire risk mitigation, ensuring a safer and ecologically vibrant future. Collaborating with Indigenous groups to create projects grounded in a blend of Indigenous knowledge and scientific evidence.   Thank you. Together we will continue to create meaningful and lasting impact.   Happy Impact Reading!

items.featured_alt: Four people standing together at the Friends of the Koala nursery opening
items.static_title: 80,000 trees to be planted to support Koala conservation
items.content:
To support Northern New South Wales’ rapidly declining Koala population, the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife (FNPW) awarded a grant to Friends of the Koala Inc to support koala conservation by expanding its East Lismore nursery by 80,000 trees for the food and shelter of Australia’s koala population. 

The grant awarded to Friends of the Koala Inc. will extend the capacity of its current nursery to plant a total of 100,000 koala trees per year. This will be a major step in supporting the recovery of the NSW North Coast and the Gondwana Rainforest World Heritage Area, of which 50% were devastated by the fires, destroying the habitats of thousands of native animals. Tree species planted will include the Forest Red Gum, Tallowood, Swamp Mahogany, Grey Gum, Grey Ironbark, Flooded Gum and Brush Box.

Conserving Koalas in Northern NSW  

Operating for over 35 years, Friends of the Koala Inc. has an established history of conserving, enhancing and preserving the Koala population and their habitat. Alongside the native plant nursery, the group operates a Koala Hospital in East Lismore and works to rescue, rehabilitate and release koalas back into the wild.

Mark Wilson, the Friends of the Koala Nursery Manager, said that this grant will enhance his team’s commitment to creating a more continuous corridor of food and shelter for koalas, particularly in the Northern Rivers region of New South Wales.

“The support of the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife has meant that we are now a step ahead in our mission to protect NSW’s declining koala population. The Black Summer was the worst environmental disaster witnessed in history, killing or displacing three billion animals, so it’s our first priority to start rebuilding habitats to protect our beloved native wildlife.”

Planting trees to support Koala habitats 

Ian Darbyshire, CEO of FNPW, said: “Friends of the Koala will play a significant role in restoring Australia’s biodiversity and our mission of planting one million trees in bushfire affected regions around Australia. This will be an integral step in supporting NSW’s koala population of which a third was severely affected. It is thanks to our partners, L’OCCITANE and One Tree Planted that grants such as this can continue to be awarded to restore our native flora and fauna.”

FNPW would like to thank global reforestation non-profit, One Tree Planted, French beauty brand, L’OCCITANE and Southern Cross University for their contribution to the Friends of the Koala Bushfire Recovery Nursery.

items.featured_alt: Group of volunteers seated beneath a shelter at a planting day
items.static_title: A Visit to the Southern Flinders Ranges
items.content:
One of the Parks 2025 projects announced by the Government is the intention to establish a new adventure based tourism destination for South Australia in the Southern Flinders Ranges.

The Southern Flinders Ranges are within easy reach of Adelaide and feature ranges, peaks, gorges and forests, including high-quality native vegetation and reservoirs, which stretch from Beetaloo to Wilmington. There are some incredible views throughout the Southern Flinders Ranges, including the 960m high Mount Remarkable which presides over the Willochra Plain. Views from the Southern Range look out over the Spencer Gulf and also take in the agricultural landscapes to the east. 

Creating the park and all of its visitor experiences is a partnership with the Nukunu Traditional Owners, the State Government and community organisations, including the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife, Northern Areas Council, District Council of Mount Remarkable, Port Pirie Regional Council and Regional Development Australia Yorke and Mid North.

As part of the Remarkable Southern Flinders project, Regional Development Australia Yorke and Mid North (RDAYMN) welcomed the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife (FNPW), on a recent tour of the Southern Flinders Ranges.

FNPW President, Patrick Medley, CEO, Ian Darbyshire and Project Committee Chair, David Pumphrey were greeted in Port Pirie by John Pirie Secondary School First Nations students for a tour of their bush tucker garden ‘Urumbula’.

The tour saw the students inform the group of different plants that have cultural significance to many First Nations people across the country, including Eremophila Longifolia which plays an important part in the local Nukunu culture.

Over two days, the group was joined by District Ranger, Danny Doyle and RDAYMN’s Alan Zubrinich who guided the group through the stunning Southern Flinders Ranges visiting the iconic Alligator Gorge in Mount Remarkable National Park and spotting 12 Yellow-Footed Rock Wallabies in Telowie Gorge Conservation Park, which is their most southern colony.

The tour allowed for members to immerse themselves in the Southern Flinders Ranges and initiated further collaboration and discussion on next steps for this conservation and tourism project, including its key projects of

  • developing an international mountain bike destination at Mt Remarkable
  • upgrading trails for hiking and cycling, including a new iconic trail, featuring multi-day hikes
  • upgrading and expanding campgrounds to provide camping for a wider variety of vehicles and camping experiences
  • upgrading visitor facilities

Stay tuned for further updates on this exciting project for South Australia.

items.featured_alt: Aboriginal site recording, Yengo National Park and surrounding Country
items.static_title: Aboriginal Site Recording Yengo NP and Surrounding Country
items.content:
In December 2020, FNPW received the final report from one of our Bushfire Recovery Grants: Aboriginal Site Recording Yengo NP and Surrounding Country. The project aimed to map 40 sites, however from May through to December the team surveyed more than 67 sites.

The area was severely impacted by the 2019-20 bushﬁres and the grant has allowed many Aboriginal sites in the Yengo NP and surrounding country to be surveyed and photographed. The team surveyed 41 known cave sites (listed AHIMS) with signiﬁcant art – drawings, artefact stencils and hand stencils – photographed and GPS conﬁrmed. In addition, there were 22 engraving sites visited and recorded with some photographed at night, with the team continuing to check on well known sites mainly in the Yengo NP. The survey list also includes many grinding groove sites, water ‘tanks’ and stone arrangements.

Highlights from the survey include unrecorded sites – two caves with signiﬁcant drawings and stencils, several stone arrangements (diﬃcult to specify quantity), engravings (some partial that could be added to known engravings at the same site) and many new grinding groove sites. Some cave sites also contained artefacts such as knapping stone ﬂakes, ochre fragments, animal bones (most likely macropod) and mussel shells.

Below are some of the photos they have taken from the sites that were mapped after the fires.

The images from the caves (Yengo 1 and 2) show art work on walls and engravings of circles believed to be in excess of 4,000 years. These caves were excavated by archeologist Jo McDonald in 1987 and are believed to be the oldest in NSW.

Most of the sites survived the ﬁres, although there was some damage to at least two caves due to the impact of eroding winds in the ﬁrestorm and trees that burnt into the cave overhangs. On the sandstone platforms, the leaf litter and fallen trees will have an impact as vegetation regrows and possibly cover engraving sites. The team has removed leaf litter on a number of engraving sites to protect the site. The team have worked with the national parks rangers and this very successful relationship will continue, especially in regard to updating AHIMS and the protection/management of cultural sites. The team are developing their skills and sharing their knowledge of photography, mapping and survey planning. A great outcome from the grant has been achieved.   This project was funded through FNPW’s Emergency Bushfire Recovery Grants as part of FNPW’s Healing our land initiative.   Top group photo shows Kiama, Ben, Liza, Jim Mitchell (team volunteer who works on survey, maps and planning), Allan Chawner (team volunteer who works with survey and photography), Carol Carter (team volunteer who works with survey, lighting and administration) and Warren Taggart, Wonnarua Elder and team leader.

items.featured_alt: Greening Australia bushfire recovery nursery, ACT
items.static_title: ACT’s Greening Australia Nursery one of nation’s first Bushfire Recovery Nurseries
items.content:
FNPW has announced ACT’s Greening Australia Nursery as one of the nation’s first Bushfire Recovery Nurseries.

In partnership with global non-profit, One Tree Planted and French beauty brand, L’OCCITANE, this is the first stage in FNPW’s mission to plant one million trees over the next five years in response to the horrendous 2019/20 bushfires.


The grant will extend the capacity of Greening Australia’s Canberra nursery by 40,000 trees, bringing its total capacity to 160,000 trees. This will be a major step in supporting the recovery of the South Coast to Gippsland Corridor, with funding also allocated towards upgrades to the irrigation system, nursery benches and trolleys, as well as essential supplies such as potting mix, trays and pots.

Mr. Graham Fifield, Operations Lead at Greening Australia said: “It’s a great privilege to be awarded a grant as part of FNPW’s mission to plant one million trees across Australia. Together with our passionate volunteers at Greening Australia, it’s our goal to play a major role in rehabilitating our fire-affected landscapes for the benefit of local wildlife and local communities.”
As part of its volunteer program, Greening Australia works with a broad cross section of the Canberra community to provide meaningful and tangible environmental outcomes through a hands-on experience. Currently, volunteers are working towards restoring habitats for threatened species including the Koala, Glossy Black Cockatoo, Scarlet Robin and Swift Parrot and planting native trees including Blackwood, Black She-oak, Myrtle tea-tree and Ribbon Gum.  

Mr. Ian Darbyshire, Chief Executive Officer for the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife said: “Greening Australia will play a significant role in our mission to restore our national ecosystem. Tree planting is essential for the regeneration of our future and plays a vital role in restoring natural habitats, native vegetation and wildlife rehabilitation efforts across Australia.”   FNPW has awarded grant funding to three nursery locations to date including Greening Australia, ACT, Hawkesbury Community Nursery, NSW and Yankalilla Community Nursery, SA. Trees will be planted in national parks across Australia, as well as other public and private lands affected by bushfires.
Since 2015, FNPW has also worked on its initiative “Plant a Tree for Me’ in response to the progressively degrading environment. A donation of just $10 will plant and maintain one tree in the Bushfire Recovery project.

items.featured_alt: Australian Government support for Wildlife Heroes
items.static_title: Australian Government announces additional support for Wildlife Heroes
items.content:
Wildlife Carers will be able to access first aid equipment, animal food and formula, fuel vouchers and mental health support as part of a $1 million funding program announced by the Morrison Government and the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife on 15 February 2020.

The funding is part of the Morrison Government’s initial $50 million bushfire wildlife and habitat recovery package and allows the Foundation to expand its Wildlife Heroes program, accepting applications from across the country.

Building on the success of the NSW program, applications are currently open in Victoria, South Australia, Queensland and the Australian Capital Territory. A Western Australian grant round will open soon. Additional support for all groups for longer term response and mental health support will be rolled out in the coming months.

Wildlife volunteers spend thousands of dollars of their own money every year to rescue, treat and rehabilitate native animals. The recent influx of injured, orphaned and homeless animals has put our wildlife heroes under enormous mental and financial strain. The Wildlife Heroes project will ensure wildlife volunteers get the help they need, so they can continue providing the best care for our amazing native wildlife.

As well as the Foundation’s role in the supply of necessities for emergency responders including safety equipment, animal food and formula, fuel vouchers, first aid equipment, medications and outdoor work equipment, the Morrison Government funding will assist in longer term care and release projects.

Importantly, $150,000 of the Australian Government funding will be used for mental health services to care for our inspirational carers who have witnessed some incredible trauma through their efforts.

Chief Executive of the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife, Ian Darbyshire said that funding will allow the organisation to support carer groups in upgrading facilities at a time of unprecedented need.

“This may include holding and rehabilitation facilities as well as post release supplementary feeding programs,” he said.

“There is an enormous challenge ahead but the dedication of so many carer groups is a real inspiration in the face of that.”

Volunteers involved in wildlife rescue and care can apply for grants through the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife: https://www.fnpw.org.au/wildlifeheroes

Thank you to everyone who has helped us reach every state and territory in need:

DONATE NOW TO SUPPORT OUR AUSSIE WILDLIFE HEROES

Photo by Doug Gimesy

items.featured_alt: Close-up of a greater glider's face at night
items.content:
Australia is known for its unique and diverse wildlife. However, did you know that many of these incredible species are currently under threat?

In fact, Australia holds the unenviable position of leading the world in mammal extinctions, with a staggering 87% of its mammals found nowhere else on Earth. Therefore, safeguarding our unique wildlife is a very important task.

With this purpose in mind, there are numerous actions we can take to prevent more animals from joining the extinction list. In this article, we’ll delve into what defines a “threatened” species, the primary dangers they face and how you can contribute to their conservation.

What is a Threatened Species?

A species is considered “threatened” if it meets one or more of these criteria:

Reduced Population Size: A significant reduction in a species’ numbers, often resulting from factors like habitat loss or disease.

Restricted Geographical Distribution: Species with limited habitats are at risk because they’re more susceptible to threats affecting their small ranges.

Few Mature Individuals: A limited number of mature individuals pose challenges to reproduction and genetic diversity, increasing their risk of extinction.

Key Threats to Australia’s Wildlife

Australia’s endangered species face their greatest challenges from:

Invasive Species: Non-native species disrupt ecosystems, displacing and competing with native species and their habitats. This is the number one threat affecting 82% of all threatened species.

Ecosystem Alterations: Changes to the natural landscape result in habitat loss, fragmentation, or degradation, affecting 74% of listed species. This includes modified fire regimes, which leave species without a suitable habitat.

Agricultural Activities: A pressing concern for 57% of listed species, especially plants, which are most vulnerable in areas where farming and urban development have made big changes to landscapes and land use.

Climate Change: The changing climate poses a significant threat to species by affecting their habitats and food sources.

Categories of Threatened Species

Threatened species are categorised at various spatial scales. The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) maintains the global ‘Red List.’ while the EPBC Act lists species nationally, with states and territories maintaining jurisdiction-specific lists.

Species under the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999 (EPBC Act) are classified as:

  • Extinct: No longer in existence.
  • Extinct in the Wild: Surviving only in captivity or managed populations.
  • Critically Endangered: Extremely high risk of extinction.
  • Endangered: High risk of extinction.
  • Vulnerable: At risk of becoming endangered if threats persist.
  • Conservation Dependent: Require active management to prevent becoming vulnerable, endangered or critically endangered.

Australia’s Disturbing Threatened Species Status

Australia’s unique biodiversity faces alarming challenges: 

  • Since European arrival, 104 Australian species have vanished under national environmental law, more than almost anywhere else on the planet.
  • Over 1,910 species are listed as threatened under the EPBC Act, increasing by an average of 8% since 2016.
  • As of June 2021, nationally 533 animal and 1,385 plant species were listed under the EPBC Act, with over half classified as Endangered or Critically Endangered.
  • Australia has the highest terrestrial mammal extinction rate globally, with 10% of all endemic species (animals that only live in Australia) lost in the last two centuries.
  • Astonishingly, more plant species than animal species are threatened under national, state, and territory legislation.

How Can You Help?

Now that you understand the challenges faced by Australia’s threatened species, here’s how you can make a difference:

Join Backyard Buddies: Learn more about your local species and discover actionable steps to protect them. Every small effort counts and Backyard Buddies is a fantastic way to get involved.

Donate to Growing Parks: Did you know you can donate to acquire land for expanding our national parks and ensuring the perpetual protection of animal and plant species?

Plant trees: Support initiatives aimed at habitat restoration to safeguard our precious biodiversity. Donations can contribute to tree planting in fire-affected areas and threatened ecological communities.

On Threatened Species Day, let us all pledge to play our part in conserving Australia’s unique and irreplaceable wildlife. By understanding the issues, spreading awareness and taking concrete actions, we can make a difference in the fight to protect these incredible species for generations to come.

items.content:
This week we are launching our Banking on the Future project in partnership with the East Gippsland Landcare Network (EGLN). The project is part of our Bushfire Recovery Program, which focuses on restoring what was lost during the 2019/2020 Bushfires. It has been funded by the Federal Government Bushfire Recovery for Wildlife Habitat & Community Grants (BRCG).

The Project

The project is providing funds to establish a central community seedbank in the East Gippsland region, which will be managed by the EGLN. The aim of the seedbank is to store seed from local rare and threatened species, which will then be available to bushfire restoration or revegetation works for the entire region. There will be a walk-in coolroom, seed cleaning machine and an igloo for drying the seed.

Why A Living Seedbank?

Living seedbanks are areas where species are planted so they are easily accessible for seed collection. The image below shows a living seedbank that has been planted in a public garden, so everyone can enjoy the plants and the local Landcare group can collect the seed when it is ready.

Maintaining a living seedbank means seeds aren’t being collected from the wild, which protects the plants and allows them to grow undisturbed. For smaller plants, such as these beautiful wildflowers from the East Gippsland mountains, the main plants can be fenced in to protect them and make it easier to collect the seed. Not all of the seed is collected from each plant, so there is plenty to disperse allowing the natural regeneration of the plants in the area.

Some plants like the Buchan Blue Wattle  are so rare that a special permit is needed to collect the seed in the wild. By growing and maintaining these trees in more accessible places like public gardens, we no longer need to disturb wild plant growth in the bush.

Want to Get Involved?

Anyone interested to learn about seed collecting can join one of the native seed collection workshops being delivered by Wildseed Nursery for communities from Bairnsdale to the NSW border. Give Wildseed Nursery a call at 0419 099 925.

items.featured_alt: Two honeyeaters perched among banksia foliage
items.static_title: The Battle in the Treetops: Feathers, Flowers and a Fight for Survival
items.content:
Across Australia’s woodlands, an invisible war is playing out in the treetops.

As eucalypt forests are cleared, fragmented, or weakened by fire and drought, nectar-feeding birds are being forced into tighter and tighter spaces, and some have turned from neighbours into rivals.

What was once a thriving chorus of species now echoes with tension. And it all comes down to the loss of their lifeblood: flowering eucalypts.

How Habitat Loss Changed Bird Behaviour

When Europeans arrived, vast grassy woodlands and forests were cleared for livestock, farming, and settlement. The understorey, made up of shrubs, native grasses, and small trees that once sheltered smaller birds, disappeared too.

This shift created the perfect conditions for one species to dominate: the Noisy Miner.

These highly social, aggressive honeyeaters thrive in open, cleared environments where trees stand alone without protective shrub layers. In colonies of hundreds, they fiercely defend their territories, dive-bombing and chasing away any bird that comes too close.

Meanwhile, species that once coexisted peacefully, like the Regent Honeyeater and Swift Parrot, have been pushed to the edge.

The Regent Honeyeater’s Struggle

Once common across the woodlands of south-eastern Australia, the Regent Honeyeater (Anthochaera phrygia) is now critically endangered. These nomadic nectar specialists follow the blooms of eucalypts like Yellow Box, Mugga Ironbark, and Swamp Mahogany, often travelling long distances to find food.

But their feeding grounds have been cut apart by clearing, and the flowering cycles they rely on are increasingly disrupted by climate change and drought.

Now, when they arrive in what should be a rich feeding patch, they are met with an army of Noisy Miners defending every branch.

The result is that the Regent struggles to feed, nest, and breed successfully. Even their nests are torn apart by the miners’ relentless attacks.

When Native Becomes the New “Invasive”

The irony is that both the Noisy Miner and the Regent Honeyeater are native species. But human-driven landscape changes have made the Noisy Miner behave much like an invasive one.

Without the dense shrubs that once provided refuge for smaller birds, the miners have spread across farmland, suburbs, and fragmented forests, creating what ecologists call “death zones” or “biological deserts” where almost no other small birds can survive.

Their dominance also sets off a destructive chain reaction:

  • Fewer bird species means less control of insect populations.
  • The miners “farm” insects like psyllids, feeding on their sugary secretions (lerp) but not the insects themselves.
  • As these insects multiply unchecked, they weaken and kill the very eucalypts both species depend on.
  • Fewer healthy trees mean even less food, and the cycle continues.

The Swift Parrot’s Story

Another victim of this imbalance is the Swift Parrot, one of only three migratory parrot species in the world.
These striking green and red birds breed in Tasmania, then cross Bass Strait each winter to feed on the same flowering eucalypts as the Regent Honeyeater.

Their threats are twofold: large-scale logging of Tasmanian Blue Gum forests in their breeding grounds, and the competition for dwindling nectar resources on the mainland.

Even more tragically, introduced predators in Tasmania have learned to attack their nests, driving numbers down further.

Short-term solutions like culling Noisy Miners have shown mixed success, as colonies quickly recolonise and the balance rarely lasts.

The true solution lies in restoring diverse, resilient landscapes that support all species.

That means:

  • Replanting flowering eucalypts and understorey shrubs to provide food and cover.
  • Protecting mature trees and allowing fallen logs to decompose naturally, enriching soil health.
  • Supporting Indigenous fire management practices that prevent catastrophic wildfires while maintaining eucalypt regeneration cycles.
  • Ensuring corridors of connected habitat so birds can move safely and freely between feeding grounds.

Through projects like Saving the Nectar Sippers, our organisation and BirdLife Australia are helping replant and reconnect these vital woodland habitats, giving endangered birds like the Regent Honeyeater a fighting chance to recover.

Why This Fight for Survival Matters

It is easy to think the loss of a few bird species is just nature taking its course.
But every species plays a part in keeping our ecosystems and our lives in balance.

Birds Are the Quiet Architects of Our Forests

Nectar-feeding birds like the Regent Honeyeater and Swift Parrot are vital pollinators for eucalypts. Each time they dip their curved beaks into a flower, they transfer pollen from one blossom to another, helping trees set seed and regenerate.

Without these birds, many of our most iconic eucalypt species would struggle to reproduce naturally. Over time, that means fewer trees, less shade, weaker soils, and less carbon stored in our landscapes.

Forests and woodlands are not just scenery. They are living infrastructure that keeps our air clean, stabilises our climate, filters water, and supports biodiversity from the canopy to the soil.

Healthy Woodlands Mean Healthier People

The loss of pollinators does not just hurt wildlife, it undermines the ecosystems that sustain human communities.

When trees die and soil degrades:

  • Erosion increases, silting up rivers and reducing water quality.
  • Biodiversity declines, which affects natural pest control, seed dispersal, and pollination of crops.
  • Carbon storage drops, making it harder to slow climate change.
  • Heat intensifies, because trees regulate temperature and create local cooling effects.

These shifts are already affecting rural communities and urban environments across Australia. When landscapes lose their diversity, we lose resilience, the ability of nature to bounce back after fire, flood, or drought.

Ecosystems Are Interconnected, Just Like Us

Every living thing in an ecosystem, from the smallest insect to the tallest tree, performs a role that supports the whole.

When one thread is pulled, such as the Regent Honeyeater disappearing from the food web, the entire system begins to fray. The plants it pollinated decline, the insects that relied on those plants vanish, and the soil organisms that depended on their leaf litter weaken. Eventually, even species that seem unrelated are affected.

Humans are not outside this web.

The air we breathe, the food we eat, and the rain that falls all depend on the natural systems that birds quietly help maintain.

Protecting birds is not just about saving wildlife. It is about safeguarding the natural processes that keep Australia alive and thriving.

By restoring woodlands, planting native species, and supporting programs like Saving the Nectar Sippers, we are rebuilding the foundation for a healthier, more resilient planet for every species, including us.

Get Involved

Everyone has a role to play in helping Australia’s birds thrive again. Whether you have a balcony, a backyard, or a whole property, small actions can make a big difference.

Here’s how you can help:

  • Plant native species like grevilleas, bottlebrush, and flowering eucalypts to provide nectar and shelter.
  • Keep some understorey shrubs because birds need dense areas to nest, rest, and escape predators.
  • Leave leaf litter and fallen branches to enrich soil and feed insects, which many birds rely on.
  • Provide water safely with shallow bird baths or small ponds under shade.
  • Avoid chemical sprays and pesticides, which can harm insects and reduce food sources.
  • Protect your patch from pets by keeping cats indoors and dogs supervised to help native wildlife survive.

If you want to do even more, you can support FNPW’s habitat restoration work.

Make a one-off donation or become a Habitat Hero with a monthly gift to help protect native wildlife year-round.

As a Habitat Hero, you’ll receive inspiring updates about the species and landscapes you’re helping to protect, from eucalypt forests to coastal bushland.

items.featured_alt: A Growling Grass Frog at the edge of a wetland.
items.static_title: Bringing Back the Growling Grass Frog
items.content:
There is something quietly extraordinary about a frog call echoing across a restored wetland at dusk. For people who know what that sound means, and what it took to get there, it carries real weight.

The Growling Grass Frog (Litoria raniformis) was once a familiar presence across the wetlands and waterways of south-eastern Australia. Today it is nationally listed as Vulnerable under the EPBC Act, its numbers diminished by habitat loss, altered water regimes, disease and declining water quality. In many parts of its former range, it has simply disappeared.

That is why what is happening at Winton Wetlands in north-east Victoria matters so much.

The species

Meet the Growling Grass Frog

Despite its name, the Growling Grass Frog is actually one of Australia’s more striking amphibians. It is large by local standards, reaching up to 10 centimetres, and is easily recognised by its bright green back marked with dark blotches, a pale belly and a distinctive dark stripe running through the eye. Its call is a low, rasping growl, which is where the name comes from, and during breeding season it can be heard carrying across open water on warm evenings.

It is also, ecologically speaking, a species that punches well above its weight. The Growling Grass Frog is considered an indicator species, meaning its presence, and its breeding success, reflect the broader health of the wetland system around it. When this frog thrives, it tells you that water quality is good, vegetation is functioning, and the hydrological cycles that underpin wetland life are working as they should. When it disappears, something significant has shifted.

The place

Why Winton Wetlands

Located between Benalla and Glenrowan in north-east Victoria, Winton Wetlands has a story worth knowing. The site was once a water storage reservoir, decommissioned and left degraded for years. Over time, sustained investment and genuine commitment to ecological restoration has transformed it into a functioning natural swamp and wetland, receiving environmental water flows and supporting ongoing woodland recovery across the surrounding landscape.

It is exactly the kind of place where careful, science-led conservation can make a lasting difference. The wetland now supports a purpose-built amphibian breeding and quarantine facility, a dedicated interpretation centre for visitors, and an active restoration program. The groundwork has been laid thoughtfully and well.

Historically, the Growling Grass Frog was present in this region. The goal now is to bring it back.

The method

How the translocation works

With support from FNPW, delivery partner Swamps, Rivers and Ranges, the Department of Energy, Environment and Climate Action (DEECA), and the Wettenhall Foundation, a carefully managed translocation program got underway in late 2025.

A cohort of 35 to 40 adult frogs was collected from an established population near Bendigo in central Victoria. After a 30-day quarantine and health screening at the Winton facility, they were released on site alongside the 25 frogs already living there, creating a founding population of 60 to 65 animals.

From there, monitoring continues through to March 2026, tracking survival, movement, habitat use and most importantly, whether the frogs are breeding. Breeding success is the real measure. It signals not just that the frogs have survived the move, but that the wetland is genuinely capable of supporting the full life cycle of a sensitive amphibian species. That is a meaningful ecological threshold.

Wider benefits

More than one species

A restored wetland that can support a Growling Grass Frog population is a wetland that supports a lot of other life too. Waterbirds, invertebrates, native fish and riparian plants all benefit from the same conditions the frog needs. Investing in the recovery of an indicator species is, in a real sense, investing in the recovery of an entire ecosystem.

It is also about building knowledge. Every translocation generates practical data on quarantine protocols, release methods and monitoring approaches that will inform future recovery efforts across north-east Victoria and southern New South Wales, where the species has declined significantly.

The long view

A Future worth protecting

The Growling Grass Frog will not recover overnight. But with the right conditions, the right partners, and sustained care for the landscape it depends on, recovery is genuinely possible.

That is what this project is about. Not just returning a species to a wetland, but demonstrating that large-scale ecological restoration, done well and done with patience, can rebuild the complexity that threatened wildlife needs to survive.

When that growl echoes across Winton Wetlands again on a warm spring evening, it will mean something.

FNPW contributed $36,000 to support the translocation and monitoring program at Winton Wetlands, delivered in partnership with Swamps, Rivers and Ranges and DEECA.

items.featured_alt: Wildlife Heroes new grant round
items.static_title: Bushfire recovery grants to support wildlife volunteers
items.content:
FNPW opened two new grant rounds on Friday, 28 August, making $800,000 available to wildlife care groups across Australia in need of new or replacement equipment and facilities.

Thanks to the Australian Government’s Wildlife Rescue and Rehabilitation initiative and the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife donors and supporters, a funding pool of $500,000 was made available for a National grant round.

An additional $300,000 was contributed by the New South Wales Government for NSW applicants, through its Environmental Trust.

Scie Hoschke, Wildlife ARC

Orphaned swamp wallaby

Wildlife carers continue to recover from the Black Summer bushfires, with many still caring for fire-affected animals. The Wildlife Heroes’ Large Durable Asset grant program will enable licensed volunteer wildlife rehabilitation groups, shelters and not-for-profit veterinary hospitals to buy or build large durable assets for use in the rescue, treatment and rehabilitation of animals as a result of emergency situations.

Sue Swain and grandchildren

Port Stephens Koalas

Sam Chatfield, Wildlife ARC

Ophaned spur winged plover

Simone Aurino, Port Stephens Koalas

Bushfire injured koala

The rounds will prioritise:

– the rebuilding and repair of fire damaged wildlife care infrastructure, including aviaries and enclosures.

– new assets that increase the wildlife rehabilitation sector’s capacity to respond to bushfire emergencies, including vehicles, trailers and treatment equipment.

Detailed guidelines and application instructions are available on the Wildlife Heroes website:

National Wildlife Heroes Large Durable Asset Grants

NSW Wildlife Heroes Large Durable Asset Grants

 

Applications close: Friday, 25 September at 5pm (AEST)

 

Header photo: Julie Harris Wildlife ARC, Orphaned wallaby

All photos courtesy of Doug Gimesy

Funded by the L’OCCITANE Ecosystem Restoration Fund, created in early 2020 by the L’OCCITANE Group to support ecosystems that are severely affected by natural disasters, $228,000* was donated to FNPW as part of an initial two-year commitment. These funds will be dedicated to planting seedlings from our Bushfire Recovery Nurseries in affected areas around Australia to rebuild wildlife habitats and other affected public and private lands.

These funds will be dedicated to planting seedlings from our strong>Bushfire Recovery Nurseries in affected areas around Australia to rebuild wildlife habitats and other affected public and private lands.

The Partnership

Pierre-Emmanuel Joffre, Managing Director, L’OCCITANE Australia, said: “Having arrived in Australia just six months before the bushfires, I was saddened by the devastation they caused to the landscapes, wildlife, and communities around the country. As a brand that originated from nature and the use of botanical ingredients, it has long been a commitment of ours to respect and support biodiversity. So, we are thrilled to be able to support the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife in its mission of planting one million trees around Australia.”

Ian Darbyshire, CEO, Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife said: “It’s thanks to partners such as L’OCCITANE Australia that we can respond quickly to the healing of our land post bushfires. Planting one million trees from our Bushfire Recovery Nurseries around Australia will be an important step in our regeneration. We appreciate the support of the wider community to help restore and protect the future of Australia.”

Currently, the Hawkesbury Nursery produces around 20 – 30,000 native plants endemic to the Hawkesbury region and supplies these plants to numerous revegetation and restoration projects. Trees grown in the nursery will include Forest Red Gum, Grey gum, Black She-oak, and Mountain Blue gum to support threatened species such as the Koala, Yellow-bellied Glider, and Glossy Black Cockatoo.

Hawkesbury Community Nursery is playing a significant role in our mission to restore our national ecosystem. Tree planting is essential for the regeneration of our future and plays a vital role in restoring natural habitats, native vegetation, and wildlife rehabilitation efforts across Australia.

items.featured_alt: Byron Bay Wildlife Hospital mobile hospital truck parked on grass
items.static_title: Byron Bay Wildlife Hospital Goes on Tour with FNPW’s Wildlife Friendly Vets!
items.content:
Australia’s largest mobile wildlife hospital, “Matilda,” owned by Byron Bay Wildlife Hospital, hit the road this month to create awareness about the wonderful work that the mobile hospital can do, and to share how veterinarians, wildlife carers and the general public can work together to give Australian wildlife the quality treatment and care they deserve.

The week-long tour, proudly sponsored by the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife and World Animal Protection Australia, began in Brisbane, then continued on to Currumbin Wildlife Sanctuary on the Gold Coast (QLD), Southern Cross University in Lismore (NSW), Grafton Racecourse (NSW) and had its final day at the Dolphin Marine Conservation Park in Coffs Harbour (NSW). At each stop, veterinarians, wildlife carers and the public were invited to tour the hospital, meet the Byron Bay Wildlife Hospital staff and engage with each other to discuss the ways in which the sector can work together to achieve positive outcomes for Australian wildlife.

The regional tour was the perfect opportunity to help provide Wildlife Friendly Vet resources to the veterinarian community, to encourage wildlife carers to nominate their own Wildlife Friendly Vets and to showcase the Foundation’s strong partnership with Byron Bay Wildlife Hospital.

items.featured_alt: The Field River valley at Hallett Cove, with open grassy slopes and scattered trees.
items.static_title: Caring for Country in Practice with Firesticks
items.content:
Indigenous Land Management at Field River

At Field River in Hallett Cove, the land tells a long story.

The river runs west from the southern Mount Lofty Ranges to the Gulf St Vincent, cutting through steep rocky valleys and open grassy slopes before meeting the sea. Today it sits within suburban Adelaide, bordered by homes, roads and walking tracks. Visitors come for coastal views and open space. But for Kaurna people, this is Kaurna Yarta. It is Country with living cultural memory.

On this landscape, the Kaurna (Kauwi-marnirla) Land Management team at Firesticks is working on Country again.

This work is practical, on-ground Indigenous land management in action. Cultural Fire, ecological restoration, weed control, seasonal observation and community engagement are all part of daily practice. It is about restoring relationship as much as restoring landscape.

Igniting Kaurna Cultural Understanding for All

The program at Field River, Igniting Kaurna Cultural Understanding for All, supports the Kaurna Firesticks Team to strengthen their knowledge, skills and reach. It builds on the broader strategy of Reigniting Kaurna Cultural Practices Through Fire and is delivered in partnership with Firesticks, Green Adelaide, National Parks and Wildlife Service and local councils.

The team at FNPW plays a supporting role, helping connect partners, secure resources and ensure that Kaurna leadership remains at the centre of the work.

Rayne Simpson, a Kaurna and Narungga man and Regional Coordinator with Firesticks, describes the approach:

“On Kaurna Yarta (Country), caring for land and water means recognising the deep cultural knowledge and responsibility that Kaurna Miyurna (People) have carried for thousands of years.

I believe that strong land management comes from genuine partnerships with the Kaurna community, where Traditional Owners guide how Yarta is cared for and their voices are central in decision-making.

By working together and respecting Kaurna knowledge, culture, and connection to Yarta, we can support healthier landscapes, protect cultural heritage, and build a shared future.”

At Field River, you can see that philosophy in action. The Kaurna Firesticks Team are leading land management work, on their own Country.

Indigenous Land Management as a Living System

Indigenous land management is often misunderstood as a single practice, most commonly Cultural Burning. In reality, it is a holistic system of care.

Land, water, fire, plants, animals and people are interconnected. Cultural Lore guides how and when to act. Deep seasonal observation informs decisions. The aim is not short-term intervention but long-term balance.

At Field River, the restoration vision recognises that before colonisation, this landscape was an open grassy woodland system. Grasses and low understorey species were maintained through regular Cultural Fire. These open systems supported biodiversity and allowed for movement, visibility and safety.

Following colonisation, agricultural clearing, grazing and later urban development disrupted these processes. When livestock were removed in the 1990s, woody weeds such as olives expanded rapidly. The absence of regular, low-intensity fire changed fuel structure and increased ecological imbalance.

Indigenous land management responds to these changes in an integrated way. Managing fuel is not separate from managing biodiversity. Water systems are not separate from plant communities. Cultural heritage is not separate from ecological health.

Each decision is made in relationship with Country.

Cultural Fire Within the Broader Practice

Cultural Fire is one tool within this broader system.

It differs fundamentally from conventional hazard reduction burning. Cultural Burning is applied at the right time, in the right conditions, informed by seasonal indicators, plant responses and knowledge held by Traditional Owners. It’s not simply about reducing fuel loads. It’s about promoting regeneration, encouraging specific species, and protecting cultural sites.

At Field River, Cultural Fire sits alongside targeted woody weed control and ecological restoration works. Together, these actions reduce extreme fuel loads while also supporting native grasslands and culturally significant plant communities.

Fire is guided by relationship, not solely by prescription.

Why This Matters in an Urban Landscape

Field River sits within metropolitan Adelaide. Suburbs such as Hallett Cove and Sheidow Park surround the valley. Visitor numbers are high, particularly during warmer months. Built assets, walking trails and adjacent residential areas increase the complexity of land management.

Historical fire management planning in the southern foothills has identified high fuel levels and the risks associated with urban interface landscapes

The Field River Restoration Plan similarly emphasises the importance of restoring ecological processes while protecting life and property.

Aboriginal land management offers a proactive pathway to resilience.

Rather than responding only when conditions become extreme, cultural practice seeks to prevent imbalance before disaster occurs. By reintroducing regular, controlled fire and addressing weed-driven fuel accumulation, the Kaurna Firesticks Team is reducing risk while strengthening biodiversity.

Governance and Cultural Authority

Central to this work is governance.

Cultural authority remains with the Kaurna Nation. Knowledge sovereignty is respected. Decisions are guided by Kaurna leadership, supported by Firesticks’ Indigenous governance structures and advisory mechanisms.

Partnerships with Green Adelaide, National Parks and Wildlife Service and other agencies are collaborative, but Kaurna leadership is not diluted within these arrangements. Practice informs policy, not the other way around.

Government agencies are engaged in conversations about how regulatory frameworks can better reflect on-ground Aboriginal land management. This includes acknowledging that traditional fire practice operates within a legal environment that has historically limited Indigenous access to Country.

Transparency and trust are foundational. This is long-term work that recognises that restoring both landscape and governance takes time.

What This Builds

At Field River, the impacts are already visible.

Fuel loads are being reduced in a way that supports ecological outcomes. Culturally significant areas are being protected. Young Kaurna people are gaining employment, skills and pathways into leadership. The broader community is learning that Aboriginal land management is not historical knowledge, but contemporary practice.

The Field River Restoration Project recognises that landscape recovery is a multi-decade process. Cultural revival operates on a similar timescale.

This work builds resilience at multiple levels: ecological, cultural, social and institutional.

Caring for Country is not an abstract concept at Field River. It is active, practical and grounded in place. It is Kaurna people working on Kaurna Yarta, supported by partners who recognise that meaningful change happens when Traditional Owners lead the care of their own lands.

In the heart of urban Adelaide, that leadership is reshaping how land management is understood and practiced.

items.featured_alt: silver banksia tree in Charleston Conservation Park South Australia
items.static_title: Charleston Conservation Park: From Ashes to Banksias
items.content:
When you step into Charleston Conservation Park today, two stories meet your eye. Charred trunks of old banksias still stand from the bushfires of 2019, stark reminders of what was lost. But around them, a new generation of silver banksias is thriving, young trees raised in nurseries and planted by volunteers now bringing the woodland back to life.

This is the landscape’s renewal in motion. It’s a story of resilience, of seed saved just in time, and of a community determined to restore one of South Australia’s rarest woodland habitats.

A Woodland Worth Protecting

Charleston Conservation Park sits in the Adelaide Hills, just 40 minutes from the city, but it feels a world away. It protects grassy and heathy woodland: manna gums, drooping she-oaks, and most important of all, the silver banksia.

Once common across southern Australia, silver banksias have vanished from much of their range. In South Australia, they hang on in scattered pockets. Charleston is one of their last strongholds.

The park was first proclaimed in 1976 at 54 hectares, and 2017, the park grew by nearly half when an adjoining grazing property was added. The new land was worn down by years of livestock, but it held potential. That same potential made the fire hit even harder.

When Fire Changed Everything

n December 2019, the Cudlee Creek bushfire swept through more than 23,000 hectares of the Adelaide Hills. Charleston Conservation Park was caught in the path.

Silver banksias, already hanging on in small numbers, were especially hard hit. Unlike eucalypts, which can resprout, banksias are usually killed outright by intense fire and rely on seed stored in old cones to regenerate. But after years of drought, little viable seed was left on the trees.

What survived was memory, and seed stored in sheds.

Walking through the park now, you can still see the blackened trunks of those lost banksias. But look closer, and you’ll notice rings of young plantings pushing up through the ash, signs of hope rising from devastation.

Community Seeds of Recovery

For years before the fire, a group of locals called the Friends of Charleston Conservation Park had been collecting seed. Quiet work. Careful work. No one knew how urgently it would be needed.

After the fire, that saved seed became a lifeline.

Volunteers, along with Kersbrook Landcare and local nurseries, grew tens of thousands of seedlings. Since 2019, more than 20,000 silver banksias have been planted by hand. That effort is rebuilding an ecosystem from the roots up.

Another 7,500 native plants have gone in too, thanks to support from programs like the Hawke’s Brewing Threatened Species Landcare Grant. Every one of those plants matters – to the woodland birds, to the pygmy possums, to the soil, and to the people who refused to give up.

How FNPW Has Helped

FNPW’s role has been to support the expansion zone, the eastern half of Charleston added in 2017. This section had been heavily grazed and needed targeted intervention. Through our funding, thousands of plants were grown in nurseries and planted into this area, helping to establish new banksia stands and restore a degraded landscape.

Our focus has been on rebuilding structure and diversity so the park’s woodland can knit back together and provide the food, shelter and resilience wildlife need.

Why Silver Banksias Matter

Silver banksias are a keystone species, producing abundant nectar that feeds honeyeaters, insects and even small mammals like the western pygmy possum. Their cones provide seed for birds, while their structure offers shade and shelter for countless creatures. For thousands of years, they also played a role in stabilising soils and supporting the balance of woodland ecosystems across southern Australia.

If silver banksias were to disappear, entire food webs would unravel. The loss of their flowers and seed would ripple across species that depend on them, leaving woodlands weaker and less resilient. Protecting and restoring this species helps ensure that both wildlife and the broader landscape have the resources they need to survive and adapt.

Signs of Renewal in Charleston Conservation Park

Today, signs of renewal are everywhere. Kangaroo grass and speargrass tussocks are spreading across the ground layer, holding soil and providing habitat for insects and small reptiles. Honeyeaters dart between young banksias, and robins perch low in the recovering woodland.

The contrast is striking: old, fire-scarred trunks stand side by side with fresh banksia seedlings, living proof that nature, given the right help, can bounce back.

Looking Ahead

Charleston’s recovery is still a work in progress. Young trees need time to mature, and ongoing challenges like drought, weeds and other impacts of climate change remain. But every new planting strengthens this landscape and every seedling brings back a piece of the woodland puzzle.

With continued care, Charleston will not just recover, it will thrive, providing a haven for threatened species and a place where the community can witness resilience firsthand.

Get Involved

Donate to our restoration work

Your support can help to fund nurseries, buy local seed, and put tools in the hands of volunteers across landscapes in need across Australia.

Become a Habitat Hero

By signing up as a monthly donor, you’ll be helping us restore and protect habitats and landscapes all year round. Your ongoing support ensures seedlings get planted, cared for, and nurtured into thriving woodlands that provide vital habitat for threatened species

Together, we can ensure Charleston’s story is one of recovery, resilience, and renewal.

items.featured_alt: David Goldman
items.content:
Hosted by: Vincent Turner

About the Guest

David Goldman is a seasoned professional in the field of environmental conservation, and a representative of the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife in Australia. With a dedication to the preservation of national parks and wildlife, David brings a wealth of insight into biodiversity and land management. Based in Sydney, Australia, his role involves collaborative efforts to expand the reach and protection of natural reserves across the country, aiming to save threatened species and enhance ecological resilience.

Episode Summary

In this engaging episode of Shape the System, host Vincent interviews David Goldman from the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife. Together, they delve into the pressing issues surrounding biodiversity, wildlife preservation, and ecosystem resilience in Australia. They discuss innovative ways of safeguarding natural habitats and the pivotal role of land conservation in maintaining a diverse and flourishing biosphere.

David sheds light on the foundation’s key projects, including the pursuit of enlarging national parks and establishing green corridors. He highlights the importance of eliminating invasive species to allow native flora and fauna to thrive, and the role of community participation in protecting and revitalizing the environment. With a comprehensive look at government partnerships and philanthropy, this episode is rich with insights into the tactical steps being taken to meet Australia’s 30×30 conservation commitments.

The conversation further explores the evolution of the foundation, which has transitioned from purely land acquisition to encompassing land regeneration and public engagement through the Backyard Buddies program. They also touch on the economics of land conservation, including engaging with private landholders and the future of sustainable revenue models for environmental charities.

Key Takeways

  • The Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife aims to protect 30% of Australia’s natural land by 2030 by purchasing and regenerating land adjacent to national parks.
  • Biodiversity preservation has a direct impact on ecological resilience, crucial for combating extreme weather events and climate change.
  • Efforts include volunteering, community nurseries, and working with local governments to eliminate invasive species and promote native ecosystems.
  • The concept of ‘Backyard Buddies’ promotes individual action, underscoring the connection between one’s backyard and larger ecological systems.
  • Innovative models for sustainable futures include leveraging carbon sequestration to fund further land acquisition, demonstrating an evolution from traditional donation-based funding.

Notable Quotes

“The federal government put out a list, continuously update that list. It’s part of the EPBC act, and currently there’s almost 2000 threatened species, both floor and fauna.” – David Goldman

“Often what our work will involve before even handing it over the land over as national park is that revegetation or regeneration of the land.” – David Goldman

“87% of the money that comes to us, we will put it back into the purpose.” – David Goldman

“I personally, and I’m sure there are a number of people at the office, don’t believe that the donor model is necessarily the long-term sustainable future.” – David Goldman

“So it’s about being a bit more clever in how we look at our future and what revenue models we put in place to ensure that we are sustainable.” – David Goldman

Resources

No specific resources or references were mentioned in the transcript.

Embark on a journey through the transformative efforts of the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife by listening to the full episode. Discover the innovative strategies that are shaping the future of Australia’s natural landscapes. Stay tuned for more episodes from Shape the System to be inspired by stories of individuals and organizations redefining how we interact with and protect our planet.

Shape the System is  an independent podcast with support from KPMG High Growth Ventures

items.featured_alt: Kosciuszko to Coast Connect and Protect glideways logo
items.content: Primary school-aged children can learn about the threatened gliding possums and other Australian animals in a new book called Drawing Australian Gliders. Created by Canberra-based artist Kate Smith and Kate’s ecologist parents, Peter and Judy Smith. Drawing Australian Gliders book aims to teach children about the habits, history, and interesting facts about threatened species of gliders in Australia such as the Greater Glider, the tiny Feather-tail Glider, and the Sugar Glider. Also, this book provides essential drawing tips and takes the readers on a drawing adventure. “By combining natural history and art, we hope to foster better awareness and appreciation of these unique and exquisite Australian animals and their magnificent forest habitats,” Dr. Smith said All of the proceeds from the book’s sales will be put back into the conservation efforts along the Kanangra-Boyd to Wyangala wildlife corridor, an important migration route between the Greater Blue Mountains and Wyangala Dam. Gliding possums can be found in eucalypt forests and woodlands extensively along Australia’s east coast and ranges, in an area known as the Great Eastern Ranges. The ranges are a 3000 kilometre stretch of land from Victoria through NSW and north Queensland. In NSW, all the gliding possums are protected species. The Greater Glider, Australia’s largest glider, is vulnerable to extinction under the Australian Government’s threatened species legislation. The Australian Government recently lifted the species’ conservation status to endangered. “The gliders are threatened chiefly by climate change and by clearing and degradation of eucalypt forests and woodlands,” Dr Smith said. K2W Glideways Petaurus Connections project is supporting the project which is jointly funded by the NSW Government Saving our Species (SOS) program and the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife (FNPW).
