items.featured_alt: remarkable southern flinders ranges
items.static_title: Southern Flinders Ranges: Where Ancient Landscapes Meet Living Culture
items.content:
Rising from the rolling plains of South Australia, the Southern Flinders Ranges is a place where ancient geology, rich biodiversity, and deep cultural heritage come together. Over hundreds of millions of years, wind, water, and shifting earth have carved a dramatic landscape of rugged ridges, deep gorges, and sweeping valleys. Today, these ranges are far more than a scenic backdrop. They are a biodiversity stronghold, a cultural treasure for First Nations peoples, and a natural refuge for plants and animals that have adapted to life in a challenging environment.

Why the Southern Flinders Ranges Matters for Biodiversity

The Southern Flinders Ranges holds a unique position in South Australia’s conservation landscape. Here, semi-arid and temperate ecosystems overlap, creating a rare blend of habitats that can support an impressive diversity of species. Many of these plants and animals are endemic, found nowhere else in the world.

This area also acts as a climate refuge, offering shelter and food in a region where rising temperatures and changing rainfall patterns are placing increasing pressure on wildlife. The ranges are also of immense geological importance, with rock formations preserving some of the oldest evidence of complex life on Earth.

Flora of the Southern Flinders Ranges

The vegetation here reflects the adaptability of life in a landscape of extremes. Ridge tops are dominated by sugar gums, cypress pines, and black oak woodlands. In sheltered gullies, you can find grevilleas, lilies, and ferns, while wildflowers burst into bloom after rainfall, carpeting the hillsides in colour.

The endangered Flinders Fingers orchid (Caladenia xantholeuca) is one of the region’s botanical treasures, found nowhere else, while wattles and native grasses help stabilise soil and provide food and habitat for wildlife.

Wildlife of the Southern Flinders Ranges

The Southern Flinders is home to an extraordinary range of animals, from kangaroos and emus to smaller but equally vital species such as dunnarts, planigales, and the cryptic streambank froglet. The Yellow-footed Rock-wallaby, with its distinctive banded tail and golden limbs, has made a strong comeback through focused conservation work.

Predator-proofing and reintroduction programs have brought species like the western quoll (Idnya) and brushtail possum (Virlda) back to the region after decades of absence. Reptiles, including goannas, dragons, and the once-vulnerable Flinders Ranges worm-lizard, add to the diversity, alongside a wealth of birdlife such as wedge-tailed eagles, parrots, and honeyeaters.

Cultural Significance to First Nations Peoples

The Wapma Thura–Southern Flinders Ranges National Park is the Country of the Nukunu people, whose ancestral connections stretch back tens of thousands of years. “Wapma Thura” means “Snake People” in Nukunu language, a reference to an important creation story.

Today, the park is co-managed with Nukunu Traditional Owners, ensuring that cultural knowledge and practices are embedded in land management. This partnership protects not only the ecological values of the ranges but also the cultural heritage that has shaped them for millennia.

Climate Challenges: Drought and Fire

Like much of South Australia, the Southern Flinders Ranges faces the growing impacts of climate change. Prolonged droughts have reduced water availability, stressed vegetation, and increased competition for resources among wildlife. Reduced soil moisture makes it harder for plant communities to recover, leaving landscapes more vulnerable to erosion.

Bushfires are another serious threat. Hotter, drier conditions have increased both the frequency and intensity of fires in the region. Fire can devastate habitat in a matter of hours, destroying food sources and shelter for threatened species, with recovery taking years or even decades in some areas.

The Remarkable Southern Flinders Project

The Remarkable Southern Flinders Project is a $10 million initiative designed to connect and protect the landscapes of the Southern Flinders. It has united previously separate reserves, including Telowie Gorge, Wirrabara Range, Spaniards Gully, and part of Mount Remarkable National Park, into one continuous conservation area.

This project is about more than protecting land. It creates a world-class nature-based tourism destination with mountain-bike trails, hiking routes, and visitor facilities that encourage people to experience the region while respecting its ecological limits.

Our role in the project includes supporting habitat restoration, improving visitor infrastructure, and working closely with Traditional Owners to ensure cultural and environmental values remain at the heart of all activities.

A Future Worth Protecting

Standing on a ridge in the Southern Flinders, you might see a wedge-tailed eagle circling overhead or hear the rustle of a rock-wallaby among the cliffs. In spring, orchids and wattles bloom in abundance. At night, quolls and possums emerge under the southern stars, continuing the cycles of life that have unfolded here for countless generations.

The Southern Flinders Ranges is a living system, an ancient geological wonder, and a cultural landscape that holds the stories of the First Nations people who have cared for it for millennia. Protecting it means safeguarding biodiversity, respecting cultural heritage, and ensuring that future generations can connect with its beauty and significance.

Your donation can support projects that restore habitats, protect wildlife, and strengthen cultural stewardship in special places like the Southern Flinders Ranges. Together, we can help safeguard Australia’s unique landscapes and the species that depend on them.

Donate today and be part of creating a healthier, more resilient future for people, wildlife, and Country.

items.featured_alt: Kosciuszko National Park recovery
items.content:
The 2020 fires devastated one-third of Kosciuszko National Park, inspiring volunteer firefighters from southern Poland to raise over $150,000 AUD to aid its regeneration. The donation made to FNPW was in recognition of Polish-Australian relations, particularly considering the national park is named after Polish military leader, General Kościuszko.

The funding which was provided to NSW National Parks and Wildlife, contractors and flora and fauna specialists, have allowed the following activities to commence works.

Fauna Surveys:

Funding has been allocated to the survey of birds and insectivorous bats over a total of 28 heavily burnt sites. FNPW is pleased to report that insectivorous bats were present at all 15 bat sites. When compared to previous data, these surveys suggest an extreme drop in the bird population. Funding has been allocated to re-survey these areas next summer. This will provide valuable information on how species are recovering and indicate long term impacts on species populations and status.

Bat Boxes:

Bats are a critical part of healthy, functioning ecosystems – small ‘micro’ bats control insect populations and large ‘macro’ bats pollinate and spread the seed of native vegetation. With the assistance of these funds and the National Parks Foundation, 200 bat boxes have been installed using a methodology to develop knowledge on the effectiveness of two box designs.

NPWS Aboriginal Discovery Ranger, Shane Herrington installing bat boxes 

Erosion Control:

The eroding slope in the sub-alpine zone of Kiandra was stabilised to assist the natural recovery process by reducing the impact of winter conditions on the exposed landscape. Water holding structures were installed at Rocky Plains Bog to combat the extensive loss of vegetation caused by the recent bushfire season.

Field officer and firefighter, Raymond Sanderson installing wind and water control measures at Kiandra. Timber stakes were then cut off for safety.

Recovery of Endangered Species:

The regeneration of the critically endangered Mountain Pygmy-Possum’s (pictured below) habitat was supported by planting approximately 3,500 plants. In addition to erosion control, water holding structures, such as native grass and sphagnum, provide a habitat for many rare native flora and fauna, such as the endangered Broad Toothed Rat. The seeds of vulnerable vegetation and species were collected from sections of unburnt forest to create a seed bank for future planting.

The critically endangered Mountain Pygmy-Possum

Looking Forward:

The remaining funds have been allocated to work scheduled for next summer and we will provide updates as the regeneration efforts of Kosciuszko National Park continue.

Unfortunately, the enormous impact of the recent bushfire season means that the scope of works required will continue to grow and require further support. If you would like to make a donation, you can do so here. 

For more information see Kosciuszko National Park 2020 Fire Recovery

items.featured_alt: Small bird perched on the smooth trunk of a eucalypt
items.static_title: Restoring the Grossmans Block: Breathing Life Back into the Southern Flinders
items.content:
In the heart of South Australia, the Southern Flinders stretch from Beetaloo to Wilmington. It is a landscape of rugged peaks, winding gorges, and ancient woodlands. More than scenery, this region is alive with rare plants, unique animals, rich cultural heritage, and a growing tourism economy shaped by nature.

One of the newest pieces of this living puzzle is the Grossmans Block – 430 hectares now protected as part of the Southern Flinders Precinct Park Complex. Securing this land is a vital step in stitching the region’s ecosystems back together.

Why the Grossmans Block matters

For decades, Grossmans was worn down by grazing and cropping. Native plants were trampled, waterholes disturbed, and fragile soils left exposed. The damage spread beyond the property, fragmenting habitats and putting vulnerable species at risk.

Now that the land is under protection, those pressures have been lifted. The difference is already clear:

  • 13 rare plant species are safeguarded.
  • 9 conservation-listed animals now have secure habitat.
  • The nationally significant Flinders Worm-lizard has a protected refuge.

The transformation has already begun. With stock removed, weeds controlled, and careful management in place, Grossmans is shifting from a degraded paddock to a thriving refuge. Looking ahead, the goal is to scale up restoration, expand habitat corridors, and strengthen First Nations partnerships across the region.

This is not just one patch of land saved. It is a critical link in restoring ecological connections across the Southern Flinders.

A mosaic of life

Grossmans is a patchwork of ecosystems. River Red Gums shade the creeks, rocky ridges hold native grasses and Yakka, and Blue Gum and Sheoak woodlands provide shelter for birds, reptiles, and small mammals. Even areas scarred by fire or grazing still hold the seeds of renewal.

These ecosystems include:

  • River Red Gum creek lines, once overgrazed, now offering nesting space for woodland birds and shelter for reptiles.
  • Blue Gum woodlands, beginning to rebound, providing food for small marsupials and pollinators.
  • Sheoak and Blue Gum woodlands, among the most intact areas, rich with insects that sustain species like the diamond firetail.
  • Open Blue Gum woodland, degraded but with strong potential to recover as habitat for the Flinders Worm-lizard.
  • Mallee pockets, small in size yet vital for ground-dwelling fauna and nectar-feeding insects.
  • Burnt Blue Gum and Sugar Gum woodland, recovering since the 2014 Bangor Fire, now offering food and perches for wedge-tailed eagles.
  • Exotic grasslands, still dominated by non-native species, but with grazing removed they can regenerate into native habitat for small mammals and ground-nesting birds.

A Bushland Assessment in 2022 confirmed the importance of this diversity, identifying seven vegetation types and awarding the site 2,724.95 SEB (Significant Environmental Benefit) points. In simple terms, Grossmans is among the most valuable conservation land in the region. With grazing gone and good rains ahead, many of these areas will bounce back quickly, creating fresh shelter and food for wildlife.

Connecting the bigger picture

On the map, Grossmans sits beside Beetaloo Reservoir and on the edge of the newly created Wapma Thura–Southern Flinders Ranges National Park. Protecting this land:

  • Closes gaps in habitat corridors.
  • Links creek lines, woodlands, and ridges into one connected system.
  • Places the block under the same protections as the wider park.

Strategic acquisitions like this do more than save individual sites. They turn scattered fragments into functioning landscapes.

A shared effort

Securing Grossmans was only possible through strong partnerships and major investment.

The Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife contributed, enabling the Department for Environment and Water (DEW) to purchase the property. Spread across four parcels, the block is now protected under the National Parks and Wildlife Act 1972 and will be managed by DEW for at least the next decade.

This project came to life thanks to the combined efforts of governments, councils, local organisations, and the Nukunu Wapma Thura Aboriginal Corporation. Together, they are shaping the Southern Flinders into a conservation stronghold and a destination for people who love nature.

Key partners include:

  • The South Australian and Australian Governments
  • Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife
  • Northern Areas Council
  • District Council of Mount Remarkable
  • Port Pirie Regional Council
  • Regional Development Australia Yorke and Mid-North
  • Nukunu Wapma Thura Aboriginal Corporation

How you can help

Securing Grossmans was just the beginning. Real restoration takes patience, monitoring, and ongoing resources. You can play a part:

  • Donate to support weed control, habitat recovery, and species surveys.
  • Become a monthly donor to provide steady, reliable support.
  • Spread the word so more people know why this land matters.

Every action helps turn Grossmans into a cornerstone of a thriving Southern Flinders Precinct.

items.featured_alt: Young eucalyptus leaves in soft green light
items.content:
Riverina Highlands Landcare nursery upgrade plans are becoming more concrete with a start made on new irrigation, shedding, and slabs. The Foundation for National Parks has made much-needed infrastructure improvements possible through a Bushfire Recovery Grant.

Compliments to the nursery such as new irrigation piping and a water tank will improve the plant irrigation and the capture of irrigation runoff, saving hundreds of thousands of liters per day. In addition, the solar array will power the pump, which will save electricity costs and decrease the environmental footprint.

This compliments funding the nursery and wider landscape have received to help stimulate the local economy and recover wildlife and habitat values after the fires. These infrastructure upgrades were not part of the criteria in other grants but were the missing piece of the puzzle needed to increase the nurseries’ production. The Foundation for National Parks contribution will allow the nursery to rise to these challenges and meet demands for replanting the links lost in the landscape, creating new wildlife corridors and animal food sources such as nectar, berries, and seeds.

The Riverina Highlands Landcare Nursery runs a thriving volunteer program which has always been integral to its operation and part of local wellbeing in this sector. It is also a potential place for healing for those who wish to take positive action after the fires and the help would be welcome in the coming two years as the nursery is upgraded and busy delivering plants across our region for Landcare volunteers. The nursery has been run successfully for many years now by volunteers from the Riverina Highlands Landcare Network as a not-for-profit venture and supported by Snowy Valleys Council.

Riverina Highlands Landcare Nursery provides a wide range of revegetation stock that is sourced from local seed and will therefore thrive in our local conditions and suit wildlife. You can find trees, shrubs, and more importantly a range of grasses and small groundcovers that make up a healthy understorey ground layer locally. These different layers provide a healthy and weed-free environment that is needed by the wide range of birds, reptiles, and mammals in this area and particularly those special creatures we have all worried about after the fires wiped out vast areas of habitat in one go, two years ago.

Riverina Landcare Nursery is also available 5 weekdays for home garden plants, with many of the local native plants suitable for the suburban block sizes and a great thing to plant to encourage local special foragers like colorful King parrots who love to visit backyards around here.

items.featured_alt: Yankalilla bushfire recovery nursery, SA
items.static_title: SA’s Yankalilla Community Nursery one of Australia’s first Bushfire Recovery Nurseries
items.content:
The Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife has awarded one of three Bushfire Recovery Nursery grants to Yankalilla Community Nursery in South Australia.

In partnership with global non-profit, One Tree Planted and French beauty brand, L’OCCITANE, this is the first stage in FNPW’s mission to plant one million trees over the next five years in response to the horrendous 2019/20 bushfires.

The grant awarded to the District Council of Yankalilla will extend the capacity of its current nursery by 25,000 seedlings, to plant a total of 40,000 trees. This will be a major step in supporting the recovery of the Mount Lofty to Kangaroo Island Connection. The funding will also provide essential resources such as fencing, nursery benches, hygiene and plumbing and potting structures.

Corey Jackson, the Coastal Conservation Officer at the District Council of Yankalilla, said “It’s a privilege to support FNPW’s mission to plant one million trees over the next five years. Our ultimate goal has always been to plant and restore native vegetation and this grant will ensure we can expand our scope to regenerate even more land affected by the bushfires.”

The Yankalilla Community Nursery was established to grow local native plants for coastal community projects and species recovery, with a separate compound provided by the District Council of Yankalilla for volunteers from the Normanville Natural Resource Centre to expand vegetation growth.

A key focus for the community nursery will be to grow the Drooping She-oak and associated plants as part of the habitat and food source recovery for the Glossy Black Cockatoo. Once common on the Fleurieu Peninsula, the cockatoos are now found only on Kangaroo Island and were heavily impacted by the recent bushfires.

Mr. Ian Darbyshire, Chief Executive Officer for the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife.said: “Yankalilla Community Nursery will play a significant role in our mission to restore our national ecosystem. Tree planting is essential for the regeneration of our future and plays a vital role in restoring natural habitats, native vegetation and wildlife rehabilitation efforts across Australia.”

FNPW has awarded grant funding to three nursery locations to date including Yankalilla Community Nursery, SA, Greening Australia, ACT, and Hawkesbury Community Nursery, NSW. Trees will be planted in national parks across Australia, as well as other public and private lands affected by bushfires

Since 2015, FNPW has also worked on its initiative “Plant a Tree For Me’ in response to the progressively degrading environment. A donation of $10 will plant and maintain one tree in a Bushfire Recovery Nursery.

items.featured_alt: Northern quoll close-up
items.content:
The Northern Quoll is one of Australia’s most unique and fascinating animals. Known for its feisty temperament, this small carnivorous marsupial plays a vital role in maintaining the health of ecosystems across Northern Australia. But this remarkable species is in serious trouble.

Today, it faces numerous threats, from habitat destruction to the deadly invasion of cane toads. Here’s why we need your help to protect them and how you can get involved. 

What Makes the Northern Quoll Special?  It is the smallest of the four quoll species, but don’t let its size fool you. Weighing up to 1.2 kg, it is a skilled predator with a striking appearance: white spots on its back and rump, and a long unspotted tail that can grow up to 35 cm. These agile climbers use their short “thumb” on their hindfeet for gripping and navigating rocky terrain.  This “native cat” is more than just cute; as a predator, the Northern Quoll helps regulate the populations of small mammals, playing an important role in balancing ecosystems. 

Why Is the Northern Quoll Threatened? 

Once thriving across the northern third of Australia, Northern Quoll populations have dramatically declined. The introduction of invasive species such as feral cats and cane toads, changes in fire management practices, and land-use alterations have devastated their habitats. 

Cane toads, in particular, pose a deadly threat. Quolls, attempting to hunt these toxic invaders, often fall victim to the poison the toad glands just underneath their skin. 

Protecting the Northern Quoll 

The Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife (FNPW) is actively supporting two vital conservation projects aimed at safeguarding the future of the Northern Quoll. These initiatives involve First Nations Rangers who are leading the charge in remote regions like Arnhem Land and the Kimberley. Here’s a glimpse into the incredible work happening on the ground: 

  • Warddeken Mayh (Species) Recovery Project: In partnership with the Karrkad Kanjdji Trust, First Nations Rangers are using advanced data and traditional ecological knowledge to protect threatened species like the Northern Quoll (Djabbo). Through controlled fire management and monitoring their numbers, First Nations Rangers are creating safe habitats for the quolls, ensuring these precious creatures can survive in a changing environment. 
  • b>Regional Ecology Support Project: With the Kimberley Land Council and regional Ecologist Marlee Hutton, Indigenous Rangers are monitoring species like the Northern Quoll and gathering crucial population data. FNPW’s support has enabled them to blend traditional knowledge with modern science, resulting in more effective conservation efforts. 

How You Can Take Action 

You can make a difference today by voting for the Northern Quoll in the Project’s “Marsupial of the Year 2024“. Every vote will help us raise funds to continue with our conservation efforts. Together, we can ensure the survival of the Northern Quoll and protect the ecosystems they help sustain.  

VOTE FOR THE NORTHERN QUOLL

items.featured_alt: Blue Mountains
items.content:
This Saturday, 18 April is World Heritage Day which recognises Monuments and Sites, with a theme of shared cultures, shared heritage and shared responsibility.

The Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife is proud to have awarded the Blue Mountains World Heritage Institute (BMWHI) with a grant to undertake a citizen science project which will monitor the impacts of climate change on the ecosystems of The Greater Blue Mountains World Heritage Area of Australia.

Following the impact of the 2019/20 bushfires, which affected approximately 80% of the million hectares of national park and wilderness, the project will monitor flora and fauna and the impact on threatened ecosystems like upland swamps, facing intensifying drought, fire and local flooding. Monitoring activities will span across Blackheath, Katoomba, Wentworth Falls, Lawson and Springwood, totalling 28 sites overall.

Photo courtesy of Roger Lembit

Dr John Merson from BMWHI said the findings will enhance community capacity and knowledge, enabling beyond-the-project monitoring programs to be maintained and developed. “We are installing new equipment, including camera traps, cameras and audio recording devices to monitor all five eco-system types including rainforest, wet sclerophyll, dry sclerophyll, heath and swamps. A new App is also being developed that will feed data into the BioCollect system for inclusion in the Atlas of Living Australia.”

Teams will make weekly site visits to record images and collect data, with the findings being published via community events, online, newsletters, reports and journal articles.

Currently, NSW National Parks and Services has closed all historic sites in response to the COVID-19 emergency, however John Merson from BMWHI encourages visitation in future.

“The biodiversity and unique ecosystems of the Greater Blue Mountains World Heritage area provide clean air and water to the Greater Sydney region, and its extraordinary beauty attracts over five million visitors a year.

Nature is slowly but surely recovering from the devastating fires of the past few months, but many species will be struggling. Much like testing for the Covid-19 pandemic, we need to gather as much information as possible to understand the impacts of more extreme fires, and weather conditions driven by climate change. During this challenging time, we are following strict distancing protocols while still aiming to gather as much data as possible, so we can continue to nurture and conserve this exceptional place.”

FNPW is also supporting a project in the Gondwana Rainforest region through the “Saving Our Species” project for the Albert’s Lyrebird and supported the acquisition of Nilpena Station fossil sites that are part of the World Heritage bid by the SA Government.

items.featured_alt: Daintree rainforest
items.static_title: Take time for nature this World Environment Day
items.content:
Each year on June 5 is World Environment Day, this years theme is biodiversity and ‘Time for Nature’. A day where we recognise the importance of the environment and nature in our world and for our own health.

As the UN World Environment Day Time for Nature campaign says:

These are exceptional times in which nature is sending us a message: To care for ourselves we must care for nature.

This World Environment Day we are asking everyone to take time and get out into nature. The more we take time to learn about the natural world around us the more we take the time to care for it.

With COVID-19 restrictions easing in each state it is a great time to take time with your family or friends to explore our national parks.

Whichever state you are in there is a national park that you can visit this weekend.

NSW 

Most NSW parks and campgrounds are open this weekend. Campground and cabin bookings are essential so check your parks website before heading out.

FNPW tip for this weekend: See if you can spot a Gymea Lily on the Old Great North Road World Heritage walk at Dharug National Park

QLD

QLD parks that were closed due to COVID-19 are now open. Some restrictions apply for visitor numbers. Bookings for camping and vehicle access can be booked online.

FNPW tip for this weekend: Step back in time to the Gondwana Rainforests of Lamington National Park and listen out for bowerbirds or catbirds, relatives to the oldest lineage of songbirds in the world.

SA 

Parks in South Australia are open! The June park of the month is Deep Creek Conservation Park, which also happens to be the location of one of our Plant a Tree for Me sites supporting revegetation for the Black Glossy Cockatoo populations of SA.

FNPW tip for this weekend: Head to Deep Creek Conservation Park and keep an eye out for whales on the horizon!

NT 

From midday Friday June 5 and unless closed for seasonal closures, parks and reserves will be open and accessible to Territorians.

FNPW tip for this weekend: Grab your binoculars and head to Litchfield National Park and count the how many of its 169 bird species you see.

TAS

Tasmanians can enjoy national parks his long weekend, with restrictions to easing from 3pm Friday, 5 June. Some visitor centres and multi-day walking tracks will be closed until June 15, so check the Tassie Parks website before you head out on your adventure.

FNPW tip for this weekend: See if you can catch the last of the fagus turning or the first winter snow at Mount Field National Park

WA

With intrastate borders still closed it’s a great opportunity for locals to explore WA. All parks are open and long term camping bookings are now available for many locations.

FNPW tip for this weekend: Grab a picnic and just relax with the grey kangaroos at Yanchep National Park.

ACT

Although Namadgi National Park remains closed due to bushfire and storm damage there are plenty of nature reserve and forest areas in the ACT that are open this weekend.

FNPW tip for this weekend: Search for a button everlasting daisy in Black Mountain Nature Reserve

Photo courtesy of Peter-Nijenhuis

items.featured_alt: Act4SDGs planting day
items.static_title: Taking Sustainable Action to Protect Parks and Save Species
items.content:
Friday, September 20, 2019 kicks off the Global Week to #ACT4SDGS. SDGs – Sustainable Development Goals – are globally agreed goals set by the United Nations General Assembly. They are a universal call to action to end poverty, protect the planet, and ensure all people enjoy peace and prosperity by 2030.

The key SDGs affecting natural habitats and wildlife that FNPW is targeting are Life on Land, Life Below Water, Climate Action, Good Health and Well Being, Quality Education and Partnerships for the Goals. Here’s how you can #ACT4SDGS this month.

1. Become a Backyard Buddy

Backyard Buddies is FNPW’s environmental education program. Sign up to receive our bi-monthly B-Mail newsletter or go to the Backyard Buddies page to learn more about this program and how you can create your own piece of wilderness, or help the many native species that are losing habitat every day.

2. Plant A Tree For The Planet!

Trees are one of humankind’s best friends. Trees not only provide habitat and food for plants and animals, they absorb carbon dioxide and release oxygen, enabling us to live on this planet. FNPW ‘s Plant a Tree for Me! initiative is a practical and effective way that you can invest in the conservation of our native wildlife and natural environment. Your donation will help grow native trees to increase biodiversity and provide vital habitat to help protect our unique wildlife.

3. Sign up to be a Corporate Volunteer

Corporate Volunteering with FNPW is a great team building experience that strengthens bonds, ignites team spirit, and creates memorable experiences for employees undertaking meaningful activities that benefit our environment. Go to our Corporate Volunteering page to learn more.

As an organisation that sees and hears about the grass roots impact of climate related issues on our parks and wildlife, FNPW is striving to #ACT4SDGS by improving outcomes for the unique landscapes and species that are part of this country. We thank you for helping us in our mission to protect natural Australia for future generations.

items.featured_alt: FNPW supporter survey
items.static_title: Thank You for Completing the 2021 Supporter Survey
items.content:
Thank you for completing our 2021 Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife (FNPW) Supporter Survey. All of us at FNPW value your opinions and your responses will help us to prioritize where we focus our impact in the years to come. Here are some of our findings.

We were so pleased to learn that the vast majority of you, nearly 82%, enjoy the Australian outdoors by visiting a national park, followed closely by visiting a nature reserve and going for bushwalks or hiking. If you are looking for some new parks to visit, we would encourage you to check out some of these hidden gems from one of our favourite articles on World Parks Day here.  

As we would have guessed, over 90% of you ranked the environment (conservation and wildlife) as the most important cause to you personally, and nearly the same percent of you (89%) ranked extinction of plants and animals as the most important environmental issue facing Australia at the moment. That being said, it is no surprise that the national parks are important to you as a place where Australian native species and wilderness areas are protected and where you know biodiversity will be preserved for future generations.

It is this mission of growing parks and saving species that inspire you to support FNPW’s work. FNPW’s core project areas of interest to you were the work that FNPW does to save endangered species and grow national parks, second only to FNPW’s Backyard Buddies educational initiative, which tells us that you value learning about our precious wilderness and wildlife, as well as protecting these species and their habitats for the future. 

Finally, we were happy to find that over half of you wanted to receive our 2020 Impact Report. We have sent out the Impact Report by email to those supporters from the survey who identified that they would like a copy. However, if you did not get the Impact Report and would like to view it, we have linked the FNPW – A snapshot of 2020 – Impact Report below.  

We would still love to hear from you

Again, thank you for taking the time to tell us what is important to you. Based on your answers, some of you might have heard from us regarding more information on some of the ways you can support FNPW through a Gift in your will or by becoming a Habitat Hero monthly donor. If you would simply like more information from these survey question subjects, we have provided additional links below.

If you did not hear from us and you would like to get in touch, we would love to hear from you! Contact us per our details in the footer or by clicking here.

items.featured_alt: A southern brown bandicoot foraging in leaf litter.
items.static_title: The Bandicoot: A Little Gardener Beneath Our Feet
items.content:
In the underbrush of Australia’s south and southeast, a small, shy marsupial is quietly performing some of the most important work in our ecosystems. The Southern Brown Bandicoot (Isoodon obesulus) may not have the fame of kangaroos or koalas, but when it comes to ecological impact, this little digger is a heavyweight.

The animal

Meet the Bandicoot

This stocky, short-snouted marsupial weighs between 400 grams and 1.2 kilograms, depending on sex and region. It thrives in low scrub, heath, and woodland with dense ground cover. Unlike the tree-dwelling marsupials we often picture, the bandicoot lives on the ground, using its long claws and sharp nose to rummage through leaf litter and soil for invertebrates, fungi, and plant roots.

Rather than simply existing within its habitat, the bandicoot transforms it.

Once a common sight across South Australia, eight species of bandicoot once roamed the state. Today, only the Southern Brown Bandicoot remains. Habitat loss caused by land clearing, infrastructure, and agriculture, along with predation from foxes and cats, has pushed this species onto the Endangered list under the EPBC Act.

Bandicoots rely on dense native undergrowth to hide from predators. As land is fragmented across the Fleurieu Peninsula and Mount Lofty Ranges, many populations have become isolated, unable to move or breed safely between bushland areas.

Ecosystem work

Why This Small Creature Matters

Soil Turning and Ecosystem Engineering

The Southern Brown Bandicoot may be small, but it moves an astonishing amount of soil. Research in Western Australia’s Yalgorup National Park found that a single bandicoot creates around 45 new foraging pits each day, shifting about 10.7 kilograms of soil daily. That’s nearly 4 tonnes of soil turned over every year by one animal.

This constant digging rejuvenates the earth. Each pit breaks up hardened soil, improves water absorption, and draws buried organic matter to the surface. Studies show that seedlings grown in soil disturbed by bandicoots grow taller, heavier, and faster than those in untouched soil. These little foragers are natural gardeners, physically transforming their environment in ways that help countless other species thrive.

Distribution, Fragmentation and Genetic Connectivity

Once widespread across southeastern Australia, the Southern Brown Bandicoot’s range has shrunk dramatically due to habitat clearing and the spread of introduced predators. Genetic studies in South Australia reveal reduced gene flow and greater isolation caused by agriculture and development. Without targeted conservation, scientists predict that up to 84 percent of local populations could disappear within a century. The loss of bandicoots would ripple through the environment, undermining the soil processes that sustain healthy, diverse ecosystems.

Habitat Use and Resilience

Despite these challenges, the Southern Brown Bandicoot shows impressive adaptability. Studies have found that it can survive in modified landscapes, including roadside reserves and drainage channels, as long as there is thick undergrowth and protection from predators. This resilience gives conservationists hope. If habitat corridors, dense vegetation, and predator control are maintained, these remarkable marsupials can continue living alongside us, quietly keeping ecosystems in balance.

In the field

Spotlight: The Bandicoot Superhighway Project

The Bandicoot Superhighway Project, a community-led initiative supported by the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife, is helping reconnect fragmented habitats and restore landscapes across South Australia.

So far, the project has achieved:

  • 44 hectares of habitat rehabilitation and restoration
  • 34,669 native seedlings planted to rebuild shelter and foraging areas
  • 100+ wildlife cameras installed to monitor local populations
  • Community workshops empowering residents to protect these important ecosystem engineers

By restoring vegetation and improving connectivity across the Fleurieu Peninsula, the project helps bandicoots move freely, breed safely, and continue their crucial role in maintaining soil health. It’s a powerful example of how science, community, and conservation can come together to heal landscapes.

Helping bandicoots helps the land recover. Through community engagement, locals are encouraged to get involved – from tree planting and wildlife monitoring to supporting ongoing restoration through donations.

How to help

How You Can Help

Bandicoot recovery starts with small actions that add up to big impact. You can help protect these unsung heroes by:

  • Planting or gifting a native tree to restore their habitat. Every native tree contributes to shade, shelter, and insect life that supports bandicoots.
  • Becoming a Habitat Hero through the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife, supporting hands-on conservation work that keeps ecosystems connected.
  • Keeping cats indoors and dogs on leads in bushland to reduce predation risks.
  • Reporting sightings to help community monitoring and citizen science programs.

Your gifted tree becomes part of a living chain that supports bandicoots, biodiversity, and a healthier Australia.

items.content:
The Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife congratulates Australia’s amazing scientific community and the deep work that has gone into researching, writing, and producing the State of the Climate 2022 report. We also acknowledge the Minister for the Environment and Water, The Hon Tanya Plibersek, on releasing this important report.

The report outlines the latest national and international climate research, surrounding observations, analyses, and future projectors, which describes year-to-year variability and longer-term changes in Australia’s climate including; the major changes in weather, from extreme heat, heavy rainfall, and coastal inundation, fire weather, and drought, will see a growing impact on the lives and livelihoods of Australians.

The Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife’s continued commitment to growing national parks and protected areas, saving species, and healing the land remains firm. Its key focus on helping to address key issues highlighted in the report includes rebuilding, protecting, and enhancing biodiversity, restoring habitat and ecological function, and improving resilience and recovery in response to drought, bushfires, and floods. Embedding and building partnerships with First Nations to manage and maintain natural landscapes is critical to the success of this commitment working into the future.

While it can seem an overwhelming task, we can also take action and personally contribute to improving climate outcomes that will benefit future generations. As we digest some of the distressing findings that the latest State of the Climate 2022 report has identified, there are a number of actions everyone can take today to help combat the challenges that lie ahead. Discover more ways to get involved and help to protect Australia here.

items.featured_alt: Volunteers planting on a grassy hillside below Norfolk pines with Trees in Newcastle
items.static_title: The FNPW Announces Next Bushfire Recovery Nursery
items.content:
The Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife is proud to welcome Trees In Newcastle (TIN), the latest community nursery to receive a grant to expand its tree capacity as part of FNPW’s Bushfire Recovery Nursery Project
Trees In Newcastle is a long-established community environmental organisation made up mainly of volunteers. Since 1989, the native plant nursery has been committed to conserving native vegetation, supporting the community with environmental initiatives and offering bush regeneration and consultation services.

To date: TIN has grown over 1.5 million plants since propagation began in 1992. Last year, its bush regeneration team planted over 26,000 native plants across the region. In 2010 alone, its education program helped build knowledge, understanding, skills and positive attitudes with 90 primary and 37 secondary teachers, 533 primary students and 380 secondary students.
TIN has over 50 regular and active volunteers who annually provide 18,500 hours of time and energy to the organisation and the community.


Since the bushfires of 2019 – 2020, TIN has been involved with landowners in the Laguna-Wollombi area, Port Stephens and Merriwa in seed collection, planting advice and the supply of native trees. With the grant provided by FNPW, the Nursery will expand its capacity by an additional 10,000 trees to plant a total of 33,000 native trees. These trees will support the Wollemi NP, Lower and Upper Hunter, Central Coast and Blue Mountains World Heritage Area regions.

The native trees, including the Grey Ironbark, Forest Redgum, Spotted Gum and Black Sheoak, will support threatened species such as the Glossy Black Cockatoo, Powerful Owl, Regent Honeyeater and Koala.
With another three Nurseries yet to be announced, FNPW is moving closer towards its overarching goal of planting a million trees in bushfire affected regions across Australia by 2025.

items.static_title: The FNPW Expands Bushfire Recovery Project Towards One Million Trees Goal
items.content:
In recognition of National Tree Day 2021, the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife is proud to continue expanding its Bushfire Recovery Project towards one million trees in bushfire affected regions by 2025.

In partnership with global non-profit, One Tree Planted and French beauty brand, L’OCCITANE, FNPW has provided grant funding to another two community nursery locations in Newcastle, NSW and Mt. Barker, SA to expand the capacity of the tree nurseries and propagate native plants for erosion prevention and the restoration of animal habitats. Seedlings will be established from indigenous tree species in each of the nursery locations and will be planted in national parks across Australia, as well as other public and private lands that have been affected by bushfires.

Our first four Bushfire Recovery Nurseries across NSW, ACT and SA have commenced planting season, which is a major step in supporting the recovery of critically impacted regions such as the Gondwana Rainforest World Heritage area and NSW North Coast, Mount Lofty to Kangaroo Island Connection, Wollemi National Park, the Blue Mountains World Heritage Area and the South Coast to Gippsland Corridor. The funding will also provide essential resources such as fencing, nursery benches, hygiene and plumbing and potting structures.

For many of us in lockdown, we won’t be able to actively volunteer and plant trees this Saturday, 1 August. However, if you’d like to get involved in supporting the future of our Bushfire Recovery project, you can virtually “plant a tree” as part of our ‘Plant a Tree for Me’ initiative where $10 will plant and maintain one tree in a bushfire affected region.

Click here to Plant A Tree.

items.featured_alt: Rocky ridges and creek country in the northern Flinders Ranges.
items.static_title: The Land Behind Australia's World Heritage Bid
items.content:
Deep in the northern Flinders Ranges, about 17 kilometres east of the small settlement of Blinman, sits a stretch of country that has been holding its breath for a very long time.

Balcoracana Paddock is part of the Bunkers Range on Adnyamathanha Country. Its gorges and creek beds hold permanent water. Its cave systems shelter yellow-footed rock wallabies. And beneath its surface lies some of the most scientifically significant fossil records on Earth: sedimentary sequences from the Cambrian period documenting more than 500 million years of life.

This land has now been permanently added to Ikara-Flinders Ranges National Park.

We partnered with the Australian Government and the SA Department for Environment and Water to acquire Balcoracana Paddock, adding approximately 4,500 hectares of conservation-significant country to the park’s protected estate. The acquisition was also supported through the Federal Government’s Protecting Important Biodiversity Areas Program.

World Heritage

A nomination a decade in the making

The timing is significant. In February 2026, Australia formally submitted the Flinders Ranges World Heritage nomination to UNESCO’s World Heritage Centre in Paris, and the nomination has since been accepted for assessment. A final decision from the World Heritage Committee is expected in mid-2027. It is a milestone a decade in the making, backed by a 368-page submission and nearly 4,000 pages of supporting documentation.

Balcoracana Paddock is one of seven properties whose geological record underpins that bid. The Flinders Ranges is the only place on Earth where the continuous formation of the earliest complex animal life, between 672 and 510 million years ago, can be observed across three geological periods: the Cryogenian, Ediacaran, and Cambrian.

Country

Adnyamathanha consent and co-management

For the Adnyamathanha people, whose connection to this Country runs far deeper than any pastoral boundary, the nomination and the acquisition carry real meaning together. UNESCO requires World Heritage bids to be supported and consented to by all relevant First Nations communities. Last year, the Adnyamathanha Common Law Holders provided that consent.

As an addition to Ikara-Flinders Ranges National Park, Balcoracana Paddock now falls under the existing co-management agreement between Adnyamathanha native title holders and the South Australian Government, expanding Traditional Owners’ formal decision-making role across the landscape.

Adnyamathanha Senior Elder Charles Jackson OAM has spoken of the importance of Adnyamathanha people coming together on this nomination, and of their cultural information placing them front and centre on the world stage. The land acquisition is part of that same commitment.

Wildlife

Somewhere to go

For wildlife, the benefits are immediate. Removing stock grazing allows native vegetation to recover across the creek beds and drainage areas where threatened plant species are already returning.

The land connects directly into the Bounceback Program’s existing predator and grazing management regime, which has driven significant recovery of yellow-footed rock wallabies, short-tailed grasswrens, and echidnas across the broader Ikara-Flinders landscape. Western quolls, successfully reintroduced to the park, have been recorded moving northeast toward Balcoracana Paddock.

This acquisition gives them somewhere to go.

Why it matters

What the case rests on

The Flinders Ranges was recently named the only Australian destination on Lonely Planet’s must-visit list for 2026. World Heritage listing, if confirmed, would cement that recognition on a global scale. But the case for protecting this country doesn’t rest on tourism or titles. It rests on what’s here: ancient fossils, rare animals, living culture, and a landscape that holds an irreplaceable record of life on Earth.

Our commitment

Growing national parks

Growing national parks is one of our three core commitments. Balcoracana Paddock is exactly the kind of acquisition that makes it real.

items.featured_alt: Murray River turtle basking on a log in shallow water
items.static_title: The secret lives of Australian freshwater turtles
items.content:
Deborah Bower, University of New England; Donald McKnight, James Cook University; Eric Nordberg, University of New England; James Van Dyke, La Trobe University; Michael B Thompson, University of Sydney, and Ricky Spencer, Western Sydney University

Australian freshwater turtles support healthy wetlands and rivers. Yet one in three turtle species is threatened with extinction. And there is still much we don’t know about them.

In today’s special issue of the journal Austral Ecology, 55 authors present the latest research on Australian freshwater turtles.

Along with other biologists, we have contributed to a series of research papers to inform ecology and conservation of freshwater turtles.

Our research reveals some fresh insights into turtle behaviour, survey methods and conservation strategies.

Spy wear and other turtle tech

In one study researchers compared data from underwater video cameras to traditional trapping surveys and achieved similar results. They detected 83 turtles from 52 hours of footage and identified all species in the study area.

Overall, baited remote underwater videos proved to be a “useful, time effective, non-invasive technique to collect relative abundance and species richness estimates for freshwater turtles”.

Another study provided the first vision of a wild saw-shelled turtle attempting to court a mate. The male sought affection from the female turtle by waving his feet and pressing his nose into her face.

Meanwhile, a different male was observed trying to mount a larger male. This was the first case of same-sex mounting seen in this species.

We are continuing to unravel curious turtle behaviour known as nocturnal basking. During the day, many reptiles regulate their body temperature by sunning themselves. But some freshwater turtles (and crocodiles) also emerge from the water and bask on logs at night.

To find out why, scientists in Queensland measured the preferred temperature of Krefft’s river turtles and watched them bask more when the water was hot. So it seems they do this to stay cool in hot weather.

Over in desert country, we recaptured Cooper Creek turtles after two decades. While we were there, the site became surrounded with floodwater – this provided a rare opportunity to find turtles moving onto the floodplain to find food.

We also found lots of baby turtles. This is in contrast to most places around Australia, which have ongoing problems with foxes eating turtle nests.

Conservation success stories

Foxes target freshwater turtle nests across Australia, reducing breeding success. Researchers are experimenting with measures to protect nests from predators.

In the New England Tablelands, temporary electric fences served to protect turtle nests from foxes over three breeding spring-summer seasons from 2019 to 2022. But in the Murray River, plastic mesh over individual nests only protected some of them.

Nest protection supports conservation of the endangered Mary River turtle. Over 22 years, more than 100 members of the local community in the Mary River Catchment have led initiatives to protect Mary River turtles. Working with communities has dual benefits – for research and for the people involved, who enjoy connecting to nature.

These collaborations have helped improve river management, informing delivery of water for the environment and improving the quality of river habitats for turtles.

November is Turtle Month for the 1 Million turtles campaign, a national citizen science program bringing together scientists and the community, to support freshwater turtle conservation initiatives.

Through the free TurtleSAT app, people can do more than just report turtle sightings. They can actively contribute to data-driven turtle management.

The app provides real-time data visualisation. The program website also provides education, helping citizen scientists protect nests, establish predator-free turtle sanctuaries, engage in national experiments, and deepen their understanding of turtles and wetlands.

With more than 18,000 records logged, 1,200 turtles saved from road hazards and 500 nests protected, this initiative is crucial in light of the growing threats faced by freshwater turtle species.

Challenges and solutions

Of Australia’s 25 freshwater turtle species, 12 are so poorly known their national conservation status could not be assessed during this 2022 review. Many of these lesser-known species occur in northern Australia.

Of the 15 species or subspecies assessed, we recommended listing a higher level of threat for eight. This included western saw-shelled turtles, which were recently uplisted from vulnerable to endangered.

Threats include habitat loss, being eaten by foxes or feral pigs, disease, fire, and moving species into new areas where they breed with existing turtle species. To manage these threats, we need to move beyond engagement to an integrated approach, where conservation advice is co-determined by First Nations people who are closely involved in implementing recovery plans and action plans.

There is immense value in establishing long-term studies to track these long-lived species. And technology continues to provide new opportunities to learn more.

Future conservation and management will require working with communities to learn more about turtles and protect them. If one million people each save one turtle, collectively we will have made a big difference.

Deborah Bower, Associate Professor in Zoology and Ecology, University of New England; Donald McKnight, , James Cook University; Eric Nordberg, Senior Lecturer (Applied Ecology and Landscape Management), University of New England; James Van Dyke, Associate Professor in Biomedical Sciences, La Trobe University; Michael B Thompson, Emeritus Professor in Zoology, University of Sydney, and Ricky Spencer, Associate Professor of Ecology, Western Sydney University

items.featured_alt: Caring for Carers podcast
items.static_title: The Wildlife Heroes: Caring for Carers podcast
items.content:
The Wildlife Heroes: Caring for Carers podcast is live! FNPW has teamed up with podcast producer Gretchen Miller, wildlife carers and psychologists to start a mental health conversation.

“The wildlife carers who manage Australia’s injured and orphaned native animals are a national asset that requires strategic nurturing with empathy, understanding, financial and psychological support if it is to remain viable and sustainable”

( A review of roadkill rescue: who cares for the mental, physical and financial welfare of Australian wildlife carers? Englefield et al., 2018)

The first five episodes of Caring for Carers are now live and accessible via wildlifeheroes.org.au, Spotify or iTunes.

Topics and guests featured in the series:

1. Climate Change – the grief we feel

How can we take care of ourselves as climate warriors and climate worriers?

Guests:
Dr Ros Irwin, a veteran carer and President of Friends of the Koala from Lismore in NSW.
Sally Gillespie, a former psychotherapist who presents talks and workshops on climate psychology and ecopsychology.

2. Personal Wellbeing – looking after yourself in order to better look after others

Wildlife care is 24/7 as we all know. So how do we make time for ourselves, and what can we do to ensure we remain well, and are able to keep caring?

Guests:
Suzy Nethercott-Watson, a carer for 20 years, and the director of Two Green Threads – a website built to support wildlife volunteers in the work they do. www.twogreenthreads.org
Sharon Draper, animal lover and Sydney based psychologist with an interest in trauma and compassion fatigue.

3. Community Conflict

The pressures are great, so what happens when we stop getting along? We consider conflict – from individual, to in the group, to with the larger community and how wildlife volunteers can build and maintain positive and supportive relationships.

Guests:
Jess Birrell, wildlife volunteer, reptile trainer and expert.
Lyn Page, TAFE senior counsellor, volunteer field psychologist with Red Cross, and a member of the disaster response network with the Australian Psychological Society

4. Catastrophic Events

Catastrophic events are all too frequent – flood and fire all take their toll on wildlife and wildlife carers are always there to pick up the pieces. So how do we best recover and look after ourselves, and our animals, after we’ve been on the front line of a traumatic wildlife rescue emergency?

Guests:
Jessi Jean Drew-Smythe, wildlife volunteer and bat carer, studying environmental biology
Lyn Page, TAFE senior counsellor, volunteer field psychologist with Red Cross, and a member of the disaster response network with the Australian Psychological Society

5. Supporting Others – looking after our carer friends

We’re all in this together – so how best to support and encourage our fellow wildlife volunteers when they struggle?

Guests:
Tilly Gray, wildlife carer who loves all animals (humans included!) and is currently working on “The Wildlife Carer Rehabilitation Manual – How to Care for Human Beings”
Sally Gillespie, a former psychotherapist who presents talks and workshops on climate psychology and ecopsychology and has written a book, Climate Crisis and Consciousness: Re-imagining Our World and Ourselves.

The podcast was funded through the Australian Government’s bushfire wildlife and habitat recovery package and is part of the Caring for Carers program that FNPW is rolling out as part of the Wildlife Heroes project.
 

Listen via: https://wildlifeheroes.org.au/wildlife-heroes-caring-for-carers-podcast/ …or on Spotify or iTunes.

And please share with your wildlife rescue and care community.

items.content:
Since 2018 FNPW has been working closely with Ricky Spencer from Western Sydney University to coordinate school engagement in the 1 Million Turtle Project.  The community conservation program aims to release more than one million turtles throughout South-Eastern Australia each year, through the creation of protected habitats and a coordinated breeding and harvesting program.

On December 16th, FNPW hosted a webinar called 1 Million Turtles: Turtle Talk. We were joined by Ricky Spencer, and Nathan Cutter from the NSW Department of Primary Industries. The webinar covered a range of information about freshwater turtles, including different species, the threats currently facing them, and what people can do to help.

You can watch a recording of the webinar below:

THE 1 MILLION TURTLE PROJECT

The project brings together world leading researchers, industry conservation agencies and community groups with the primary goal of restoring turtle populations that are in major decline throughout SE Australia. This team was part of the first global assessment of the world’s turtle and tortoise species, which revealed that half of all 360 turtle and tortoise species worldwide face imminent extinction.

In Australia, attacks from invasive predators, road mortality, habitat destruction, water quality degradation and drought, are the primary factors contributing to the decline of Australia’s most common turtle species by up to 91 per cent over the last 40 years.

The aim of the 1 Million Turtles Project is to place schools, teachers, and school children at the centre of the community conservation program. It will create hands-on classroom experiences, as well as outdoor field-based conservation initiatives to:

  • Establish school communities as a major focal point for freshwater turtle conservation initiatives helping restore declining turtle populations
  • Assess the importance of hands-on classroom engagement with animals to facilitate on-ground conservation initiatives and engagement
  • Provide accredited curriculum and training to schools in a range of disciplines, including environmental sustainability, citizen science and animal husbandry
  • Assess the role of children as “agents of change” for the environment through their family and friend networks.

TURTLE TOOLS

Through citizen science tools and engagement the project aims to raise awareness of turtle populations across South-Eastern Australia and support long term conservation of species. You can help by using some of the tools of the project to monitor and support turtles.

 TurtleSat

TurtleSAT is a Citizen Science mapping tool produced by the 1 Million Turtles Community Conservation program. TurtleSAT allows communities to map the location of freshwater turtles in waterways and wetlands across the country.

Download the TurtleSat app to record sightings of turtles when you are out and about.

Download TurtleSat

 

Wildlife Rescue Handbook – the first 24 Hours

The FNPW Wildlife Heroes Project has developed a handy booklet to help you if you find injured wildlife, including turtles.

Download the booklet or print it and keep a copy in your car so that you will know what to do whenever you find injured wildlife.

Download the Rescue Booklet

FNPW is excited to support the United Nations Day School Program and encourages all schools to participate in inspiring young people to be kind, perseverant, and motivated global citizens.

Program Aims

• Inform students on the critical work of the United Nations and the Global Goals
• Engage students through activities/events across different grade levels which encourage them to take action for the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)
• Strengthen the school’s commitment to nurturing global citizens and leaders of tomorrow

About the program

The United Nations Association of Australia (UNAA) NSW invites all NSW schools to join in the United Nations Day celebrations on 24 October 2022. 

Peace People Planet is an annual celebration of the United Nations mission in schools and the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). 

With less than eight years left to achieve the 17 Sustainable Development Goals and 169 universal targets known as Agenda 2030, the UN encourages schools to get involved. You can participate by:

– Teaching SDG integrated lessons or choosing an SDG campaign as a lead-up to the UN Day

– Organising a Blue Mufti Day on 24 October 2022 or participating in events, teacher workshops, and more!!

Upon signing up, schools will receive a welcome pack with FREE resources filled with exciting classroom ideas and project-based learning.

For more information and to sign up, please visit https://www.unaansw.org.au/un-day-schools-program/

items.featured_alt: Rainforest walking track restored through the Currumbin Wildlife Sanctuary bushland
items.static_title: We must act now: IPCC AR6 Synthesis Report
items.content:
As the east coast of Australia says goodbye to La Niña and braces for a potential El Niño season, climate change continues to be a hot topic across the country. Further highlighting this is the recently released report from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) AR6 Synthesis Report, Climate Change 2023. 

The purpose of the IPCC AR6 is to summarise the state of knowledge of climate change, including its widespread impacts and risks as well as climate change mitigation and adaptation. It’s an essential resource to help governments and policymakers, as well as communities, businesses, and society more broadly to understand the current environment. 

Key findings

Some key findings of IPCC AR6 include: 

  • Global surface temperature was 1.09°C higher in 2011-2020 compared to 1850-1900 
  • human influence has unequivocally warmed the atmosphere, ocean, and land. 
  • The likely range of total human-caused global surface temperature increase for this time period is 0.8°C–1.3°C, with a best estimate of 1.07°C  
  • methane levels are currently higher than they have been at any other time in the last 800,000 years. 
  • CO2 concentrations are currently two million times higher than they have been at any other time in the past two million years. 

While these numbers paint a catastrophic picture independently, the anecdotal evidence also demonstrates the dire circumstances the world faces. Climate change has caused substantial damage, and increasingly irreversible losses in ecosystems, with increases in the magnitude of heat extremes driving hundreds of local losses of species. In fact, mass mortality events have been recorded on land and in the ocean.  

Moreover, the vulnerability of human mortality to ongoing climate change is increasing, as more than three billion individuals reside in regions highly susceptible to its effects. The report notes that human mortality from floods, droughts and storms was 15 times higher in vulnerable regions, compared to regions with very low vulnerability. And whilst increasing weather and climate events continue to put considerable development constraints on communities, reducing the potential to mitigate risk in such vulnerable regions. 

While the report summary paints a devastating picture of where we currently are and what’s to come in terms of environmental damage and the effects of climate change, there is still time to reduce the more disastrous impacts.  

What actions are necessary to be taken?

While much needs to be done globally to help mitigate the risk of climate change and reduce the overall human impact on the environment, there are a number of steps that can be taken locally to ensure Australia is on the front foot. One of the most effective and impactful steps that can and should be taken is to reduce the conversion of natural ecosystems. 

By changing the conversion of the land, for example from native vegetation to agricultural usage, carbon is released from the soil which contributes to greenhouse gases and climate change. At the same time, it eliminates the native and natural vegetation and its capacity to sequester carbon, which effectively doubles down on the impact this has on the environment. 

While up to one-fifth of global greenhouse gas pollution comes from deforestation and degradation, protecting land from clearing helps to preserve soil quality which stores three-times more carbon than the atmosphere or terrestrial vegetation. As such, buying land to expand national parks and protect and preserve as much land as possible is key in the fight against climate change.  

Additionally, protecting land and natural ecosystems can help to reduce the loss of wildlife which is essential to help spread vegetation and continue its growth. Habitat loss, fragmentation, and degradation of land is the number one driver of species loss in Australia, so it’s essential that steps are taken to reduce this potential.  

While the window to create effective change is closing, Australia already has the requisite knowledge, technology, and tools to begin to make an impact locally. However, a whole of system approach that prioritises collaboration is needed, in conjunction with an increase in funding, to enact effective change. 

How FNPW can help

The Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife partners with national parks and wildlife services across Australia to help safeguard the nation’s valuable ecosystems, wilderness, and flora and fauna now and for future generations. As a non-government organisation, the Foundation works in partnership with First Nations, government agencies and organisations, as well as local communities and community conservation groups, to help support conservation projects around Australia and protect the country’s unique environment and to directly combat environmental change.  

For more information on how your organisation can partner with the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife to help make a positive impact for the future of Australia, contact the team today.

items.static_title: Why Expanding National Parks Matters for Australia’s Future
items.content:
From the air, Australia’s landscapes look vast and uninterrupted. But on the ground, many ecosystems are now broken into smaller and smaller pieces.

A woodland might survive on one side of a road, while cleared paddocks stretch out on the other. A wetland may still fill with water after rain, but the surrounding habitat that once supported birds, fish and amphibians has disappeared. A forest may remain standing, but the animals that once moved freely through it now encounter fences, farmland or towns.

For wildlife, these invisible boundaries matter.

Animals that once travelled kilometres across a landscape in search of food, water or breeding partners now find themselves confined to isolated pockets of habitat. Over time, those pockets shrink, species disappear and ecological systems begin to unravel.

Expanding national parks is one of the few tools we have to reverse that process.

When land is added to the national park estate, those fragments begin to reconnect. Landscapes become larger and more continuous again. Rivers flow through protected catchments. Forests link to woodlands. Wetlands reconnect with floodplains.

Instead of protecting nature in small islands, we begin protecting whole systems.

National parks are not simply scenic places set aside for recreation. They are landscapes where ecological processes are allowed to continue largely uninterrupted. Fire cycles, animal migrations, pollination, seed dispersal and soil regeneration all play out across space and time.

And when these processes are protected, nature has the chance to recover.

The basics

What a National Park Actually Is

Across Australia, national parks are areas of land legally reserved for conservation. They are established under state and federal legislation and managed to protect biodiversity, ecosystems and cultural heritage.

Unlike most other land uses, conservation becomes the primary purpose of the landscape. Development pressures are reduced, and long-term management plans guide how the park is protected and restored.

Australia’s first national park, Royal National Park south of Sydney, was created in 1879, making it one of the earliest national parks in the world. Over time, the system expanded to include alpine regions, rainforests, arid landscapes and marine ecosystems.

Today, national parks form part of Australia’s protected area network, which conservation scientists consider the most effective tool for ensuring threatened species and ecosystems can survive and recover.

New protection

What Changes When Land Becomes a National Park

When land is added to a national park, its future changes dramatically.

Instead of being managed for agriculture, development or extraction, the focus shifts to ecological protection and long-term restoration. Park managers develop detailed management plans to identify the landscape’s key ecological values and the threats that need to be addressed.

These plans guide everything from fire management and weed control to wildlife monitoring and habitat restoration.

In many cases, newly protected landscapes require significant ecological repair. Areas that were previously cleared or heavily grazed often need revegetation and soil stabilisation before native ecosystems can return.

Over time, natural regeneration begins. Native plants recolonise the landscape, soil health improves, and habitats become suitable again for wildlife.

Species recovery

Bringing Wildlife Back

One of the most important roles national parks play is supporting the recovery of threatened species.

Australia has lost more mammals than any other continent since European settlement. Many species declined after habitat clearing and the arrival of introduced predators such as foxes and feral cats.

Protected landscapes allow conservation programs to reverse some of these losses.

In South Australia’s Flinders Ranges, the long-running Bounceback program removed feral goats, foxes and rabbits from national parks to allow native ecosystems to recover. The work has helped restore habitat and made it possible to reintroduce locally extinct species.

In recent years, species such as western quolls and brushtail possums have been successfully reintroduced to protected areas in the region and are now breeding in the wild again.

These kinds of projects show what becomes possible when landscapes are protected and actively managed.

National parks also support wildlife corridors that allow animals to move between habitats. This connectivity is increasingly important as species shift their ranges in response to climate change.

Whole systems

Protecting Entire Ecosystems

Conservation is not only about individual species. It is about protecting the ecological systems that sustain life.

Healthy ecosystems are built on complex interactions between plants, animals, insects, fungi and microorganisms. Pollinators support flowering plants. Fungi recycle nutrients. Vegetation stabilises soils and protects waterways.

National parks protect these relationships by safeguarding large areas where natural processes can continue.

These landscapes also provide important environmental services that people rely on. Intact ecosystems help filter water, store carbon, reduce erosion and buffer the impacts of extreme weather.

In a warming climate, protected areas can also act as climate refuges, providing cooler, more stable habitats where species can persist as surrounding landscapes change.

Culture and Country

Protecting Culture and Country

Many national parks are also places of deep cultural significance.

Across Australia, protected landscapes contain Aboriginal cultural sites, rock art, ceremonial grounds and places tied to thousands of years of cultural knowledge.

Increasingly, national parks are being co-managed with Traditional Owners. These partnerships recognise the role First Nations peoples have played in caring for Country for tens of thousands of years and ensure that cultural knowledge continues to guide land management.

Traditional fire practices, seasonal knowledge and cultural stewardship are increasingly recognised as critical parts of modern conservation.

Scale matters

Why Expanding National Parks Matters

Land outside protected areas can change quickly.

It can be cleared, developed or fragmented as economic pressures shift. National park designation provides a stronger level of long-term protection and ensures landscapes are managed primarily for ecological health.

Expanding protected areas also improves connectivity across landscapes. Larger, linked ecosystems allow wildlife populations to move, adapt and maintain genetic diversity.

For conservation scientists, scale matters.

Small, isolated reserves can protect individual sites, but large connected landscapes are far more effective at sustaining biodiversity over the long term.

Where we come in

Creating Space for Nature to Recover

At FNPW, expanding protected areas is a key part of how we help nature recover.

By acquiring and protecting land adjacent to existing national parks, we can strengthen entire landscapes rather than protecting isolated pockets of habitat. These additions expand wildlife corridors, protect critical ecosystems and allow restoration work to occur at scale.

Healthy ecosystems take time to recover. But when land is protected, given space to regenerate and managed carefully, nature has a remarkable ability to bounce back.

Expanding national parks is ultimately about giving that recovery a chance.

Because protecting landscapes today helps ensure Australia’s wildlife, ecosystems and natural heritage continue to thrive long into the future.

items.content:
The NSW Wildlife Heroes Project is managed by the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife with funding from the New South Wales Government through its Environmental Trust.

Wildlife Heroes is proud to announce its latest grant round aimed at assisting wildlife rehabilitation volunteers in their essential work. This funding opportunity will be open from 11th November until 11:59pm 11th December, 2022. Grants for up to $15,000 per wildlife rehabilitation group, and $4,000 per independent wildlife rehabilitator, will be available to eligible NSW applicants in need of medium to large sized assets.

Goals of the grant round are to:

• Enable volunteers to acquire, build, repair, or upgrade medium to large sized animal enclosures.
• Enable volunteers to acquire assets that will alleviate reliance on volunteers’ personal property e.g., storage containers and car trailers.
• Enable volunteers to purchase specialised assets that will result in positive wildlife welfare outcomes e.g., misting systems for bat heat-stress events, fitting out trailers for emergency wildlife response.
• Increase the capacity, and improve the capability, of volunteers to accomplish their critical work of wildlife rehabilitation.

This grant round has been tailored to reflect feedback given during volunteer consultation earlier this year. Applicants are encouraged to consider versatility when planning their application i.e., assets that are relocatable, multi-purpose and/or able to be shared between rehabilitators. This is to ensure the items remain within the wildlife rehabilitation sector into the future.

For more information and to check eligibility criteria, go to:

https://wildlifeheroes.org.au/nsw-wildlife-heroes/
